<note>This page consists of four intricate geometrical constructions used to model the movement of stars and planets. In the era before telescopes, astronomers used these "paper instruments" to calculate where a planet would appear in the sky.</note>

***

### Top-Left Diagram
A large primary circle containing three concentric inner circles. A horizontal and vertical diameter intersect at the center, with several additional lines radiating outward like spokes. A small <term>epicycle<note>original: "epicyclus" — a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in pre-Copernican astronomy to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backward.</note></term> is positioned on the second innermost ring, demonstrating how a planet might revolve around a point that is itself in motion.

### Top-Right Diagram
A large circle representing a <term>deferent<note>The main circular path that carries the epicycle of a planet.</note></term> with a horizontal diameter. Two smaller circles are placed on opposite sides of the vertical axis, likely illustrating the "eccentric" nature of an orbit—where the center of a planet's path is slightly offset from the Earth.

### Bottom-Left Diagram
A circle containing horizontal and vertical diameters. Several smaller circles of varying sizes overlap and intersect both the central point and the outer boundary. This complex arrangement likely represents the intersection of different celestial spheres, such as the <term>ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note></term> and the celestial equator.

### Bottom-Right Diagram
A sophisticated construction featuring a large circle with a horizontal diameter. Two small circles are depicted, with lines connecting their centers back to the central point of the large circle. Various arcs and intersecting lines (<term>chords<note>Straight lines connecting two points on a curve.</note></term>) suggest a model used to calculate the specific <term>celestial mechanics<note>The branch of astronomy that deals with the motions of objects in outer space.</note></term> of a planet's longitude.

# Treatise on the Sphere and on Other Matters <note>Latin: "Tractatus de sphera et de aliis reb." In the Middle Ages, a "Treatise on the Sphere" typically referred to the study of the heavens and the Earth's place within the cosmos, often based on the work of Johannes de Sacrobosco.</note>

<column-break/>

->Vatican Latin Manuscript 4087<- <note>original: "4087, Vat." This is the library's official identification number for the volume.</note>

<summary>This is the title page of a medieval manuscript focusing on astronomy and the structure of the universe, identifiable by its Vatican Library catalog number.</summary>

<keywords>Astronomy, Celestial Sphere, Vatican Library, Medieval Science, Manuscript Studies</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page serves as the introduction to Johannes de Sacrobosco’s "De sphaera mundi," a foundational medieval astronomical textbook. It establishes the structure of the work and defines the basic geometry of the cosmos.</meta>

<margin>Treatise</margin>
We divide the treatise on the sphere into four chapters, stating first what a sphere is, what the center is, what the axis of the sphere is, what the pole is, how many spheres there are, and what the form of the world is. <gloss>The sphere according to Euclid <note>original: "Spera secundum euclidem"</note></gloss> In the second chapter, we discuss the circles from which the material sphere is composed, and that super-celestial sphere which is imagined <gloss>to be composed</gloss> or understood through it. In the third, the rising and setting of the zodiac signs, the division of days and nights, and the division of climates. In the fourth, the circles and motions of the planets and the causes of eclipses.

---

The sphere is therefore defined otherwise thus <gloss>by Euclid</gloss>: A sphere is the result of one full revolution of a semi-circle while the diameter remains fixed, until it returns to its starting position. That is to say, a sphere is a <gloss>solid</gloss> round body, from whose central point all lines drawn to the surface are equal; and that point is called the center of the sphere. A line passing through the center of the sphere and touching the surface at both ends is called the axis of the sphere. The two points terminating the axis are called the poles of the world.
<margin>Definition of a sphere. A straight line coming through the center to each extremity is called the axis, and the points are called poles.</margin>

---

Furthermore, he divides the sphere according to its substance into two parts, <gloss>namely</gloss> the celestial region and the elemental region. According to motion, it is divided into two, <gloss>namely</gloss> the first sphere <term>Primus Motus; the "first movement" or outermost sphere that drives the daily rotation of the heavens</term> and the sphere of the planets and the firmament, moving from east to west upon the poles of the world, which are called the world poles. The part containing the planets, however, moves in the opposite direction from west through the east.
<margin>Into the celestial part and the elemental region, and according to two motions: where the east and west are.</margin>

---

<margin>and the end of the whole [R]</margin>
The right sphere and the oblique sphere have been observed <gloss>right and oblique</gloss>. For those are said to have a right sphere <gloss>who</gloss> live under the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note>. <unclear>To whom</unclear> it is called "right" because their horizon cuts the vertical circles at right angles. However, those are said to have an oblique sphere who live outside the equinoctial line, such as those for whom one pole is elevated and the other is depressed. And it is called oblique because their horizon <gloss>artificially</gloss> intersects the equinoctial line and cuts it at right and oblique angles.
<margin>right and oblique</margin>

---

The universal <gloss>machine</gloss> of the world is divided into two: the ethereal and the elemental regions. The elemental region <gloss>which is namely</gloss> subject to change; the first are water and earth <gloss>which are called</gloss> Earth, situated in the center in the middle of all things. Around it is water, around water is air, around air is pure and untroubled fire reaching the orbit of the moon <gloss>and Acheron <note>Acheron refers to the sublunary realm, often associated with the limit of elemental change</note></gloss>, as Aristotle says in the book *Meteorology*; for thus did the glorious and divine God arrange them. These are also the elements which <gloss>mutually</gloss> change and decay. <gloss>And these</gloss> simple bodies cannot be divided into parts of different forms. From their mixing, various species are generated. The parts of the earth surround the globe on all sides; in the fourth [chapter] of the treatise, the earth resists the moisture of the water to protect the life of animals. All movable things of the earth remain stable, which, like the center of the world, by its own weight flees from motion toward the lowest extremities and possesses the shape of a round sphere. <gloss>And this</gloss> does not <unclear>depart</unclear> <note>Likely "recedit" in source text</note> as is evident through water; and from this it is clear the center is placed in the middle <gloss>location</gloss>, as is said in Book 2 of *On the Heavens and the World*. In the middle of the whole world, the earth is placed <gloss>as if</gloss> as the point toward which all universal motions tend, just like at the center of a circle.
<margin>Wherefore the earth is immobile</margin>

<summary>This opening page of Sacrobosco’s treatise introduces the fundamental geometric and physical definitions of the medieval geocentric universe, outlining the four elements and the distinction between the celestial and elemental realms. It establishes the Earth as the immobile center of the "universal machine," surrounded by the nested spheres of the planets and the firmament.</summary>

<keywords>Sacrobosco, De sphaera mundi, cosmology, astronomy, Euclid, Aristotle, celestial spheres, elemental region, center, axis, poles, primus motus, firmamentum</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial mechanics and transitions into proofs for the sphericity of the Earth and the sea. It builds upon the previous page's definitions of the "First Movement" by detailing the secondary motions of the planets and the geometric necessity of a spherical universe.</meta>

Each sphere is moved by two motions: one is the movement of the heaven <margin>carries with it <note>original: "rapit secum"</note></margin> through the two extremities of the axis—namely, the Arctic pole and the Antarctic pole—from East to West and back again to the East, which the <term>equinoctial circle|The celestial equator, which divides the sky into two equal halves</term> divides through the middle. There is, however, another motion of the lower spheres, opposite and oblique to this one <margin>through the oblique circle of the world <note>Referring to the Ecliptic, the path the sun appears to follow</note></margin> upon their own poles, which are distant from the first poles by 23 degrees. By its force, the first motion carries all the others with it once in a day and a night around the Earth. While they strive to obey the first motion, they also resist it with their own <margin>here is the figure through the middle</margin> motion. Because of this, the various spheres are carried by their own proper motion against the motion of the heaven through different spaces of time. For example: Saturn in 30 years; Jupiter in 12; Mars in 2; the Sun in 365 days and a half; Venus and Mercury in proportional times; and the Moon in 27 days and 8 hours. <insert>D E</insert> However, that the heaven revolves from the East is shown by the figures of the stars, which rise and gradually diminish until they come to the middle of the sky; they are always in the same proportion and distance from each other, and thus they set continuously and uniformly at different times. Another reason is proven by the fact that the Arctic pole, which is always visible to us, moves from here and provides a path by which it describes its circles through equal distances of proximity to each other by these two motions <margin>in its own [motion]</margin>.

<margin>Solitude is more convenient and necessary.</margin> Although the spheres tend toward the East, the firmament nonetheless moves from East to West. The firmament is round or spherical, and its motion is in the likeness of [the letter] N, because the sensible world was made in the likeness of the archetypal world <note>A philosophical concept that the physical universe reflects a perfect divine plan or "archetype."</note>. Therefore, there is no point lacking in the perfection of this world, for they are of a round form, which has neither a designated starting point nor an end. This shape is also most convenient, because among all solid bodies, the round form is the most capacious; and since the world is greatest, a round shape—being most capacious—is useful and convenient for it to contain all things. Necessity also determines this round form, for if it were a many-sided shape like a square or a triangle, two inconveniences would follow: namely, that there would be a vacuum in some place, or a body without a place, both of which are false, as is evident in the angles and curvatures. As <term>Alfraganus|Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani, a 9th-century Persian astronomer whose works were translated into Latin and became standard textbooks in Europe</term> says, if the earth were flat, some part of the heaven would be closer to us, such as that which is over our heads; and so the same star would be closer to us at its rising or setting. But we see the contrary; for the Sun, like any other star, appears larger at its rising or setting than when it is in the middle of the sky. In truth, this is not actually so; it only appears that way because of the vapors rising from the earth. Our sight of the Sun and stars through these vapors is like looking through a translucent body that dilates our visual rays, making the object appear larger, just as a coin appears larger at the bottom of a basin of water. By this similarity of the refraction of rays, it appears larger, even though it is not so in reality. That the Earth is round appears here through the fact that the stars do not rise and set equally for everyone everywhere. For example, an eclipse of the moon which appears to us in the first hour of the night appears to people in the East in the third hour of the night; it appears later to them because of the "swelling" of the Earth <note>The Latin "tumor terre" refers here to the physical curvature or bulge of the Earth's surface.</note>. Thus, this "swelling" is demonstrated on the surface. Furthermore, those traveling toward the North pole see certain stars in perpetual appearance, while for those traveling toward the Antarctic pole, other stars appear toward the South. If the Earth were flat from East to West, the stars would rise as quickly for those in the West as for those in the East, which is false. If the Earth were flat, certain stars would always be visible to everyone, which is also false. Thus, it is proven that the Earth is not a plane.

<insert>D E</insert> The sea or water also has a "swelling" <note>curvature</note> toward roundness. If someone is placed on the shore of the sea <margin># because of which it is truly said / the swelling at the top of the mast / the ship descends / that the swelling of the water... / is seen... because of the swelling... / because of the swelling of the water</margin> and a ship departs from the port, as it moves further away, it can no longer be seen by the eyes of the person on the shore. However, if that person climbs to the top of the mast, the ship can be seen. This is because the "swelling" of the water blocks the view. If the water were flat, the ship should be visible from the shore just as well as from the mast, but the curvature of the water opposes the sight. Water is a homogeneous body, and the whole appears to follow the same roundness.

<meta>This page continues the geometric proofs regarding the Earth's shape and its position at the center of the universe. It transitions from the physical behavior of water to the mathematical measurement of the Earth's circumference and the definition of the primary celestial circles.</meta>

...to each of them. But parts of water, just like any other liquid, naturally seek a round form; a part seeks the same form as the whole of which it is a part. It is said, moreover, that the Earth is situated in the middle of the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars</note>. 
<margin>The Earth appears to be in the middle</margin>
Thus it appears that the visible surface is of such a quantity because it is in the middle; for through this, the Earth by its rising seems to obey [the celestial laws] because the Earth is equally distant from them. If the Earth were closer to the firmament in one part than another, someone standing on the part of the Earth's surface that was closer to the firmament would not see half of the heavens. But this is against Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer of antiquity</note> and all the philosophers, who say that wherever a person stands, six signs [of the Zodiac] rise and six set, and half of the heavens is visible while the other half is hidden. <margin><insert>The Earth's size is as nothing</insert></margin> This same fact proves that the Earth is like a center and a point in respect to the firmament; for if the Earth were of any significant size in comparison to the firmament, it would not be possible for half of the heavens to be seen. Likewise, if one imagines a flat surface passing through the center of the Earth, it divides both the Earth and the firmament into two equal parts. Even though our eye is on the surface and not at the center of the Earth, the distance from the surface to the center is so small compared to the vastness of the firmament that it is considered insensitive <note>Meaning "immeasurably small" or "negligible"</note>. Alfraganus <note>Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani, a 9th-century Persian astronomer</note> likewise says that the Earth is the smallest of the fixed spheres and that the whole Earth is like a single star in respect to the firmament. Because the Earth is in the middle of the world, it is held immobile, for since it is heavy—as is seen by its own nature—everything heavy tends toward the center. The center is a point in the middle of the firmament; since the Earth is supremely heavy, it naturally tends toward that point. Item, [as noted by ancient authors], the Earth does not move from its position. 
It is expressed that in that time [of calculation], the circumference of the entire orb of the Earth is attested by the authority of Ambrose <note>Likely referring to St. Ambrose or a geographical authority cited in his works</note>, who followed the physical teachers; they established 20,000 [leagues] for all the distances, assigning 700 stadia <note>A "stadium" was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</note> to each of the parts [degrees] of the Zodiac. For by taking an astrolabe on a clear night and looking through its sights at the pole, then traveling directly [North or South] until the pole stands one degree higher, the space of that journey is measured and judged to be 500 stadia. Then, by multiplying this by the 360 degrees [of a circle], the circumference of the terrestrial orb is told. From these things, just as the rule of circles and diameters goes, the diameter of the Earth can be found: subtract a twenty-second part from the whole circumference, and the remainder... [the result] is 80,181 and a half stadia, which is the diameter of the Earth's orb.

There are two kinds of circles: those which are called major and those which are minor. A major circle of the sphere is one which, described on the surface of the sphere, has the same center and divides it into equal halves. A minor circle is one which, described on the surface, does not divide it into two equal halves but into unequal parts. Among the major circles, we must first speak of the **equinoctial**. The equinoctial is a circle dividing the sphere into two equal parts, being equidistant from both poles in every part. It is called "equinoctial" because only when the sun passes through it—which happens twice a year, namely at the beginning of Aries and Libra—is there an equinox <note>When day and night are of equal length</note> across the whole Earth. Hence it is called the "equator of day and night," because it makes the artificial day equal to the night; it is also called the "angle of the first movement" of the sphere. Here it should be known that the "first movement" is the motion of the <term>Primum Mobile|The 'First Moved' sphere, the outermost part of the universe that drives all other rotations</term>, that is, the ninth sphere or the ultimate heaven, which always returns from the East through the West back to the East. It is also called "rational" because of its similarity to the movement of reason which is in the <term>microcosm|'Little world,' a term for a human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe</term>, which occurs through the contemplation of the Creator through His creatures. Where the Creator is fixed, the motion of the firmament is contrary to this, returning from the West to the East... divided also is the angle of the first movement because it divides the first motion into two equal parts equidistant from the poles. There are two points called the poles of the world: the one visible to us is the North pole, also called Arctic or Boreal; the second is not named [visible] to us and is called the Antarctic, Southern, or Austral pole.

<image-desc>A small, hand-drawn circular diagram of a celestial sphere occupies the top center of the page. It features a horizontal line (the equator) and a vertical axis connecting the poles. To the right of the diagram are several columns of numerical calculations in Hindu-Arabic numerals.</image-desc>

I say that the stars located in the Bears <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor</note> move more slowly the closer they are to the pole, as is commonly said. Those are the northern dwellings; if "dwellings" encompasses those regions around the Arctic pole, which is named from *arktos* <note>original Greek: ἄρκτος</note>, which is interpreted as "bear," and it is located near the Great Bear. It is called "Boreal," however, because the North Wind <note>Latin: *boreas*</note> comes from that direction. The opposite pole is called the "Antarctic," as if placed in opposition to the Arctic, and it is also called "Meridional" <note>Southern</note> because it is in the direction of the midday sun; it is also called "Austral" because the South Wind <note>Latin: *auster*</note> comes from that part. Therefore, these two points fixed in the firmament are called the "poles of the world," which terminate the axis of the sphere. The world revolves around them. One of these appears to us, while the other is hidden, as described by Virgil: "One pole is always high above us; but the other, beneath our feet, the dark Styx <note>The river of the underworld in Greek mythology</note> and the deep shades of the dead hold." <note>A paraphrase of Virgil's *Georgics*, Book I, lines 242–243</note> And there is another circle intersecting the sphere at the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator</note>; it intersects it into two equal parts, and one half of it inclines toward the north and the other toward the south. That circle is called the "Zodiac," from the Greek *zoe* <note>original Greek: ζωή</note> meaning "life," because all life of lower things exists under it due to the motion of the planets; or it is called *azodias* <note>from *zodia*, "small animals"</note> because it is divided into twelve equal parts which are called "signs," and they take their names from animals <note>The constellations of the Zodiac</note> because of some shared property, or because of the arrangement of the fixed stars in those parts resembling living creatures. In Latin, this section is called the "Sign-bearer" <note>Latin: *Signifer*</note> because it carries the signs. It is the same thing referred to in the book *On Generation and Corruption* <note>A work by Aristotle</note> as the "oblique circle," where it is said that through the approach and retreat of the sun in the oblique circle, the generation and decay of lower things occurs. The names, order, and number of the signs are clear in these verses:
*The Ram, the Bull, the Twins, the Crab, the Lion, the Virgin. The Balance, the Scorpion, the Archer, the Goat, the Water-pot, the Fishes.* <note>The Latin names used are: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Architenens (Sagittarius), Caper (Capricorn), Amophora (Aquarius), and Pisces</note>
Each sign is divided into 30 degrees, so that in the whole Zodiac there are 360 degrees according to the astronomers. Again, each degree is divided into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds, and so on. This division of the Zodiac is performed by astronomers just as any circle in the sphere, whether large or small, is divided into 360 similar parts. Therefore, while every circle in the sphere is understood as a line, the Zodiac circle is understood as a surface having a width of 12 degrees of the kind we have just discussed. Hence, when they speak in astrology saying the signs are "quadrate" (not using the name improperly), they mean the same as square or quadrangular. Each sign has 30 degrees in length and 12 in width.

<margin>The Ecliptic line</margin>
The line dividing the Zodiac in the <unclear>middle</unclear>, such that 6 degrees are left on one side and 6 degrees on the other, is called the "ecliptic line," because when the sun and moon are linearly positioned under it, a solar or lunar eclipse occurs. The sun always runs directly under the ecliptic. All other planets, however, decline either toward the north or toward the south under the ecliptic. That part of the Zodiac which declines from the equator toward the north is called Northern, or Boreal, or Arctic; those six signs from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo are called the Northern signs. The other part of the Zodiac which declines from the equator toward the south is called Meridional or Austral; the six signs from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces are called Meridional or Austral signs. When the sun is in the beginning of Aries or any sign, it is said to "rule" under the Zodiac... <note>The text here becomes more technical regarding the "surface" of a sign</note> a vertex is in the center of the earth, and because of this, we can say whether planets are in a sign or not. We should understand this as an eminent circle passing through the poles of the Zodiac and the beginnings of the 12 signs. This circle divides the entire surface of the sphere into 12 broad parts in the middle, but narrow toward the poles of the world; each such part is a "sign" and has a special name from the name of the constellation that is near it... according to this definition, it is clear that there are poles of the world and signs...

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical description of the celestial sphere. Following the discussion of the poles on the previous page, the author now defines the great circles (colures), the meridian, and the horizon, using both classical authority and medieval folk etymologies.</meta>

<margin>equal</margin>
If first, through a point or part which we take, the whole world is divided into four equal parts which are called "quarters," and there are 48 degrees <note>likely referring to the width of the habitable zone or the span between the tropics</note> in the world and in any sign similarly. There are another two smaller circles passing through, which show by their positions how to distinguish points; these are called "equinoxes" or the "colure" <term>colure: one of two principal meridian circles that intersect at right angles at the poles</term>. It is named *acoloros* <note>original Greek: ἀκόλουρος, meaning "docked" or "curtailed"</note> because it is "without a tail" or "maimed," and by you rustic people in your manner it is called the "ox-tail," because it is made of the proper members of a circle and yet is not a perfect circle. Thus, it appears to us as imperfect, although it is the colure of medicine(?). This colure distinguishes the solstices <term>solstices: the two points in the year when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon, resulting in the longest and shortest days</term>; it passes through the poles of the world, through the poles of the Zodiac, and through the greatest declinations <note>the angle between the celestial equator and the ecliptic</note>.

<margin>summer</margin>
This colure also passes through the first degrees of Cancer and Capricorn. The first point of Cancer, where the colure intersects the Zodiac, is called the "Summer Solstice" because when the sun is in it, the sun is nearest to the heat. Whence it is called <unclear>it happens</unclear> to perfect <unclear>Christians</unclear> <note>original: "fianis," likely a contraction for "Christianis," though the astronomical context suggests a possible technical term for observers</note> this first is said to be the **Summer Tropic**, which is so called because it is then that the sun turns back toward the upper hemisphere <note>The word "Tropic" comes from the Greek "tropos," meaning "a turn"</note> to return to us! Therefore, the sun being in the point of Capricorn, it is the **Winter Solstice**. By the rotation of the firmament, it describes a certain circle which is said to be described specifically toward the Antarctic pole; whence it is called the **Winter Solstice Circle**, or the **Winter Tropic**, because then the sun <note>original: "tropicus hyemalis"</note> declines from the equinoctial toward us, and the Zodiac <term>Zodiac: the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, marking the sun's annual path</term> is at its furthest point from the equator, and the pole of the Zodiac is distant from the pole of the world. Therefore, as the whole sphere and the Zodiac move together—which is positioned through the points of Aries and Libra—then the points of the Zodiac are moved with the poles of the world, and that circle which the pole of the Zodiac describes in its rotation is now called the **Arctic Circle**.

Likewise, the other circle which the other pole of the Zodiac describes around the Antarctic pole of the world is called the **Antarctic Circle**. However great the maximum declination <term>declination: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</term> of the sun is, such is the distance of the pole of the world from the pole of the Zodiac. This is evident if we take the colure <term>colure: one of two great circles intersecting at the celestial poles</term> which distinguishes the four divisions and the poles of the world and the poles of the Zodiac. Since every quarter of the same circle is described through the equator, the quarter of this colure which is from the equinoctial up to the pole of the world will be equal to the quarter of the same colure which is from the point of Cancer up to the pole of the Zodiac. But from these equals, if the common arc which is from the point of Cancer to the pole of the world is removed, the remainders will be equal: namely, the maximum declination of the sun and the distance of the pole of the world to the pole of the Zodiac. Therefore, the Arctic circle is as far from the pole of the world as the point of Cancer is from the equator. Because of this, the sun is between the points... <note>The text here performs a geometric proof using Euclidean logic to show that the distance from the celestial pole to the Arctic Circle is equal to the sun's maximum tilt</note> ...is double the maximum declination of the sun, namely the arc that falls on the colure which is intercepted between the Arctic circle and the Arctic pole of the world, which is equal to the maximum declination of the sun. Since, however, the colure (like other circles in the sphere) consists of 360 degrees, a quarter of it will be 90 degrees. Since, therefore, the maximum declination of the sun according to **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Almagest" was the standard text for the Middle Ages</note> is 23 degrees and 51 minutes, and the arc between the Arctic circle and the Arctic pole of the world is the same number of degrees, if these two are joined together they make 43 degrees <note>The scribe's math is slightly off or using a different convention; 23°51' doubled is 47°42'</note>; then subtracting from 90, there will remain 43 degrees, which is the size of the arc of the colure between the point of Cancer and the Arctic circle. And so it is clear that the arc of the Arctic is double the maximum declination of the sun. Note that the equinoctial and the four smaller circles are called "parallels," of which five are distant from each other... as is evident here. But because these two circles taken together are equal to the point which is distant from each other, they are called: the **Equinoctial Parallel**, the **Summer Solstice Parallel**, the **Winter Solstice Parallel**, the **Arctic Parallel**, and the **Antarctic Parallel**. Note that by these smaller parallels—namely, the two Tropics, the Arctic parallel, and the Antarctic parallel—five zones or five regions are distinguished in the sky.

> Whence **Virgil** says: Five zones the heavens contain, and as many regions on the earth are directly subject to them. <note>original: "Quinque tenet caelum zonae..." from Virgil’s "Georgics," Book 1, line 233</note>

Whence the regions of the earth are placed according to the Zodiac. That region which is between the two tropics is said to be **uninhabitable** because of the heat of the sun constantly passing between the tropics. Similarly, the region of the earth directly opposite to it <note>the southern equivalent</note> is said to be uninhabitable because of the sun's heat always passing over it. However, those two zones which are circumscribed by the Arctic circle and the Antarctic circle around the poles of the world are **uninhabitable** because of excessive cold, on account of their maximum distance from the sun. Similarly, this is true of the regions of the earth directly beneath them. However, those two zones, one of which is between the Summer Tropic and the Arctic circle, and the other between the Winter Tropic and the Antarctic circle, are **habitable and temperate**, balancing the heat of the torrid zone against the two tropics and the cold of the zones which are at the extremes.

One of these circles divides the world into two equal halves through the poles of the world. However, the daytime arcs <note>the path the sun travels above the horizon</note> are not equal to the nighttime arcs, unless one is positioned under the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note>. For this reason, for those living in any part directly beneath the equator, the sun passes directly over their heads. In an <term>oblique sphere</term> <note>the sky as viewed from a latitude where the pole is tilted, such as in Europe</note>, the horizon divides the sun’s equinoctial path into two equal parts. Therefore, when the sun is at the point of **Aries** on the equinoctial, the arc of the day is equal to the arc of the night; this is the equinox, and it occurs across the entire earth.

Beyond this, the oblique horizon does not divide other circles into equal parts. Thus, in all the circles located between the equinoctial and the **Tropic of Cancer**, the daytime arc is greater than the nighttime arc. Because the arcs above the horizon in the northern region follow the sun's movement from the start of **Aries** through **Cancer** until the end of **Virgo**, the days increase over the nights, and they increase more the closer the sun approaches **Cancer**. In the region of those circles between the equinoctial and the **Tropic of Capricorn**, the arc below the horizon is greater and the arc above is smaller; thus the daytime arc is shorter than the nighttime arc, and the day is shortened in proportion. The closer the circles are to the winter tropic <note>Capricorn</note>, the more the days are shortened.

From this it is seen that if there are two circles equidistant from the equinoctial on opposite sides, the length of the daytime arc in one is equal to the nighttime arc in the other. Consequently, it appears that the <term>natural days</term> <note>a full 24-hour cycle</note> are equal throughout the year at points equally remote from the height of the equinoxes on opposite sides; the length of the <term>artificial day</term> <note>the time from sunrise to sunset</note> for one is exactly the length of the night for the other. 

However, this is according to the common perception of the earth's horizon... <note>The text here discusses technical adjustments of 11 parts regarding the sun's removal</note> because they divide the firmament more accurately within the slant of the **Zodiac**. The more the pole is elevated above the horizon <note>the further north one goes</note>, the shorter the summer days are in which the sun is in the northern signs. But the sun lingers longer above the world in its slanted path, and thus the days are numbered as being much longer than the nights. The same occurs for the signs closer to **Cancer** through the line to the end of **Sagittarius**; they are [longer] afterward, just as they are greater in their <term>right ascensions</term> <note>the time a sign takes to rise at the equator</note>. This is true of the signs from the beginning of **Capricorn** through **Aries** to the end of **Gemini**, due to the aforementioned difference between right and oblique movement. From this it is seen that the slant falls upon the ascending... and a certain part is born for the descending... more directly than we see in the <unclear>southern</unclear> measure. But when the sun is in the region of **Cancer**, it rises where the signs rise directly by night, or six rise obliquely; for us, the day is most proportional in the year. If the sun is in the region of the start of **Capricorn**, then that part which rises obliquely rises by day, and not directly. Hence, when the sun <unclear>falls</unclear> from either point of the equinox, the signs rising directly and those rising obliquely by night perform their cycles, and so on.

In a short rule: let it be established that whether it is night or day, the signs rise directly, and by night in proportion; as the night or day is short or long, more or fewer signs rise. From these things it is gathered that because the hour of birth is a space of time in which half a sign is placed in any artificial day, and similarly in the night, these are <term>natural hours</term>. In the rising or in other circles, anything otherwise on the equinoctial, whether on the southern or northern side, increases or decreases the days; as we have said, more or fewer of the signs falling directly or obliquely occur by day or by night.

The zodiac can be demonstrated: when the sun is in the first point of Cancer <note>the summer solstice, around June 21st</note>, there was one day of 24 hours for them; through which it is said the earth is not in the region [where] the sun then persisted on the horizon, emerging in that amount as it does for the night. For those whose zenith is between the Arctic circle and the Arctic pole of the world, the horizon intersects the zodiac at two points equidistant from the <note>original: "apinegeo"</note> perigee to the horizon. In the revolution of the firmament, it advances degree by degree through the portion of the zodiac intercepted above the horizon. While the sun is in that portion above the horizon, there is one continuous day; and if that portion were the size of one sign <note>30 degrees of the zodiac, roughly one month</note>, it will be a "proper day" of that length, and similarly for the night. And if it were the size of two signs, the proper day would be the length of two months, and so on. 

Similarly, the foundation of the argument is the same: that the portion intercepted by those two equidistant points remains below the horizon; namely, when the sun is in that intercepted portion, there will be one "proper night" <note>original: "nox propria"</note> for a duration as great as the quantity of the zodiac intercepted. 

However, the remaining signs, when they rise so they may set, they rise so that they approach [the horizon]. They rise according to their property here: Capricorn(?) or before the moved ones, Aries before Pisces, and [Pisces] before Aquarius. Yet their opposites rise in the right way and set in reverse, such that Scorpio rises before Libra, Libra before Virgo, Virgo before Leo; and so the signs here recede from the right path of the sun. 

Alternatively, because the zenith is at the Arctic pole, their horizon is identical to the equinoctial <note>at the North Pole, the horizon and the equator are the same line</note>; namely, the equinoctial intersects the zodiac into equal parts just as their horizon does. Thus, it is said that one half of the zodiac is above and the other below. When the sun runs through that half which is from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo <note>the spring and summer months in the Northern Hemisphere</note>, there will be one "proper day" or night. And when the sun runs through the other half, which is from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces <note>the autumn and winter months</note>, there will be one "proper night." 

Wherefore, one half of the entire year is one single artificial day <term>artificial day</term> <note>the time the sun is actually above the horizon</note> and the other half is one night; thus, in the whole year, there is one natural day <term>natural day</term> <note>a full cycle of light and dark</note>. Just as it is never <unclear>more</unclear> in <unclear>123</unclear> degrees, the sun is under the horizon, but it is thought and seen that there it is day even during the night. For with us, it is considered "day" even before the sun rises above the horizon <note>twilight</note>; however, this is <unclear>with respect to</unclear> our senses and is held as a common natural saying. 

According to physical reasoning, a day is not just from the rising of the sun until its setting below the horizon. It is seen to be a perpetual day [at the poles]; however, it is found that the air there is cloudy on account of <unclear>shallows(?) over 2</unclear>...

It must be noted that the sun moves through a circle by which it is moved through the surface of the ecliptic, and it is eccentric. For a circle is called **eccentric** <term>eccentric: a circle whose center does not coincide with the center of the Earth</term> when such a circle of the sun is said not to have its center in the center of the Earth, but outside of it. The point in the eccentric which is closest to the firmament <note>the highest point in the orbit</note> is called the **aux** or **augis**, which is interpreted as "elevation"; the opposite point, which is furthest from the firmament, is called the "opposite of the augis." Moreover, there are two motions of the sun from west to east: one is its proper motion slowing through the eccentric, which moves in a day and night by almost 59 minutes; the other motion is slower, that of its own sphere upon the poles of the zodiac, moving by a motion equal to the fixed stars, namely one degree in 100 years. Thus the sun, by these two motions, completes its course in its proper circle...

For any of the other planets except the sun, there is a circle besides the equant, a **deferent** <term>deferent: the main orbital circle of a planet</term> and an **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a smaller circle whose center moves along the circumference of the deferent</term>. Equally, however, the lines are revolved... through the surface of the ecliptic. ...is called the **dragon** <note>original: "draco"; refers to the path shape formed by the intersection of orbital planes</note> because it is wide in the middle and narrower toward the ends. That intersection through which the line moves from the south to the north is called the **head of the dragon** <note>the ascending node</note>. The other intersection, through which it moves from the north to the south, is called the **tail of the dragon** <note>the descending node</note>. The deferents for any planet are equal, and the epicycle, though it differs in quantity. For Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, the centers are in the surface of the ecliptic, and those two are in the same surface. In any of the planets, there is an epicycle. And the epicycle is a small circle through whose circumference the body of the planet is carried, and the center of the epicycle is carried in the circumference of the deferent. If two lines are drawn from the center of the earth so that they touch the epicycle, one on the eastern side and the other on the western side, the point of the stations on the eastern side is called the **first station**, and the point of contact on the western epicycle is called the **second station**. And when the planet is at the height of these contacts, it is called **stationary**. The upper arc of the epicycle, interpreted between the two contacts, is called **direction**; when the planet is in that arc, it is called **direct**. The lower arc of the epicycle between the two stations is called **retrogradation**, and the planet existing there is called **retrograde**. To the moon, however, no station, direction, or retrogradation is assigned; hence the moon is not called stationary, direct, or retrograde, because of the velocity with which it is moved in the epicycle.

Two tangent lines from the Earth to the epicycle define the points of 'statio pma' (first station) and 'statio sda' (second station). From this it is clear that the moon in a solar eclipse [moves] by its own proper motion. It must be noted that when there is an eclipse of the moon, it is an eclipse for the whole earth; but in an eclipse of the sun, it is not so, in as much as it is an eclipse in one climate <note>a latitudinal zone</note> and not in another, which happens because of the diversity of perspectives in different climates. **A**ll things that have proceeded from the primordial origin of matters were formed by the logic of numbers. For this reason, in the same way that they are to be known, the <term>science of numbers</term> <note>original: "numerorum scientia"</note> is necessary for the knowledge of all things in the universe. Anyone should know that what is called <term>Algorismus</term> <note>The term "Algorism" refers to the system of decimal arithmetic using Arabic numerals, named after the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.</note> should be noted in the mind as an introductory art before studying numbers. Number is defined in two ways. Naturally, a number is a collection of units or a multitude made of units. In its proper <unclear>logic</unclear>, every single thing is called a "one." However, one kind of number is a <term>digit</term>, another is an <term>article</term>, and another is <term>composite</term>. A <term>digit</term> <note>original: "digitus"</note> is any number less than ten. An <term>article</term> <note>original: "articulus"</note> is a number divisible into ten equal parts so that nothing remains as a remainder <note>i.e., multiples of ten like 10, 20, 30...</note>. A <term>composite</term> or "mixed" number is one that consists of a digit and an article. It should be known that every number between two adjacent articles is a "proposed" [composite] number. Furthermore, there are [several] species of this new art, namely: <term>numeration</term>, <term>addition</term>, <term>subtraction</term>, <term>mediation</term> <note>halving a number</note>, <term>duplication</term>, <term>multiplication</term>, <term>division</term>, <term>progression</term>, and <term>root extraction</term>. And this last one is done in two ways, both for square and cubic numbers. Among these, we shall speak first of numeration and afterwards of the others in order.

## On numeration

**N**umeration is the artificial representation of any quantity belonging to a system of figures. For a figure, a place and a line are here set forward. But for the discovery of the aforementioned, a figure is set forward because it differs from the four [others] pertaining to this; not because it is seen through those, but because it clearly shows what kind of figure follows. "Place" is the name of the space in which it is written; "Line" is the name of the ordered path for the representation of any number. It should be known that nine limits are found as significant signs or figures representing the nine digits, which are as follows: 

-> 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 <-

The tenth figure is called <term>theca</term>, or a circle, or a <term>cipher</term> <note>original: "cifra"</note>, or the figure of nothing, because it signifies nothing by itself, yet when placed it allows the others to signify. For without a cipher or ciphers placed before them, an article cannot be written. Against <unclear>infinity</unclear>, through these nine significant figures joined to <unclear>those</unclear> <unclear>prescribed</unclear> <unclear>above</unclear>, any number can be represented. More figures are not necessary. It is noted, therefore, that for every digit, only one figure proper to itself is to be made. Every article, however, is denoted by a cipher and a digit, for any article is named from a digit: as ten from units, twenty from two—and so with the others. Every number, in that it is a digit, is said by its own figure. Every article is represented by a cipher <unclear>placed before</unclear> and a number from 10 to 100 so that it is contained by two figures; and thus it denotes by itself and is intended by the cipher placed in the first place. Similarly, the figure which signifies a digit denotes an article when placed behind. It can be <unclear>placed</unclear> according to <unclear>how</unclear> the digit behaves, and by itself that number is placed so the article is illustrated as before. Every number between 100 and 1,000, as a mixed number, should be viewed through these three figures. Every number from 1,000 up to ten thousand through four figures, and so on. It is noted that any figure placed in the first place signifies its digit. In the second place, it signifies ten times its digit; in the third, a hundred times its digit; in the fourth, a thousand times its digit; in the fifth, ten thousand times its digit; in the seventh, a million times <note>original: "millesies millesimus"</note>. And thus it ends by multiplying by ten... 10 | 100 | 1,000... any figure placed in the following place signifies ten times as much as it did in the preceding one. And if I make it above any figure placed in the place of thousands, <unclear>they are placed</unclear> by a point to denote how many thousands the representation of the figures should have, according to how many points were passed to the left. We write in this art toward the left, in the manner of the inventors <unclear>Theodore(?)</unclear> or <unclear>Arabs(?)</unclear>, so that in the reading process we arrange the number according to the <unclear>greater</unclear> order.

## On addition

**A**ddition is the aggregation of numbers to numbers so that a growing sum may be seen. For addition, at least two rows of figures and two numbers are necessary.

When the addition of two numbers to each other must be done, the number to which the addition is to be made is the one that receives a value from the other, and it should be written in the upper position. The number to be added, however, is the one given by the other, and it should be written below. It is proper that the smaller number be written below and the larger above; however, if it is done the other way around, it should be corrected as it ought to be, though it makes no difference to the result. Therefore, just as a number is written in addition, the number to which addition is made is placed in the upper row, and the numbers to be added are written in the lower row, spaced out so that the first figure of the lower is directly under the first of the upper, the second under the second, and so on for the others.

Once this is done, let the first figure of the lower row be added to the figure above it. If the result of the addition does not exceed a <term>digit</term> <note>A single-digit number from 1 to 9.</note>, an <term>article</term> <note>A multiple of ten, such as 10, 20, or 30.</note>, or a <term>composite number</term> <note>A number made of both a ten and a digit, like 15 or 22.</note>, let it be written in the place of the upper figure, which is deleted <note>In medieval arithmetic, often performed on a "dust board" or erasable slate, old figures were literally wiped away to be replaced by the new sum.</note>. If the result is a digit that exceeds ten, or an article, let a <term>cipher</term> <note>original: "cifra"; the number zero.</note> be written in the place of the deleted upper figure, and let the digit from which that article is named be transferred to the left and added to the next figure following it. If no figure follows it, then place it in the empty space. If it happens that the next figure to which the article’s digit should be added is a cipher, let that be deleted and the digit of the article be written there. 

If the figure is a <term>nine</term> <note>original: "novenarius"</note> and a unit must be added to it, a cipher should be written in place of that nine, and the article transferred as before. If, however, it results in a composite number, let the digit which is part of that composite number be written in the place of the deleted upper figure, and the article be transferred as before. This done, let the second be added to the second as before, and the work should proceed as previously described. It should be noted that in adding, etc.

<margin>Regarding Subtraction</margin>
Subtraction is an operation by which one [number] is taken from others in the upper row, each from the figure corresponding to it. **S**ubtraction is the operation of two numbers against each other to find the greater excess. Or, subtraction is [taking] one number from another so that the remaining sum is seen to be smaller; or a smaller can be subtracted from a larger, or an equal from an equal; but from a smaller, a larger can by no means be taken. Therefore, that number is greater which has more figures or a greater value in its leading part. If there are as many figures in one as in the other, it must be judged by the last or the second-to-last figures, if the last are equal, and so on for the rest. In subtraction, two things are necessary: the number from which the subtraction is to be made, and the number to be subtracted. Let the number from which subtraction is made be written in the upper row with its proper spacing. Let the number to be subtracted be written in the lower row in its own [spacing], so that the first is under the first, the second under the second, and so on for the others. Subtraction is [taking] the first of the lower row from the figure placed above it. That upper figure is either equal to the one below it, smaller, or larger. If it is equal, let it be deleted and a cipher written in its place, provided a figure following it signifies a number. If it is smaller, let as many units as are contained in the lower figure be deleted from it, and let the remainder be placed there. 

If it is larger—because a larger cannot be subtracted from a smaller—let one be borrowed <note>original: "mutuetur"</note> from the next following figure, which is worth ten with respect to the preceding figure. From that ten and the figure from which the subtraction was supposed to be made, joined together, let the lower figure be subtracted and the remainder placed in the spot of the deleted figure. If the figure from which the unit was borrowed was itself a unit, let it be deleted and a cipher put in its place, so that the following figures do not [mistakenly] signify a number. And then it is necessary to proceed as before. If the figure from which a unit must be borrowed is a cipher, one must go to the last significant figure and borrow a unit there, and returning, in the place of every cipher passed over, the figure <term>nine</term> <note>original: "novenarij"</note> should be placed. For if a ten is intended for that figure, a ten remains, but from that ten... a figure nine is left behind for each place passed through. This is because a unit borrowed from the third place is worth one hundred with respect to the figure from which subtraction was made. But in the place of the passed-over cipher, a nine is left which is worth 90; thus a ten remains [to be used in the current column], and the same logic applies to the preceding places.

Now, for the operation of multiplication, two numbers are principally necessary: namely, the multiplied number <note>The "multiplicand."</note> and the multiplying number <note>The "multiplier."</note>. The number to be multiplied is seen to receive the application of the other. The multiplying number is that which is, to speak literally, fixed. When we divide a number, the product is sometimes called the "result" of leading one into the other. The method by which a multiplier can produce many results by multiplying is always to keep the same sum, and this is what is said of two numbers in the following multiplication. There are, however, six rules of multiplication:

[1] When a <term>digit</term> <note>A single-digit number from 1 to 9.</note> multiplies a digit. The smaller digit is subtracted from the <term>article</term> <note>original: "articulo"; a multiple of ten (10, 20, 30, etc.).</note> denoted by the difference of the larger's proportion to ten, with ten counted as well. For example, if it is eight times four <note>The text uses a specific medieval mental math rule for multiplication based on differences from 10.</note>, eight is two away from ten; four times two is eight, which subtracted from forty <note>the article</note> leaves 32, the sum of the whole multiplication. 

[2] When a digit multiplies an article. The digit is led by the value denoted by that article, and each unit will be worth ten; or one hundred, if the article is one hundred. 

[3] When a digit multiplies a <term>composite number</term> <note>original: "numerus compositus"; a number consisting of a ten and a unit, like 12 or 25.</note>. It must be led into both parts of the composite number, so that the digit multiplies the digit according to the first rule, and the article according to the second, and the results are then added together to give the sum of the whole. 

[4] When an article multiplies an article. The digit by which one is denoted is led into the digit by which the other is denoted, and each unit will be worth one hundred; or one thousand, if the article is one hundred. 

[5] When an article multiplies a composite number. The digit of the article must be led into both parts of the joined number, and the sum will be evident. 

[6] When a composite number multiplies a composite number. Each part of the multiplier must be led into each part of the multiplicand: the digit twice (once by the digit and once by the article), and the article similarly twice (once by the digit and once by the article). 

In this, everywhere, let the article be extended to the principal articles. If you wish to multiply any number by itself or by another, write the number to be multiplied in the upper row and the multiplying number in the lower row. Arrange them so that the first digit of the lower row is placed under the last digit of the upper row. This done, the last digit of the multiplier is led into the last digit of the multiplicand. From that multiplication, there may come out a digit, an article, or a composite number. If a digit results, let that digit be written above the multiplying figure. Let this be done for all the multiplying numbers until you come to the first, which is to be led into the last of the multiplicand. From this, if a digit, article, or composite number results: if a digit, write it in the upper place; if an article, write a cipher in the upper place and transfer the article. Similarly, if it is a composite, write the digit of that composite in the upper place and transfer the article as before. This done, move the figures of the multiplying number one place to the right, so that the first is under the penultimate of the multiplicand, and the other figures in their prior order. Similarly, let the first be placed forward; this done, the last of the multiplier must be led into that part of the multiplicand under which is the first [digit] of the multiplicand. If a cipher occurs between the first and last figures of the number to be multiplied, the row of figures for the multiplier must be moved forward by two spaces, because nothing results from multiplying any figure by a cipher. Thus, because the cipher should not be beneath the figures being multiplied, the forward-shifting is performed, just as was said regarding the multiplier. Then, after this operation, a vacant space is left between the two rows of figures, so that whether adding or subtracting, nothing else is committed to memory.

### On Division

Division of a number by a number is, generally, the distribution of a larger number into as many parts as there are units in the smaller number. Note that in division, three numbers are necessary: namely, the number to be divided <note>The "dividend."</note>, the dividing number or **divisor**, and the number denoting how many times <note>original: "denotans quotiens"; the "quotient."</note> or the "resulting" number. 

The number to be divided must always be larger than, or at least equal to, the divisor, so that the division may be performed in whole numbers. Likewise, when one number is divided by another, the number to be divided should be written in the upper row and the divisor in the lower row, placed beneath the dividend, so that the last figure of the divisor is under the last of the dividend, the penultimate under the penultimate, and so on for the others. This should be done as exactly as possible. 

If, however, it cannot be done in such a way that the last is under the last—either because the last figure in the lower row cannot be subtracted from the last figure above it because it is smaller, or because although the last in the lower row can be subtracted some number of times from its upper figure, the remaining figures cannot be subtracted as many times from those placed above them—then we must arrange the lower row so that its figures are placed one step further to the right. Once these are thus ordered, beginning from the last figure of the divisor, one must see how many times that figure can be subtracted from the figure placed above it, so that it can be subtracted just as many times from all the figures placed above the others and from the remainder. 

Note that it may happen that it is subtracted several times, but never more than nine times nor less than once. Having seen "how many times," the number denoting the quotient should be written in a second row directly above that figure under which the first figure of the divisor is placed. This figure signifies the subtraction of those figures in the lower rows from those in the upper rows. This being done, the figures of the divisor are moved forward by one unit’s distance, as was done above, and the business is conducted as before. If it should happen after moving forward that the last figure of the divisor cannot be subtracted from the figure placed above it, then a **cipher** must be written in the row of the quotient, and the figures moved forward as before. Similarly, let it be done everywhere a cipher occurs; wherever the divisor cannot be subtracted from the dividend, a cipher must be placed <unclear>how</unclear> and the figures moved forward.

Once this is done, either the remainder is added, or nothing remains if nothing was reserved. If, however, you wish to work with an improper fraction, a change will be made in the dividend. Thus, multiplication proves division. Likewise, if a multiplication has been performed, let the product be divided by one of the original numbers, and the number denoted by the other figure of the multiplier will result.

**Progression** is the gathering of numbers according to equal increases, starting from unity or from another number, so that each number follows the next by a specific addition. Moreover, one type of progression is **natural** (or continuous) and the other is **interrupted** (or discontinuous). 

**Natural progression** is when one begins from unity and no number is omitted, such as:
-> 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 and so on. <-
In the naming of the following numbers, the progression proceeds by single units. 

**Interrupted progression** is when numbers are omitted after unity, such as:
-> 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 <-
and similarly from any other starting point, such as:
-> 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 <-
and so on for others, if the progression proceeds by two units or more. 

It should be noted that for natural progression, two rules are given. When a natural progression ends in an **even number**, multiply the last number by half of the number that follows it <note>The text describes the formula for the sum of a series 1 to n: Sum = n × (n+1)/2</note>. For example: 1, 2, 3, 4. Multiply four by two <note>The text is slightly garbled here, but the intended result is 10</note>, and it will result in 10, which is the sum of the whole progression. 

But if a natural progression ends in an **odd number**, multiply the total number by its "larger portion" <note>For an odd number n, the "larger portion" is (n+1)/2</note>. For example:
-> 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 <-
The multiplication of five by three results in fifteen, which is the sum of the whole progression. 

Regarding interrupted progression, there are similarly two rules. When an interrupted progression ends in an **even number**, multiply half of that number by the number representing the next half-portion. For 2, 4, 6, 8, multiply four by five, and it will result in twenty, the sum of the progression. 

When, however, an interrupted progression ends in an **odd number**, multiply the "larger portion" <note>The position of the number in the sequence</note> by itself. For example: 1 | 3 | 5. The larger portion <note>three, as it is the third number in the sequence</note> is multiplied by itself (three times three), and nine will be the sum of the whole progression.

</margin>

Next follows the **extraction of roots**. First, it must be seen what a **square number** is, how many types of square numbers there are, and what a "root" is. 

According to **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose "De Arithmetica" was the standard medieval textbook on number theory.</note>, one type of number is **linear**, another **superficial**. 
A **linear number** is one considered only by its points; it has no regard for divisions and has only one dimension, namely length. 
A **superficial number** <note>an area or plane number</note> is that which comes from the leading <note>multiplication</note> of one number into another. It has two dimensions, namely length and width. 

But it should be known that a number can be led into another in two ways: either once or twice. If a number is led once into a number, it is either into itself or into another. If it is led into itself, it is a **square**, and it is called "square" because when written, it has four equal sides like a quadrangle. If it is led into another, it becomes a superficial number but not a square; for example, two led into three constitutes six, a superficial number but not a square. Therefore, every square number is superficial, but not vice versa. A square number is produced from the leading of a number into itself, such as "twice two are four"; four is the first square, and two is its **root**. 

If a number is led twice into a number <note>multiplied twice, e.g., a × a × a</note>, it creates a **solid number**. It is called "solid" because it occupies space like a body and has three dimensions: length, width, and depth. This can also happen in two ways: either into itself or into another. If a number is led twice into itself—or once into its own square, which is the same thing—it becomes a **cubic number**.

<summary>This page concludes the rules for division and introduces arithmetic progressions and the geometric classification of numbers (linear, superficial/square, and solid/cubic) based on Boethian theory.</summary>

A number is named **cubic** from the noun "cube" <note>original: "cubus"</note>, which is also called a **solid**. A cube is a body that has surfaces, eight corners <note>vertices</note>, and 12 edges. Just as some numbers are derived in this way, so a number is called solid and not cubic <note>The author distinguishes between general solid numbers (products of three factors) and perfect cubes (where all three factors are equal)</note>, where three factors constitute twelve. **N**ext follows the extraction of roots in cubic numbers. Here it must be seen that, just as in the method for squares, any <term>cube root</term><note>A number that, when multiplied by itself twice (e.g., 3 × 3 × 3), produces a cubic number.</note> is a cubic number produced from another. A cubic number is the product of something led into itself and then led [multiplied] twice into itself, just as once into its square. A cube root is that number which is thus twice led into itself so that once it results in four <note>likely referring to the geometric dimensions or a specific example</note>; a cubic square has the same root as was said before. 

Let the cubic root be extracted from the proposed number to find the cubic root. If the proposed number is a perfect cube, well and good; if it is not a cube, then one should seek the largest cube below the proposed number. The method of finding this for a proposed number—which to some seems very difficult—is by calculating and setting aside the figures by <term>thousands</term><note>original: "millenarij"; medieval mathematicians grouped digits by threes when extracting cube roots, similar to how we use commas for thousands today.</note>, placing the last thousand under the place of the last figure. One must find a digit which, when led into itself cubically, deletes the whole proposed [number] above it as much as possible. When this is done, that digit must be tripled, and the <term>tripling</term><note>A specific step in the medieval algorithm for cube roots involving multiplying the current root by three and shifting positions.</note> must be placed under the third figure toward the left, and under the triple, and under that triple. Then a certain digit must be placed under the figure before the tripled one, which is then multiplied by the tripled value. 

After this, the triple must be led into the preceding [digit] with respect to itself as closely as possible, so that when led into the cubic root it deletes the whole [number] placed above it. Once this is done, that digit must be tripled, and the tripled value placed under the third figure as before, and the sub-triple under it. One should not then enter into the first tripled value and its sub-tripled value the difference; instead, a certain digit should be placed under the figure before the tripled one. <note>The Latin here describes the complex manual "shifting" process of the Hindu-Arabic algorithm for cube roots, involving repeated tripling and subtraction across columns.</note> 

Note that when we perform the multiplication from the product of the leading digit and the sub-triple, and after that the sub-triple into the product, and again the product produced from the product of the leading digit into itself cubically, these can be added and simultaneously subtracted from the total number placed above. This is as if a division were being made. When this is done, there will either be a remainder or nothing. If nothing remains, it stands that the found [root] was the cube root. If that last digit led under the sub-triple—which is the root—is led into itself [three times], it will result in the same figure that was there before. If there was a remainder, it stands that the number was not a perfect cube; the last digit and the sub-triple represent the root of the largest cube standing under the proposed number. If that root is led into itself and then into the product, that largest cube standing under the proposed number will emerge. And if the remainder is added to that cube, the result in the table will be the same figure as before. 

If any digit after the calculation cannot be placed, a <term>cipher</term><note>original: "zefira"; from the Arabic 'sifr', meaning zero. Medieval texts often treated zero as a placeholder rather than a number in its own right.</note> must be placed. This cipher is put under the fourth figure... and if in the proposed number there are no places of thousands, it must always be noted under the first figure. When the white god <note>original: "deus albus", perhaps a metaphor for a blank space or a clear result</note> stands from his two-fold [part],
They report through all things, and the multiplication serves you.
For it will pass, turning, and it must be driven back.

<margin>On the multiplication of a digit by a digit <note>A "digit" is a single-unit number from 1 to 9.</note></margin>
If you desire to multiply the articles by themselves, note
Those digits which you will multiply by themselves;
Hence there will be as many hundreds in the unit number.

<margin>On the multiplication of an article by a digit <note>An "article" is a multiple of ten.</note></margin>
Multiply the article by the digit, and note:
The article of the digit remains by the multiplier;
They shall increase in the unit [place], the result says.

<margin>On the multiplication of an article by an article</margin>
In this, if there were digits, they shall lead.
Let that which is related be assigned, let the "dogonia" <note>A corruption of "diagona" or a similar technical term for the layout.</note> be made
Of the article and the digit, and through it unless <unclear>therein</unclear>.

<margin>On the multiplication of a composite by a digit <note>A "particulus" or composite is a number containing both tens and units, like 12 or 25.</note></margin>
The article being led into the mixture of the work,
You discern from the distinction, for you enjoy the said law.
In all these articles, here the rule is unless it is missing,
The joiner of the mixture and of the multiplications.

<margin>On the multiplication of a composite by a composite</margin>
Let the digit be led with the rule in the digit.
After this, as if the article brings it to the article,
Afterwards in the article, as if by the digit.
Add this at the same time to the leading result from the part.
From here, if the leads are of the dust <note>original: "pulueris", referring to the sand or dust board used for calculation.</note>, let it be mixed.

In your time, unless you are good or the work is for one.

Here ends the Metric Alexander on
numbers, in the year 1460, by Balthasar,
on the day of Saint Dionysius.

# Geometry

**Geometry** is divided into **theoretical** and **practical**. **Theoretical** geometry is that which contemplates quantity, its proportions, and the causes of measurements by mental speculation alone. **Practical** geometry, however, is that by which we measure an unknown quantity by sensible experiment. According to custom or art, the measurement of spaces is carried out through: namely, **altimetry**, **planimetry**, and **cosmometry** <note>The text likely refers to the measurement of the world/universe; often paired with stereometry in this period</note>. 

**Altimetry** is the method by which we are able to measure the height, length, and the horizon of things. **Planimetry** is that by which we measure the width <note>original: "latitudinem," referring here to the surface area of a plane</note> of things. **Stereometry** <note>original: "Steriometria"</note> is that by which we investigate the width and depth of things. In the first mode, we measure linear dimensions; in the second mode, we measure superficial area; and in the third mode, we measure density or solidity.

In this instruction, therefore, we describe a composite measuring instrument called a **director** <note>original: "pītro directori’," likely referring to a "Directorium" or a specific variation of a quadrant</note> for measuring. We divide it into parts; for in the fourth part of a circle, it shall be terminated. It is adapted for the proportion of a **quadrant** <term>quadrant: an instrument shaped like a quarter-circle used for measuring angles and altitudes</term> and is said to be the distinct fourth part of a circle. 

In the figure where this is experienced and described, and in the square which is contained in the instrument's fourth part of a circle and its points, we are able to determine the degrees of the sun, the declinations of the stars, the latitude of regions, and the hours of the times. Likewise, we can find the altitude of cities, the distances of lands, the depth of wells, and the depth of pits. Any line that is variable may be reduced to the form of a fourth part of a circle. 

Thus, let a circle be made on such a flat plate, whose fourth part is made equal to a quadrant. From that arc, the fourth part of the arc shall be most straightly cut. By these sections, let a quadrant be made. On the sides of the square, let a space be marked out by two straight lines which make a right angle <note>original: "angulum... rectum"</note>. In the first corner of the square, let it be marked with the letter **a**. Let a second point be made, and let a line be drawn from the angle called **b** to the angle **c**. Let it be divided into two equal parts at the middle point. Let one part of a compass <note>original: "circinus"</note> be fixed there, and the other part extended to some point above **a**. From that point, let a straight line be drawn over the sides of the quadrant... which returns directly to the solid fifth part of the circle. And let the end of the arc hang from the mobile part and remain straight.

Afterward, let that first point be moved toward **b** and **e**, and let the place be marked on the dotted line at the distance where the mobile compass touches that line at the point mentioned above **a**. Then, at the point stretching above **b** and **c**, let two lines be drawn, and they include between them five equal parts upon the right angle, one being the fourth part of the circle. And by drawing an arc-line <note>original: "linca’ arcufacialē"</note> which contains the fourth part of a circle most straightly. 

And that lower part of the quadrant, where that arc-line is marked, is called the **limb** <term>limb: the graduated outer edge of an astronomical or geometric instrument</term>. Likewise, let the two other parts be called the letters of the square... across the table... equally distant from the lines **a** and **c**. And within the circumference, lower than **f**, **b**, and **c**, let two circular lines be drawn equidistant from each other, within which certain spaces are delimited. In these, the space above the line contains the degrees, and the number of degrees will appear in the figure.

Let the lower line **f**, **b**, and **c** be divided into two equal parts at the middle point. Through point **a**, let a straight line be drawn leading the quadrant into two equal parts. The line **c-b** is divided into nine equal parts, so that each part is further divided into three equal parts... these are the lines of superficial dimensions from the lower arc-line to the upper line. And let each be divided into five equal degrees. Let the lines of division be made from the lower circular line to the other arc-face, occupying the first space... until there are 90 degrees in total, which completes the fourth part of the circle. This space, thus distinguished, is called the **limb**. 
<insert>Composed and Compended</insert>
The space is delimited to the quantity of two diagonals, and similarly... let a circular line be drawn distinguishing the upper superficial space. Let that figure be marked **f** and **g**. Let that line be divided into 40 equal parts, and let the upper points be called by the sequence **a**, **z**, **k**, **l**, **m**, **n**. Then let the quadrant be placed on a flat table, totally signed and fixed so that it does not move from its place. Then let another similar table be joined to it on an equal surface.
