# The Apogee, the Perigee, and the Carrying Sphere of the Planet

These things must be declared: the <term>apogee (aux)</term> <note>original: "aux"; the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note>, the <term>perigee (oppositum augis)</term> <note>original: "oppositus augis"; literally 'the opposite of the apogee', the point closest to Earth</note>, and the <term>deferent</term> <note>original: "deferens"; the circle that carries the planet or the sun's path</note> of the planet. I say that the apogee is the point most remote from the center of the world, located upon a straight line that passes through the center to the point opposite the apogee. The perigee is the point closest to the Earth. Regarding this apogee, it is demonstrated that these two points are diametrically opposed within the spheres of the planets. It is said to be a shape of a single form whose thickness is nowhere unequal.

And concerning the deferent of the planet, which pertains to its motion: it is moved not by itself, but by the motion of the higher sphere <note>referring to the outer celestial spheres</note>, which is moved above the fixed stars from west to east by its own motion along the pole of the zodiac. It completes its revolution in a year, and in this, it moves by one degree every <insert>hundred years</insert>. <note>This refers to the slow movement of the apogees or the precession of the equinoxes, often calculated as 1° per century in medieval astronomy.</note> From this it follows as a corollary that the sun alone moves under the ecliptic through the path of the deferent and through its poles and the great circles of the spheres, up to the question of the motion of the solid body through its velocity.

But the <term>apsis</term> <note>original: "asard," likely a corruption of 'apsis' or 'axis'</note> of the apogee is not from any one surface, but is a plane. And there are those two informal surfaces. Wherefore the thickness and magnitudes are situated in the proposed place. Meanwhile, the apogee and its opposite describe the seat through which they move throughout the points of the year.

But will that point which is now the apogee remain the apogee hereafter, or will it be another? It is clear that it will be one point then another. And so we say that the apogee of the sun, which is currently at the furthest point, will later be at another point. And they move with their own velocity through the <term>minutes</term> of the deferent of the apogee <note>original: "seraphim"; possibly a poetic reference to the highest heaven or a transcription error for a technical term</note>. The tangent apogee moves the deferent from west to east upon the poles of the zodiac by its own will at a single velocity: one degree in 100 years. The same applies to the apogees of the other seven planets.

From what has been said, it follows that we may speak of these points through three motions:
1. The **daily motion** <note>diurnal motion</note> over the poles of the world.
2. The motion upon the **eccentric**, which moves from west to east under the ecliptic every 24 hours. <note>This refers to the relative solar motion.</note>
3. The **slowest motion**, which moves the stars and apogees only one degree in a hundred years.

Now, to briefly declare the aforementioned <term>theory</term> <note>original: "paratheoris"</note> in a word: since there are three orbs, the sphere of the sun is shown to be one, through the uniform deferent of the sun marked **a** and **b**. The other two deferents are moved with a shared motion, marked **a** and **c**. It is established that the sphere of the uniform deferent of the poles can be moved in one and the same way. These two points will regard each other eternally, as point **d** will be in the apogee and point **z** will be in the perigee. Thus, as is evident, there is neither a vacuum, nor the penetration of bodies, nor compression <note>This reflects Aristotelian physics, which argued that the heavens were full of solid but transparent "ether" spheres that could not overlap or leave empty space</note>, because of the motion of the poles and the apogees. It appears as one thing: that which is near the pole and the earth is sometimes remote from the earth, as is shown in the diagrams.

Thus I describe the zodiac around the center, which shall be **b**. And as is proven, a straight line is drawn from the center to the center of the zodiac, which is **a b c**, which the planet follows in a continuous duration on both sides.

# Geometric Proofs of the Eccentric Orbit

Regarding the two points | wherefore I prove that the four points associated with these two **eccentric** <term>eccentric (eccentrica)</term> <note>A circle whose center is offset from the center of the Earth.</note> circles are extended in a single line, which is **b. c.** This line passes through both centers at the very points where they are distinguished on either side; they meet at the point of contact according to the **third book of Euclid** <note>original: "tertiam euclidis"; referring to Book III of Euclid’s *Elements*, which deals with the properties of circles.</note>. Because that contact is increasing, the line **b. c.** is the greatest of the lines whose endpoints are within a circle of Euclid. If this were otherwise, the line passing through both centers would be impossible, because according to the diagonal **a. d.**, **b. c.** would be greater. From this, according to the 21st proposition of Euclid <note>original: "21 per Euclidem"</note>, the two sides **b. g.** and **b. c.** are longer than **h. e.**, wherefore **a. c.** is greater than **b. c.** This holds the argument because those two sides together are equal to **a. c.**, and thus it is found everywhere.

I would demonstrate this again because the given line passes through the two centers, both for and against, and meets at the point of the <term>apogee (augis)</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> and through that which is opposite the apogee, or the point of closest approach, as was previously alleged regarding the diameter. Let it be granted, therefore, elsewhere at point **g.** Then, from point **c.** to point **g.**, the lines **c. g.** are drawn, joined from point **b.** Let **b. g.** be drawn and argued thus: therefore **e.** is greater than **c. d.**, wherefore **g.** is not the <term>perigee (oppositum augis)</term> <note>original: "oppositum augis"; the point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note>. Alternatively, by drawing so that it is centric, since the center is **a.** and the <term>center of the world (centrum mundi)</term> <note>The Earth, considered the center of the universe in this model.</note> is **b.** Then the points on the diameter, since they are not one arc toward **a.**, are **e.** and **c.** Similarly, for the portion toward **f.**, it is **f. d.** Then, having moved to those two points **c.** and **d.**, I will prove the two lines **a. c.** and **b.** From the center of the world, I draw two other joined lines, let them be **b. c.** and **b. d.** Then, by arguing from the angles made at the center of the world, they are unequal because the angles **e. a. c.** and **f. a. d.** are equal, since they subtend equal arcs and produce **c. a. d.** Let it be smaller than angle **a. b. c.**; then angle **b. a. d.** will be greater than **a. b. c.** And because angle **f. b. d.** is greater than **b. a. d.**, then angle **f. b. d.** will be greater than **a. b. c.** Thus, just as the second part proceeds to **d.**, then the opposite angle is not met by the diameters, wherefore this cannot be.

It is said that the line **c. d.** is more advanced than any other drawn from **c.** to another point of the circumference of the eccentric, which appears in the second part of the 17th [proposition] of the 3rd [book] of Euclid, and thus they are as proposed.

# The Equal Motion of the Moon
**On the orbit beneath the sun**
**placed in the great [circle]**

To the notice of others, it should be understood that the moon does not have a turbulent velocity of motion through the **signs** <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note> when it is found in various locations; rather, the moon does not establish that motion by itself, as is clear from the astronomical tables. 

And first, it must be known that regarding this sphere—just as the **apogee** <term>apogee: the point in the moon's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth</term> is carried along—the moon is not moved by that motion in its own right, but rather it is measured by a strict leading. This velocity is moved by that motion such that it covers **one degree in 10 years**. And when the moon has traversed the **deferent** <term>deferent: the large circular path around the Earth upon which the center of the smaller epicycle travels</term>, it completes this motion in 12 days according to the records <note>original: "notulas"; likely referring to observational notes or table entries.</note>. It follows the movement of the apogee by two degrees, or while in that motion, the moon is not notably fast. But this is not seen in its total motion because, at least over a long period of time, it would be **perceptible**. Therefore, when the first **opposition** <note>Opposition occurs when the moon and sun are on opposite sides of the Earth.</note> is of the true moon, it moves according to the motion of the deferent over the poles of the world; and whenever the moon's apogee is brought into a falling [position], the moon is seen not moving toward the **east** but toward the **west**, as it appears when it is not descending in the deferent toward the east. 

Since the motion of the **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a small circular path used to explain the moon's deviations from a perfect circle</term> is nearly the same as the motion of the first center, the absolute motion of the moon from its point is nearly that of the night, having a very modest [variation]. It appears clearly from the following:

->The fourth motion is from the part of the one sphere of the world while the other<-
->carries the motion toward the west.<- 

The **fifth motion** is attributed to the moon from the part of its **apogee** <note>original: "augis"</note>, moving toward the west and always having its points oriented around the **center of the world**.

The **sixth and last motion** of the moon is attributed to its own proportion, as if it moves by one degree; then, through the moon's proximity to these motions, it does not seem to resist, as is clear from what was said above. 

I say first that the center of the moon's epicycle and the apogee follow a certain mode of motion. And this is seen in the fact that those [points] are in the same place—namely, the line from its [center] extends toward **a) the east** and **b) the center of the city** <note>Likely referring to the observer's meridian or a specific reference point like Toledo or Paris common in medieval tables.</note>. The signs for the points of the apogee through the whole sphere are **a, p, b, c** and one point such as **b, c**. The point of the apogee is moved by the line of the poles toward the west by 12 [units], while at that time the sun is moved toward the east by one degree. <unclear>Certainly that</unclear> motion corresponds to this double correspondence which determines the centers of the **equal [motions]**.

<margin>
Note that when the apogee of the moon is not reached, there are two points that are distinguished from the apogee toward the west. Others [say] that during the first correction and through a long time, the moon does not [move] toward the east, but rather in that position, the points are [aligned]. If they are all aligned, either the sun is in the middle or it is in opposition. 
What can be deduced concerning the motion of the stars and the points: and further, first, that the moon is led through point after point, not staying in the same place, and the motion of the moon is measured always by the moon [itself] coming to those points from the distant [heavens].
</margin>

Or it is not. The pole is distinguished in the middle so that it has the division of the bodies. If not for all [points], then for whichever distance they are distant from the orbits... <note>The Latin here becomes highly abbreviated and technical, referring to geometric distances between the observer, the pole, and the lunar apogee.</note> ...it does not equal the distance from the origin. The apogee is not the same as the pole... if the epicycle were at the mean motion. Therefore, the pole is not the [same] motion. And if it is distant from the origin, or at the diametrically opposite [point], or not distant... it does not seem that the diameter of the moon's body is distant.

# Here begins the letter of Masha'allah concerning the matters of lunar eclipses, the conjunctions of the planets, and the revolutions of the years, briefly elucidated.

There are, therefore, twelve chapters. 
**The first chapter** is on the manner of the circle and the stars, and how they operate in this world. 
**The second chapter** is on the diversity of the tracks and the work of the stars in the regions of the earth. 
**The third chapter** concerns the estimation of their natures, namely hot and cold, and whether they are fixed, mobile, or nocturnal. 
**The fourth chapter** is on the revolution of the years. 
**The fifth chapter** is on lunar eclipses and their significance. 
**The sixth chapter** is on the changing of seasons and the shifting of rains in the "rainy" and "heavy" signs. 
**The seventh chapter** is on solar eclipses and their significance. 
**The eighth chapter** is on the conjunction of the planets and its effect. 
**The ninth chapter** is on the generation of rain as it occurs. 
**The tenth chapter** is on the "minor conjunctions." 
**The eleventh chapter** is on the "middle conjunctions." 
**The twelfth chapter** is on the "great conjunctions" <note>In medieval astrology, conjunctions between Saturn and Jupiter were classified into minor, middle, and great cycles to predict historical shifts.</note>.

## The first chapter: on the manner of the circle of stars and how they operate. 
**Masha'allah** <note>original: "messehalla"; Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815 AD) was a Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer whose works were foundational to European "science of the stars."</note> said that the most high Lord made the Earth in the likeness of a sphere, and He made the circuit around it revolve. He placed the Earth fixed and immobile in the middle of the circle, inclining neither to the right nor to the left. He placed the mobile elements [within it] and made them move through the motion of the planets. The **head** <note>likely referring to the "head of the dragon" or the ascending node</note> and the direction of the signs and all the stars participate in the motion of the planets, their works, and their nature. 

Therefore, the work of the planets in this world is similar to a **lodestone** <term>lodestone: a naturally magnetized mineral (magnetite), used here to explain how stars influence Earth from a distance</term> and iron. Just as iron is drawn to this stone even across a distance, so all creatures and all things upon the earth are affected by the motion of the planets and the universal things above the earth, whether they be holy things or animals. 

Both **good fortune** and **impediment** <note>original: "fortuna... i pedimenti"; in astrology, an "impediment" is a planetary condition that weakens a star's positive influence.</note>, and those things which happen "to the right," arise from their motions in their workings. The greatest significance of this is the conversion of the hours in their own air, bringing both good and bad fortune. For we see that some rational people are naturally good, while others are both foolish and "good" by luck. This does not happen without a signifying cause; good or bad fortune does not occur without the choice and will of Him who produces the fortunate and the unfortunate. All of this is by the nod of God—the work of the planets and the fortune of the hours.

## The second chapter: on the diversity of the stars' work in the regions of the earth.
Know that the work [of the stars] is varied according to the diversity of the **climates** <term>climates: latitudinal zones of the Earth, each believed to be ruled by different planetary influences</term>. For in certain climates, certain portions of fortune occur, while in another climate, evils occur in different orders. Therefore, every rational person must understand the reasons of the climates and regions. Consider the region of the **Ethiopians**, where there is always heat, and the land of the **Sdanorum** <note>original: "sdanorū"; likely a scribal error for "Sclavorum" (the Slavs) or a reference to a specific northern people.</note>, where there is always cold. 

When the significance of a star brings excessive cold over Ethiopia, their air is tempered [made milder] and it signifies fertility; but if [excessive heat] is found in their air, their habitation will perish. Because of this, the science of the great climates, regions, and atmospheres is necessary. Know that the science of the stars is very heavy [difficult] and that **Dionysius** was able to know it because it is a universal and plural thing—such as the revolutions of years and eclipses, which intend the significations of all men. This cannot be done except through the knowledge of the nature of the stars, what each one signifies by its mixtures and all its affairs. We have spoken of this most clearly in our books, but now let us return to this part briefly, and now we begin by the help of God.

## The third chapter: on the natures of the signs.
There are twelve **signs** <note>The signs of the Zodiac.</note>. In every single sign, there are 30 degrees; in every degree, 60 minutes; and in every minute, 60 seconds; and so on down to the quantity of a point—that is, unto infinity. And these are their names: Aries, Taurus, and the rest. Their significations are over fire, air, water, and earth.

For three of them are fiery: Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius. And three are earthy: Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn. And three are airy: Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius; and three are watery: Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces. The signs are also categorized so that three are hot and the watery ones are cold. The others indeed are cold and the airy ones are hot. And know that all hot signs are masculine, and the cold ones are feminine. All masculine signs are also diurnal <note>Diurnal signs are associated with the day; nocturnal signs with the night.</note>, and the feminine are nocturnal. Know that of the signs, four are "mobile" <note>In modern astrology, these are called "Cardinal" signs; they mark the start of the seasons.</note>—in which the season is moved—which are Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn; and four are "fixed," in which the season is established, such as Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius; and four are "common" or "two-bodied" <note>Now called "Mutable" signs; they occur when one season is transitioning into the next.</note>, in which two seasons are joined, such as Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces. These are the natures of the signs; understand them.

## The fourth chapter: on the introduction to the revolutions of the years.

When you wish to know what will happen in the world regarding rains, winds, and other matters, establish the ascendant <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note> at the hour of the sun’s entry into the first point of Aries <note>The spring equinox.</note>, and establish the "parts" <term>Arabic Parts: mathematical points calculated from the distance between planets to predict specific outcomes, like the "Part of Fortune."</term> for that same hour. Having made the chart, consider which of them will be ahead; if it is strengthened, the season will be [well-tempered]. If indeed a planet is poorly placed, as was predicted, the world will be [troubled or corrupted]. Similarly, you may know this for the quarters of the year and the months. And know that if most of the planets are in watery signs at the revolution of the year, it will signify a multitude of rain. And in fiery signs, it will signify an excess of heat and dryness, or the barrenness of the earth. In airy signs, it signifies a multitude of winds; and in earthy signs, it will signify dryness and snow. Similarly, in the quarters of the year when the planets are in cold signs, it will signify the severity of cold and the lessening of heat. Know also that when Mars and Saturn behold each other <note>original: "conspicient"; this refers to an astrological aspect, or angle, between the two planets.</note> and do not behold a "fortune" <note>A "fortune" or benefic planet, like Jupiter or Venus, was thought to soften the negative effects of "malefics" like Saturn or Mars.</note>, it will signify a multitude of wars and the destruction of the world. Likewise, if Mars is the lord of the summer quarter and is in any of the houses of Mercury, it will signify a multitude of rain and pestilences. And just as specific dryness and the barrenness of the earth or the scarcity of grain [is predicted], if the "part" is not in the ascendant in fiery signs, understand this from the "part" according to what we have distinguished everywhere.

## The fifth chapter: on the eclipse of the moon or sun.

As Masha'allah says, you must consider the year of the eclipse. Observe which planet is in the ascendant at the midpoint of the eclipse, and the condition of the ascendant and its chart. For if the planet is "evil" [a malefic], it will signify [toil] and destruction. If indeed it is a "fortune," it will signify restoration. And know that if an eclipse of the moon occurs in cold signs, it signifies the weight of the cold. And in watery signs, an abundance of rain, especially if it occurs during the winter season. If indeed it is summer, it will signify a tempering of the air; understand the rest accordingly. Understand that if the "fortunes" behold the moon and "receive" <term>Reception: a favorable relationship where a planet is located in a sign ruled by another planet, which then "receives" it like a guest.</term> it, there will be a great benefit in those things which regard the good and the profitable.

## The sixth chapter: on the changing of seasons and the movement of planets according to their weight.

Masha'allah said: When you wish to foreknow the weather amidst the various corruptible changes in the revolution of the world, know the sign of the "heavier" planets <note>original: "plus ponderoz"; in medieval science, the outer planets (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) were considered "heavy" because they moved more slowly through the zodiac.</note>, whether they are hot or cold. If they are hot, it will signify heat in summer and a tempering of the air in winter. If they are in cold signs, it will signify [severe cold] in winter and a tempering in summer. Similarly, consider when they are in watery signs: it will signify excessive rains and a corruption of the air through too much rain in winter, and a tempering of the air with a multitude of dew in summer. And according to this manner predicted through the number of planets: the heavy planets are Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars; one must also join the Sun to them. Know finally that when the heavy planets are directly over some region, it will signify prosperity or the barrenness of the earth. When they are far from it, they signify a multitude of rains... as they are in northern signs or according to their length in the southern ones. Know also that when the heavy planets are all "oriental" <note>Rising in the east before the sun.</note>, it signifies prosperity; and whenever they are all "occidental" <note>Setting in the west after the sun.</note>, they signify a multitude of rains in winter and a tempering of the air in summer. And similarly, their rising signifies a fitting state of the air in winter and general prosperity in summer.

## Chapter seven: on the eclipse of the sun and its significance. Masha'allah said: Know that
an eclipse of the sun cannot happen except through the significance of one of these seven accidents according to the
quantity of the point itself <note>The "point" refers to the degree of the zodiac where the eclipse occurs.</note>. This is [determined by] in which quarter of its body it occurs, and if it is a total eclipse
or a partial one. And you should know the ascendant <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the eclipse.</note> of the middle of the eclipse, and the planets aspecting the
signs of the eclipse. If these are "malefics" <term>Malefics: planets considered traditionally harmful or challenging, primarily Saturn and Mars.</term>, they will signify evil, loss, and the death of kings, and
what is said [thereof]. And if they are "benefics" <term>Benefics: planets considered traditionally helpful or lucky, primarily Jupiter and Venus.</term>, they will signify good fortune and the suitability of those things. And
know that if a solar eclipse occurs in Aries, it will signify the death of kings, coming
droughts, or almost total sterility, and hunger; and I understand this to be the case in all fiery signs. In watery
signs, however, it will signify a multitude of rains or damage caused by them; I also understand that the
benefics that aspect [the eclipse] will diminish the evil of the matter in that which appears. For they will increase and decrease
the fortune. Know that in a solar eclipse, if the moon remains until [the time] of another [event], it will signify
what has been observed; and when they remain until the degree of another great [event], such as infirmity and
increase, as appears above regarding the benefics.

## Chapter eight: on the conjunction of planets and their effect. Masha'allah said: because the planets signify
accidents of this kind, and the things that are so established at the time of all the planets, whichever they may
be. And the benefics will signify fortune and a good effect and will favor the appearance of all [good things];
likewise, if the malefics prevail, they will signify evil and a bad effect. You should know that as much as they are in
any of the signs, it will signify loss, and a multitude of loss according to the substance of that same sign.
That is, if the conjunction <term>Conjunction: an astronomical event where two or more planets appear very close to each other in the sky.</term> occurs in watery signs, it will signify damage from rains and [affect] professions; and
so in the other signs. Just as it is said, if it occurs in feminine signs, they will signify pestilence among
women and the female sex of animals; and the same for the masculine. Know also that when a conjunction or eclipse
of the moons occurs in fixed signs <note>Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius.</note>, it will signify the durability of evil and loss; and
if it occurs in mobile signs <note>Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn.</note>, it will signify a lack of durability of that evil and that state;
and know that if they are in common signs <note>Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces.</note>, it will signify a moderate evil, and the same is said of the good.

## Chapter nine: on the union of the superior planets. Masha'allah said: Know that the greatest and most
extraordinary things happen from the alignment of the superior planets <term>Superior Planets: the planets with orbits outside that of Earth; in medieval astrology, these were Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</term>; and this happens because of the slowness of their motion. When
these three are joined in one term <note>A "term" is a specific subdivision of a zodiac sign.</note> so that they appear with the sun, they will signify the
destruction of rulers and kingdoms and their change, and very great matters according to the quantity of the forces
joining upon their signs. And this is because their greatest conjunction signifies prophecy and matters concerning
the various climates <note>In ancient geography, "climates" referred to latitudinal zones of the Earth.</note> and great events. And especially if any of the earthly planets are involved with them.
And know that the significator will be stronger than the others when it is a benefic; it will signify
fortune. And if it is a malefic, it will signify evil and tribulation. Understand that when the
planets are at their "exaltations" <term>Exaltation: a specific sign where a planet is thought to be at its most powerful or most dignified.</term>, it will signify good and a suitable time, and
a multitude of movements of wars and the demonstration of miracles. But if they are joined in
all the [difficult] points, it will signify loss, and drought, and almost total sterility, and hunger,
most especially according to their strength. And know that when the conjunction is in a fiery sign, it will signify drought
and sterility; and in a watery sign, a multitude of rain. In an airy sign also, they will signify the
strength of the winds; and in an [earthy] one, an excess of cold and loss. And indeed, if
they are in masculine signs, it will signify the loss of masculine souls; and likewise for the feminine.

## Chapter ten: on the minor conjunction. Masha'allah said: we have already narrated that the principal matters

rules in the sign. If there is a benefic, it will signify good and a suitable time; and
if there is a malefic, loss and drought, as well as almost total sterility. And you should know that...

## Chapter eleven: On the intermediate conjunction. Masha'allah <note>original: "Messalla"</note> said.

The intermediate conjunction is the conjunction of Mars and Saturn, and this signifies accidents <note>In the philosophical sense: events or external changes.</note> of the kingdom and wars, and it hastens whatever contradictions you may desire. The minor conjunction is the conjunction of Jupiter and Mars, and this signifies accidents which occur in many things and the competition of matters; and those things that remain will be overcome in their order by a "fortune," it will signify good fortune; if it stands in an evil state [it signifies evil]. ### Chapter on letters and rumors.

When you are questioned about a letter or about rumors <note>original: "rumoribus," here referring to news or reports</note> as to when they shall arrive, look at the messenger <note>the planet or house representing the bearer of news</note>. If it is in the **Ascendant** <term>Ascendant: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the question</term>, or if it is intending to move toward the Ascendant, or if the **Moon** is joined to the Lord of the Ascendant, or joined to the Lord of the Moon's house—so that the Lord of the Moon's house is joined to it—or if **Mercury** <note>Mercury is the traditional planet of communication and messengers</note> is joined to the Lord of the Ascendant, the letter shall come. And if the messenger is not in the Ascendant at the hour of its entry, the letter shall still come if the Moon is joined to Mercury at the hour of their meeting, or at the hour of the Moon's arrival at the Ascendant. If the Moon is carrying [the influence] from Mercury into the degree of the Ascendant, which belongs to the Lord of the Ascendant, then the letter shall arrive. 

And then, when the bearer reaches the one to whom it is delivered and you are asked when the letter was written, look at the degrees that are between the Moon and the planet from which it is separating; and say that it was written according to the number of those degrees in days. Similarly, look at the degrees found between the Moon and the planet to which it is joined; according to those [degrees] shall be the time of the letter's arrival.

The Tenth Sign <note>original: "Signū . 10 ."</note>, in which **Masha'allah** <note>original: "messeallah," referring to the 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer Masha'allah ibn Athari</note> speaks: Look at the hour of the reception of this king whom the messenger enters, as if by the testament of the reigning Lord or the time of his questioning; from this, you shall know the magnitude of his movement in work and what has been enlightened for him by God. And then, if the election <term>election: the choosing of an astrologically favorable moment to act</term> is confirmed for him, his honor and victory shall be known. Whatever profit or nobility is accustomed for us in the preceding planets that signify kings in any matter without the Ascendant, it is said in the discourse to be for the king. 

And if the Lord of the Ascendant is among the planets, look at the house of the king. If you find no planet there having the line of testimony <note>a specific astrological strength or corroboration</note> when an evil influence arrives there, he shall see destruction. <meta>This page transitions from the astrological "interrogations" of the previous page to the practical mathematical foundations required for such work. It provides rules for calculating "vulgar" (common) fractions and "physical" (astronomical) fractions, which use a base-60 system. Such calculations were essential for a medieval scholar to determine the precise positions of planets.</meta>

**Common fractions** <note>original: "Diminutio vulgaritū," literally "common diminutions," referring to standard fractions like 1/2 or 3/4</note> you shall write with the numerator above. Below, write the **denominator**, such as 3/4. In **astronomical** <note>original: "phīsice," likely referring to the "physical" or astronomical method of calculation used by natural philosophers</note> or diminished numbers, you shall write only the numerator and the place in which the diminished number is positioned, and [use] a mark for the denominator. For example: 20 seconds; the first number preceding the seconds is the place of the whole number <note>the integer</note>, then the minutes, seconds, thirds, and fourths; and so on, because they are similar diminished numbers.

To reduce **dissimilar fractions** to the same denomination so they may be made equal: Multiply the denominator of one fraction by the denominator of the other, and the result will be the **common denominator**. Then, multiply the numerator of the first fraction by the denominator of the second; the result will be the new numerator. [Divide] the result by the common denominator and you will have a value equal to the first fraction. Then multiply the numerator of the other by the denominator of the first; the result will be a numerator of equal value. For example, if 2/3 and 3/4 are proposed: I arrange these dissimilar denominators to be the same, therefore I multiply them as was said.

To reduce any **whole numbers** <note>original: "Integra"</note> to a common vulgar denomination: multiply the denominator by the number of wholes, and the result will be the numerator. If you place the given denominator under that numerator, you will have completed the task. For example, three times seven is 21; therefore, 21 sevenths are equal to 3 wholes.

<margin>Chapter Four</margin>
**Astronomical denominations** <note>original: "phīsice de noiaciōm"</note> are reduced to seconds and so forth by multiplying the number of wholes by 60, and then the result by 60 again if necessary, and so on as many times as needed. For example: 20 wholes, if you reduce them to minutes, will be 1,200; if you reduce them to seconds, they will be 72,000 <note>The OCR reads 12,000, but 1,200 * 60 is 72,000</note>; if you go to thirds, you will find they equal 4,320,000 thirds, and so on.

To reduce **common sums** to wholes, divide the numerator by the denominator. The number of times [it goes in] will be the number of wholes. If any remainder is left from the division, you cannot find a whole number for it, but it remains a fraction of the whole.

**Parts** <note>referring to minutes or seconds</note> are reduced by dividing by 60, and this as many times as needed until you reach whole numbers. When this is done, you can proceed thus: the remainder must be divided by a value of a coarser <note>larger</note> unit... for example, if you divide 648 seconds, it results in 10 [minutes] and 48 seconds remaining <note>648 divided by 60 is 10 with a remainder of 48</note>. Note this case: so that you may be certain how many wholes these seconds equal; 3/4 is equal to the nearest whole.

If there is a debt of common fractions, such as 3/4 seconds and so on, but you wish to know precisely what wholes are equivalent to the said quantity: Take the division for the whole, such as 31... <note>The text here becomes a series of complex arithmetic examples involving remainders and the choice between rounding up or down</note>... it is better in this case to remain with smaller units than larger ones.

To reduce **finer** <note>original: "subtiliores," meaning smaller units like seconds or thirds</note> quantities to **coarser** <note>original: "grosiorez," meaning larger units like minutes or wholes</note> ones, use the rules just mentioned. To reduce numbers to finer ones, multiply by 60 as often as necessary, as was shown in the first part. When you are given quantities of different kinds to be reduced to finer ones, the coarsest are reduced to the level of the finer ones, and so on as often as necessary. For example: 20 [minutes], 39 [seconds], and 40 [thirds]... <note>The text lists numerical strings that appear to be calculation exercises</note>.

To reduce a **common fraction** to a finer one: find the smaller numbers in the proportion of the numerators and denominators... and you will have the result. For example, 20 [minutes] equals 2/3 [of a whole], and 15/32 of a sixty-part <note>a minute</note> equals 11 thirtieths... you can thus reduce to coarser quantities.

If this is not sufficient for you, to reduce to coarser quantities, divide the numerator by the parts of the minutes and the denominator by those same parts... they are equal. Therefore, you reduce all of these to coarser units to find what is proposed. For example, 42 is like 4/7... it is necessary that each 1 equals 4.

6. **thirty-thirtieths** <note>original: "trecessimas," likely referring to units in a base-30 or base-60 system common in medieval tables</note> and one, which is worth 21 thirtieths; for they equal thirtieths and this [is so]. In the third part he places the years; in the first part, the **Year of our Lord**. For it is said through the years of our Lord 3, 3/4, and 11 thirtieths. If you wish [to convert] all days to the diminished astronomical [fraction] <note>original: "inminutam phisicam," referring to sexagesimal fractions used in physics and astronomy</note>, it is not changed by the addition of whole numbers except in this: be careful here because the root is properly for its own part—namely, the seconds are added through the day, and the thirds through the 4th and 5th/3rd for the doubling and halving of substances. The astronomical [method] communicates well, for it says that which is indicated.

->**Why do astronomical fractions achieve more precision over coarser numbers when they extend further than elsewhere?**<-

In **adding common fractions** <note>original: "minucias vulgare," standard fractions like 1/2 or 1/3</note>, even if they are of the same denomination, if you aggregate them, you shall make a numerator from the numerators and place the denominator [underneath]. And if they are not of the same denomination, reduce them through the part to which they belong, and then they will be of [the same] denomination. For example, as with 4 and 2/3: first you will settle the two parts, and thereafter, with that aggregated sum, you will perform a similar calculation with the third.

If however you wish to **double**, **divide**, or **subtract**: if they have the same denomination, you shall subtract the numerator. You must do what is necessary in subtraction by communicating the numerator from the larger remainders to the smaller ones, so that the denominated fractions remain. For a minor subtraction, as in 3 elevenths from 8 elevenths: for 4 elevenths will remain.

**Doubling** a common fraction is also done this way: you shall double the four <note>the numerator</note> and the denominator will be evident.

<margin>Chapter 7 and 9</margin> **Halving**, however, is similar: you will divide the numerator or double the denominator, just as 1/2 becomes 1/4; or 1/3 [doubled] to 1/2 becomes 3/2.

In **multiplying astronomical fractions** <note>original: "minuciis phisice"</note>, for both the multiplier and the multiplicand, by the art of reduction to the same kind of number, you shall lead one numerator into the other. The product will make a number of fractions as far distant from one revolution as it is distant from that into which it is led. [For example], 2 [times] 3 become 6; where they are 4 distant, they become 6 from the whole numbers <note>integers</note>. Just as 2 and 3 [minutes] from the whole numbers [become] 6 [seconds]. And there are 4, because not [just] fractions of 4. It was seen [that] 2/3 and 3/2 and 4/3 would become 12/2, and the joined whole number makes 2/4 and 4. Just as before, you shall do what was said of the thirds, which similarly makes 8. Because of this, 3 and 4 are [used], because the product of 7 and 1/3 sevenths was 12; one from 3 and 1/3 and 2 and 1/2 was 4 and 2/8, which is 20.

In this, they also lead the numerator of one into the numerator of the other, so that the product makes the numerator. Similarly for the denominators: the product will make the denominator, and you will have an increasing fraction. For example, lead 2/3 into 1/2; they become 2/6. This is called multiplying a fraction of a fraction of a whole number, said in its own way. When a fraction of the whole is given, then the astronomical fraction [makes] the numerator; similarly, the denominator is placed in a specific way. For example: I ought to multiply 3 and 2/3 and 1/3 into 2/4. I multiply into two 5s; 3 into 2, and they become 5; 4 [times] 7, they become 20. This sum, because it is 6 twentieths of the whole, you shall therefore lead 6 twentieths [into] 1/6 sevenths, and they will be 30 one-hundred-and-fortieths. In the same way, you will proceed if there are many parts in the multiplicand; likewise if in both; and this as often as it shall be necessary. There is no other process.

To **divide** in astronomical [fractions]: just as in multiplication, the whole must be reduced to one kind [of fraction]. If they are not similar, then just as in multiplication, the product is divided. You shall act so that they are of the same kind as the rest, reducing it to the more subtle <note>smaller</note> part, which you shall do excellently so that the fractions...

<meta>This page shifts abruptly from the mathematical calculations of fractions found on the previous page to a treatise on judicial astrology, specifically the nature and portents of comets. This transition is common in medieval miscellanies where mathematical tools were often applied to the "science of the stars."</meta>

Comets, or **tailed stars** <note>original: "caudate stelle"</note> as we see them, are not true stars. Instead, they are ignited vapors rising from the earth in the manner of stars. It is said that every planet [produces] such likenesses at certain times through its own humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term> which arrive as a flame; thus, it appears as a large star and is of a dry nature. This is how all such comets are formed.

The comet that comes from **Saturn** is not very black in color, but is like bright lead. This comet signifies strange and terrible events, dangers in the world, the mortality <note>original: "mortalitatem," referring to widespread death or plague</note> of kings, princes, and other lords, and many destructions. For this reason, everyone should fear the coming of this comet.

The comet that appears in a bright and silver color comes through the influences of **Jupiter**. This signifies a [good] fate for the people because it makes the earth germinate and fills it with all fertility and great utility—especially if Jupiter is in its exaltation <note>the sign where a planet's influence is strongest</note>, namely in Aries, Sagittarius, or Leo; likewise when in its [other] exaltation in Cancer or Pisces.

The comet of a red and fiery color, which drags a <unclear>long</unclear> [tail] behind it, is generated by **Mars**. For those in the world, it signifies deaths and <unclear>prostrations</unclear> <note>original: "prostraciones," meaning the downfall or collapse of people</note> among human natures. This is because it dries out the blood and the veins. While the earth is normally [moistened] by dew and moisture, this color signifies that the blood becomes dry of all other humors. Where the humors were once held in a healthy temperament <note>original: "i temperamento," the balanced state of the body</note>, this comet's power and color multiplies the choleric humor, leading to death. This occurs because it dries the blood in the veins and increases the bile. This comet turns its head toward the East, and its arrival in the world brings <unclear>adversaries</unclear> to the East, little rain, pestilence, and famine; there will be <unclear>obstacles</unclear>, falls, groans, and laments. However, when people see it, they should strengthen their nature and virtue, as it [eventually] indicates peace.

The comet that appears and moves around the **Sun**, which has a horrible and red appearance, signifies the <unclear>denotation</unclear> of vegetation, such as plants, and the dry mortality of kings and the wealthy.

The final comet is one that drags a great number of rays behind it. If it joins with any planet, it signifies something to us; for example, if it joins **Saturn** or the **Moon**, then deaths remain. If it joins **Mars** or **Mercury**, it signifies the death of children. Just as Mars causes war, this [comet] of Mercury signifies the death of the literate <note>original: "litteratorum," meaning scholars or educated men, over whom Mercury presided</note> and the virtuous, and it weakens humanity <unclear>near</unclear> [these] events.

There are yet three more comets:
1. One is like the star of **Venus**, which is white and has "hair" <note>original: "crinas," referring to the coma of a comet</note> and natural rays like a star.
2. A white one, round like the **Moon**, which is in favor of men.
3. Another which is small but drags many rays behind it; these signify actions in the world and move without [bad] accidents, by which piety is designated.

Note that although all these comets signify the things mentioned above in the world, they must be understood by the specific points in which they appear and are seen, and how the "breath" [of the vapor] deviates. Furthermore, there are three comets shaped like columns <note>original: "ad modum columpne," a classical classification of comets</note> which <unclear>destroy</unclear> <unclear>regimes</unclear> and bring them to nothing. In whichever city they appear, they signify novelties, the <unclear>prostrations</unclear> of kings, and strife among them. Furthermore, we ought to know the sign of each [planet] above these comets in the <unclear>lands</unclear>...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial portents. While the previous page categorized comets by planetary influence (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars), this page transitions into the physical and spiritual nature of "falling stars" and the mechanics of how atmospheric vapors are ignited to create these signs.</meta>

It reveals diverse things because they will soon fall; for if some part of the thing appears in the east, that which they rule <note>original: "Regulisant," likely a corrupt form of "regulant" or a reference to the star Regulus</note> appears quickly, and if it appears in the west, it will bring wind.

**C**ertainly, these are noble and spiritual creatures; they neither fall nor pass away, but remain in the firmament just as we see during the day when it is hot, or on a clear night like a **falling star** <note>original: "stella decurrens"</note>. Indeed, that is not a true star, because it would then have the appearance of a star; rather, it is a **little fire** <note>original: "igniculus"</note> fallen from the ether by heat and fieriness. It is called <term>Assub</term> <note>from the Arabic "ash-shihāb," a term used in medieval science for a meteor or shooting star</note> when it is said to have a tail, and when it appears pointing downwards it is called a <term>Comet</term> <note>original: "Cometes"</note> as mentioned above. By some, it is called <term>coram</term> <note>possibly a corruption of "crinita," meaning long-haired</note>, and it is a sign of the death of some beloved person, though this is not a settled rule. Among those things appearing in the middle, they are formed of what is called <term>air</term> <note>original: "aer"</note>, as the discussion here concerns wind. It is true that there are <term>Rising Assub</term> and <term>Falling Assub</term>. This is prohibited for such a cause because a very strong wind reigns plainly in the pure, clean, and perfect air. From another depression, as it is then purified from the **impressions** <note>original: "impressionibus," a medieval term for atmospheric phenomena like meteors or rain</note> which cease in the <unclear>nature</unclear> of the air <unclear>Lecuntum</unclear>. And this wind, through the two aforementioned [causes], could perhaps be raised by opacity and would return from those heights which it reaches by ascending, dragging with it that fire in a downward state. When it drags with a long tail in the manner of fiery torches, this also happens through a **malignant spirit** <note>original: "spiritus malignus"</note> or a **good Angel** <note>original: "bonus Angelus"</note> descending for some splendor by the command of the Lord. Then [the lights] can fall, yet the high stars remain immobile.

It distinguishes between the stable stars of the firmament and these transient "impressions" in the air that signal earthly events like wind or death.</summary>

-> To find the degree of the ascendant <note>symbol for the Sun</note> and the other four houses <-

First, equate the days and hours of the Sun using the Table of the Equation of Days <note>The "Equation of Time" accounts for the fact that the Sun's apparent motion is not perfectly uniform</note>, which is used for the nights, and double the entry as is done in the Alfonsine Tables. Take the degrees and minutes found there, and for every degree, take 4 minutes of an hour, and for every minute, take four seconds of an hour. Add this to the appointed time to get the <term>equated time</term>.

Therefore, take the hours you have after the completed days and multiply them by fifteen, if they are <term>equal hours</term> <note>Hours of exactly 60 minutes, as opposed to "unequal hours" which varied with the season</note>. Do the same for the fractions of the hours separately. From the hours multiplied by 15, you will get degrees; from the minutes of the hour, you will get minutes of the degrees. If you divide the minutes of the degrees by 60, it becomes a degree, and if you divide the seconds of the degree by 60, it becomes a minute in the quotient; thus convert them and save the result. If, however, the hours were <term>unequal</term>, multiply them by the parts of the hours you took for the degree of the sun in the table of the ascensions of the signs. Take the remainder and that minute which corresponds in the table with the double entry, and convert both into the degrees you resolved. If the time is at noon, take the ascensions of the degree of the sun on the <term>right circle</term> <note>the celestial equator</note>. If the time is at midnight, take the ascension of the <term>nadir</term> <note>the point directly opposite</note> of the sun on the same circle. If the time is from the hours of the night, take the ascension of the nadir of the sun in the table of your region. If the time is from the hours after sunrise, take the ascension of the degree of the sun in the table of your region. Once these are taken, add the degrees and minutes to which you reduced the time. By doing this, you will have the ascensions of the sign and the degree of the ascendant in your region.

In the double entry, you must subtract and multiply by the minutes of the argument; if there is a remainder after subtracting the degrees, convert it to minutes, then divide by sixty, and the quotient will be the proportional part. Add this if the first value was larger, or subtract it if it was smaller.

When you are ready to calculate the houses, first enter the table of the right circle with the ascensions found to find the degrees of the hours; this will give you the 11th and 12th houses by adding the small parts of the hours found in the ascensions. Afterward, to find the 2nd house, enter the same table after subtracting that time from the part of the hours from 60; by joining the remainder to the 2nd house in the entries for the 3rd house, and adding the same part of the hours, you will have the 3rd house. All houses are found through these methods.

To find the minutes for each house, operate thus: subtract the smaller value from the closer ascension with which you entered (or the number from the sum of degrees you had), convert the remainder into seconds, and divide the result by the excess of the larger value over the smaller. You will have the number and minutes in the quotient. Do this for each of the houses. Note that if you find a number greater than 30 when entering for the sun, subtract 30 and enter with the remainder; if you find more than 360 in the ascensions, subtract 360 and keep the remainder.

Note that you must subtract the value you entered from the one you should have entered, and convert the result into seconds. Then subtract the number you entered from the next larger value, and convert that remainder into minutes; divide by these minutes and save the result.

Note that when you converted the hour into degrees, you had to add the degrees of the hours to the degrees of the ascensions. Then enter the table for the <term>6th climate</term> <note>A latitudinal zone, roughly corresponding to the latitude of northern France or southern Germany</note> and take the parts of the hours to save. Then let it be referred back to the east and the same ascensions. Afterward, for a single house, add the doubled parts of the hours as was said above, etc.

<meta>This page continues the technical astronomical instructions, shifting from the calculation of the "Ascendant" to the geographical principles required for these computations. It establishes the prime meridians and coordinate systems used in the tables, specifically addressing the differing definitions of "West" and the location of the world’s center, Arim.</meta>

With these rules, you must have tables of the longitude and latitude of regions.

Note that the habitable degrees, where the longitudes of regions are calculated, span 180 degrees and 30 minutes from the West and define the longitudes starting from the center of the world. By adding 90 degrees to these, you will have the longitude from the far East. Indeed, a discrepancy exists: in some tables, the longitude of Toledo <note>original: "Toleti"</note> is recorded as 11 degrees because those tables calculate from the <term>islands</term> <note>original: "insulis," referring to the Fortunate Isles or Canaries, a common medieval prime meridian</note>. In others, where that is not the case, the longitude of the same city is 28 degrees because it calculates from the West of the world. However, doubt remains regarding other locations where a similar difference is not specified.

If you wish to find the distance between regions and cities: take the difference in longitude and latitude for each, multiply each by itself, add the results together, and then find the square root <note>The author is describing the Pythagorean theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$) to find the straight-line distance between two points on a coordinate grid</note>. For every degree of the resulting root, assign 100 miles, and you will have the measurement of the journey between the cities or regions here. Furthermore, a greater longitude indicates a position further from the West, and a greater latitude indicates a position further north from the <term>equator</term> <note>original: "equatorali"</note>.

**Rule:** In the tables of longitude and latitude of cities, longitude is measured from the habitable West, and latitude from the equator toward the North. Know, therefore, that "West" is understood in two ways. One way is by taking the point from the extreme edge of the habitable land in the far West; this is called the "Habitable West," and it is 72 degrees and 30 minutes from the city of <term>Arim</term> <note>A mythical city or "World Cupola" located at the center of the world in medieval geography, derived from the Sanskrit 'Ujjayinī'</note>, which lies on the equator and is 90 degrees from the East. These tables of cities follow this "Habitable West."

The second way is the "True West," from which point there are 180 degrees to the East; in this case, Arim is exactly in the middle, 90 degrees and 30 minutes from both the East and West. Therefore, if anyone wants the longitude of cities from the True West, they should add 17 degrees and 30 minutes to the longitude given here, and they will have the longitude from the True West. And if anyone wants the longitude of these cities from the East, let them subtract the longitude given here from 172 degrees and 30 minutes, and they will have the longitude from the East. Note that for one minute of arc, the measurement corresponds to <unclear>z p 1/2 7/8 mansu</unclear> <note>Likely a reference to leagues or "mansiones," which were standard day-journey units of measurement</note>.

# The Moon

**THE MOON** is closer to the earth than all the aforementioned planets and has a shorter celestial orbit, which it completes more quickly. For while the Sun <note>The text uses "ipse" (it/he), likely referring to the Sun or the solar year</note> completes its transit through all the signs of the zodiac in one year, through degrees and minutes, the Moon completes this in one month—specifically in 27 days and 8 hours. It should be known that Saturn remains in each single sign for 30 <note>The manuscript says "diebus" (days), though Saturn actually takes about 30 years to orbit the zodiac; this is likely a scribal error or a specific calculation</note> days, 10 hours, and a half-hour, plus two points. The Moon, however, stays in one sign for two and a half days and <term>two-thirds</term> <note>original: "bisset," a technical term for two-thirds of an hour</note> of one hour. The Moon receives its highest light from the light of the sun, for it is certain that it does not have its own light, but receives it from the sun, just as the sun <unclear>shines</unclear> from the heavenly <unclear>throne</unclear> where the Trinity shines—and it is said that the sun rules the kingdoms in its aspect. The firmament <unclear>through</unclear> a <unclear>second</unclear> light reveals itself to us in various forms according to the stars; at whatever time the Moon is seen, it is the <unclear>sign</unclear> of the sun, larger than the wandering stars and brighter—behold, although it is <unclear>rightly</unclear> through the sun, it nevertheless appears to us to have a greater light and to be round, as it is said, in the middle of the sky. I say it receives the whole sign from the sun—because <unclear>like a certain daughter</unclear> <unclear>but</unclear> <unclear>from</unclear> iron and bath water, iron is in the <unclear>fire</unclear>... it has no radiance of its own but <unclear>rises</unclear> to the sound of the sun—it demonstrates its <unclear>sign</unclear> in its <unclear>age</unclear>... the Moon illuminates but <unclear>life</unclear> is not... of another... through the same fire or heat and <unclear>motion</unclear>... And the closer it is to the fire, the less <unclear>perceptible</unclear> it is. Because the lord of fire is he who inflames by his strong virtue. But if it is excluded far from the fire, it is far from that burning, and immediately becomes <unclear>perceptible</unclear> and radiating and dark, like the Moon at night and not in the day <unclear>because of the sun</unclear>...

They have said that the Moon <unclear>is</unclear> like the sun itself. But the Moon is in the middle, or at least a part of it is in the way; the Sun, diverting itself, creates various forms and shows those created forms to us. And thus he shapes her—at first so that she appears <unclear>two-horned</unclear> <note>original: "bicornis," referring to the crescent moon</note>—just as... <unclear>half</unclear>. Others have said the Moon is only like two clouds in the manner of two parts, and it becomes round like a ball—from which clouds <unclear>come</unclear> or go away. The Moon <unclear>shows</unclear> herself to the world... Others have said the Moon is a round and fiery body <unclear>suitable</unclear>... but so that it is produced from him, and as much as it <unclear>is far</unclear> from the sun, its heat is increased. For it is not when he is opposite to her... but it returns the images of the sun—which <unclear>is seen</unclear> and thus her <unclear>gift</unclear>... as the sun is first, the Moon is equal in light. If she <unclear>is placed between</unclear> the clouds... and thus they are seen to be filled. For indeed, as this Moon rises, the <unclear>ocean</unclear> is seen <unclear>to rise</unclear>... <unclear>Moisture</unclear> and every <unclear>spirit</unclear> of temporality is stirred because the ocean <unclear>is moved</unclear> by the heart <note>The author links the lunar cycle to the tides and the "humors" or fluids of the body</note>—just as in a small failing, it is seen in the soul that the genital heat is matured. For certain Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to non-Christian / Classical pagans</note> said the Moon was **Diana** and said she was what they call Apollo’s <unclear>sister</unclear>—just as Apollo [the Sun] was thought to be close to his life and the Moon close to his body—He said she was seen as a **virgin**, because she is a virgin who is depicted with horns, because as horns are movable... so she is movable. Holding the form of horns above, as this image is depicted... two <unclear>burning</unclear> horns like two <unclear>torches</unclear>. For this reason, just as the sun is held in the sky... the **lamp of the moon** shines and holds the light by which the air is clarified—as if a teacher... after the lamp of the moon... of the night in which in the darkness... when every man coming into this world is illuminated. She is depicted above... her course is made swift by night, because she is swifter in her course than the sun, and so she is depicted in a certain <term>two-horse chariot</term> <note>original: "biga"</note>... let there be one white horse, like the sea, which signifies... and soon, as it is in summer and winter, because the figure shines more clearly then in summer—in winter, and in spring, and in autumn, and in the night she <unclear>smiles</unclear>. Now the Moon is called by two modes: **Luna**, **Lucina**, and **Proserpina**, then **Diana**. She is called Diana for this reason: because she appears rightly by day as by night—

# The Nature and Influence of the Moon

The **Moon**, which shines on behalf of <term>Proserpina</term> <note>original: "serpena," likely a corruption of Proserpina, the goddess of the underworld often identified with the lunar cycle</note> as she shines in the night among those in the lower regions, is clearly fashioned in a triple night; thus it is triune. With certain of its rays, the stars appear as <term>two-ox chariots</term> <note>original: "bigas per boves"</note> for the oxen grazing on the herbs through those things which provide pasture. As the moon waxes, it undergoes a movement of operation, then through a reversal of its carriage, the same pair of oxen endures continuous labors. By drawing this sign, it relates that in the burdensome time of autumn, they are permitted to sleep; then, as if in a <unclear>glade</unclear>, they are led out to pasture.

Concerning the aforementioned oxen in the day: I shall describe one Virgin of the hour of the day, that is, the celestial and the terrestrial. As was stated above, during the increase of time, the grasses in the territories feel the worn-down <unclear>redness</unclear> through all the years, smoking with a pure moisture that grows in them, as is evident in the lands. Both by clean hands and by dirty ones in the eggs from the part of the rising, through the whole.

But regarding trees, in the waxing of the moon, it is said they might die without <unclear>growth</unclear> because they are corrupted by the <unclear>centio</unclear>; the reason is that they become hollowed out as is seen in pipes, because the moisture is not taken into the outer bark but reaches the center of the moon itself. The <term>midday storehouse</term> <note>original: "midianus armarius"</note> remains in the woods because hunters do more at night than in the day, such as wolves, foxes, and the like. Just as the owl and the unicorn, such things sleep with the <unclear>crowd</unclear> in the day, but are awake at night. Other things are of the earth today, according to the custom of others who are awake in the day and seek food. Wherefore the wolf hates the sheep; through <unclear>egaric</unclear> the birds of the day hate the birds of the night, as is clear in the fowling of the <term>zoographer</term> <note>one who depicts animals</note>. With the fowler <unclear>her mheoicorem</unclear>, it is understood by the builders that trees are ruined if they are placed in buildings after being cut, unless they are felled before that same year; they take on a <term>corolla</term> <note>a ring or decay</note> in their nature, seeking it because of weakness, as they have an abundance of the power of the seed. It is understood from the prize that there is a precious gem of wondrous virtue to be disturbed, clearly extending the movements of the moon or its variety. By excessive heat and form in the same, the <term>moon-apple</term> <note>original: "lune pomum"</note> of the day is transformed, just as the name is "Moon" which is formed through its figuration just as through demons...

# Astrology

The **Zodiac** is divided principally into twelve signs. A sign is divided into 30 degrees and into 60 minutes. A minute into 60 seconds. A second into 60 thirds, and so on. First, let us deal with the natures of the signs, and afterwards the planets. Finally, concerning the signs and their properties.

**Aries** is the <term>house</term> <note>the zodiac sign where a planet has the most influence</note> of Mars, the setting <note>fall</note> of Venus, and the <term>honor</term> <note>original: "honor," meaning the exaltation</note> of the Sun in <unclear>ag...</unclear>. ## On the nature of the seven planets and their complexions; first, on the Sun

The **Sun** is the power of the day, temperate in nature, hot and dry. It has power over the life of the soul and the entire right side of the body: the heart, the brain, and the right eye by day (but the left eye by night). It is fortunate in <term>aspect</term> <note>the geometric relationship between planets</note> when at a 3rd, 7th, or 6th position <note>likely referring to trines and sextiles</note>. It is mediocre when in <term>square</term> <note>a 90-degree angle, considered stressful</note> and unfortunate in <term>opposition</term> <note>a 180-degree angle</note>. In other positions, it is considered "fortuitous" unless in <term>combustion</term> <note>when a planet is too close to the Sun and its power is "burnt up"</note>. It is masculine. Its color is white <note>meaning bright or clear</note> and its taste is sweet. Its light extends 4 degrees before and behind it. It has power over the father and is the star of kings and rulers. Under its influence is gold, the management of kingdoms, and <unclear>high status</unclear>. Its day is Sunday. Its "years" <note>astrological periods used for prediction</note> are: Small 10 years, Mean 39, Great 120, and Greatest 1,460.

### On the complexions of the Moon

The **Moon** is the power of the night, temperate by nature, cold and moist. It holds its power relative to its square and opposition to the Sun. It signifies the mother and older sisters. It rules the stomach, the lungs, the left side of the brain, and the entire left side of the body. In the day it rules the <unclear>left</unclear> eye, and by night the right. It can signify all good things, but its nature is joined to the planet it is near. It is significant in illness, in questions, in the third house of joys, and in changes of the weather. Its metal is silver. Its "years" are: Years of trust 9, Small 24, Mean 29, Great 118, and Greatest 520.

---

Its places are madhouses, prisons, pits, and solitude. Under its influence are ruins and poisonous animals. It is an "infortune" <note>a planet that tends to bring difficulty</note>. Its power in the body is in the right ear and the spleen. Its animals are the ass and the pig; its metal is iron. Its day is Saturday and its night is Mercury's. Its "years" are: Years of trust 11, Small 30, Mean 48, Great 434, and Greatest 464.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of astrology, moving from the specific descriptions of the planets (Mars, Venus, etc.) into the geometric relationships between them, known as "aspects," and the factors that determine a planet's strength or weakness in a chart.</meta>

The aspects of the planets <note>original: "Aspectus planetarum"</note> are as follows:
First, there is the **Opposition** <note>original: "oppositiōe"</note>, when one star is seen 180 degrees away from another. This aspect is fully realized in the moon; if they possess latitude <note>distance north or south of the sun’s path</note> from one part to the other, it does not cease to be a "full" aspect. 

The second aspect is called the **Square** <note>original: "quadratu"</note>, which occurs at a distance of 90 degrees. It is called a "square" <term>quadrature</term> because it represents one-fourth part of the zodiac. This is considered an aspect of "middle light." Whether they have latitude or not, they possess this influence within a range of 4 degrees. 

The third aspect, occurring at a distance of 120 degrees, is called the **Trine** <note>original: "trina"</note>, because it represents one-third of the zodiac. This aspect is said to be "clothed in light." 

The fourth is called the **Sextile** <note>original: "sextilis"</note>; these are distant by 60 degrees, which is the sixth part of the zodiac. These four aspects are categorized as "semi-plex" according to **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Tetrabiblos" was the foundation of medieval astrology</note>. 

The square is calculated when it is at this distance. It is said that the aspect is determined by these specific degrees. For all planets in opposition, the influence is most complete within 5 degrees or perhaps 3; beyond 5 degrees, the aspect is "imperfect." Thus, the limit of an aspect's influence is generally defined within 5 degrees. However, according to the truth of the timing, one should consider the aspect for as many degrees as occur before the conjunction...

## On the variability of the planets’ strength and weakness

When two planets are joined at the same point, and they have latitude together... every planet is stronger in its own latitude. When their altitude increases, as in their <term>epicycles</term> <note>the small circular paths planets were thought to move along while orbiting the Earth</note>, even if they are 6 degrees apart, they are considered to be in conjunction. And when they are 6 degrees apart, their power is light. 

All planets, as far as the Sun is concerned, find their strength <note>original: "fortid’i"</note> increased or decreased by their distance from it. Within 6 degrees, they are "burnt" <term>combust</term> <note>when a planet is so close to the Sun it is "blinded" or weakened by its heat</note>. From 6 to 12 degrees, they are under the Sun's rays. 

From the eastern horizon up to 15 degrees, planets are called **Oriental** and are very strong. Up to 30 degrees, they are Oriental and of "moderate" strength. From 60 degrees onward, they are Oriental but "weak." At their <term>station</term> <note>the point where a planet appears to stop before moving retrograde</note>, their virtue is captured, and from there until they reach opposition with the Sun, their strength is destroyed. From opposition back to the first station, their virtue begins to return. 

At the second station, up to 30 degrees, they are **Occidental** and very strong. From 30 to 60 degrees, they are Occidental and moderate. When they fall under the "combustion" of the Sun, they are weak; from that point until they are fully "burnt," their power is destroyed. **Venus** and **Mercury** follow these rules with the Sun. When they are **retrograde** <note>appearing to move backward in the sky</note>, their power is suppressed. When Oriental, they are weaker than when they are Occidental.

## On the significations and strength of the planets

Regarding the **Moon**, its signification is that when it is moving fast, the planet’s effect is fast; when it is slow, the effect is slow. Its "moderate" speed is what it travels in one day according to its mean motion. If it travels more, it is fast; if less, it is slow. 

The **Sun**, from its <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in orbit furthest from Earth</note> to 90 degrees, is slow; if it travels more, it is moderate. All planets are stronger when ascending than when descending. For example, the Sun from **Aries** to **Cancer** is ascending, and from Cancer to **Libra** it is descending. 

Regarding the **Dragon** <term>Lunar Nodes</term> <note>the points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path; the "Head" is the North Node, the "Tail" is the South Node</note>: from the **Head of the Dragon** to 90 degrees, it is ascending; from there to the **Tail of the Dragon**, it is descending. From the Tail to 90 degrees, it is descending further toward the Head, then it begins ascending again. When a planet is with the Moon, its signification is great; if the light is small, the signification is moderate. When it is 90 degrees from its apogee, it is moderate; if more, it is great, increasing toward the opposition.

### The Twelve-Part Division

The Indians <note>A reference to the Indo-Persian "Dwadasamsa" system, where each zodiac sign is divided into twelve segments of 2.5 degrees each</note> divide the ascending sign into 12 parts, so that each part is 2 and a half degrees. With two [degrees] and a half ascending, the prediction was pronounced in the proper sign; and as they hold themselves, the other two and a half which follow, so in the progress of the prediction will be the proper measure, and so for the rest. Therefore, the 12 [divisions], at 2 and a half degrees each, show the whole of a single sign to signify judgments of good or evil... for if those two degrees are healthy... it signifies the judgment of the Latins is disposed...

<meta>This page transitions from the general meanings of the twelve houses to specific techniques for calculating the "length of life" (longevity) based on the "Givers of Life" in a birth chart. The Master of astrology says there are two **givers of life** <note>original: "vite auctores". If many planets aspect it, look to that planet which has the most "dignities" <note>original: "plures vices". And it is to be judged whether it is in its own house, or in a masculine or feminine sign. 

If the **Sun** is in the 1st, 10th, 11th, 7th, or 9th house, or if one of the lords of its sign aspects it, the calculation begins from the **Sun**. <unclear>Except</unclear> truly from the **Sun**, it is also the place of the Lord. If no one aspects it, then it is aspected when it is in a feminine sign. And when it is said <unclear>chono</unclear>, it is because it is in the 9th or 12th [house] and should not be chosen. If it is between <unclear>foler[um]</unclear> and not the ascendant, the future will be less; not if the **Sun** is not above the earth. Let someone from the lords of its sign in which it is aspect it; look to the end, and if it does not aspect, do not take it. 

If the **Sun** is in a place from which it cannot be taken, the location should be sought from the following: the 10th house or the 7th house—specifically the 7th—and let the **Moon** be aspected by either of the two lords of the sign in which she is. The calculation should be taken from her and from her lord. If she is in the sign of the **Ascendant** under the earth, such as in the 3rd house, or if she is in the 11th or 5th, and any of her lords aspects her, she is taken. 

If we find neither the **Sun** nor the **Moon** in a place from which they can be taken, look to the degree of the **conjunction** or **opposition** <note>original: "uncio[n]e... oppoiciois".
