### The Eighth House

<margin>8</margin>The Eighth House is that of death and inheritance. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> says that it is in some way a place detrimental to life, and whatever sign it may be, that sign is of an inimical nature, because a detrimental place appears in its power.

Astrologers say: if the Lord of the Eighth House is in a sign of human likeness <note>Signs of human likeness include Gemini, Virgo, Libra, and Aquarius.</note> and it is **Mars** or **Mercury**, and it is in the angle of the Ascendant or in the angle of the Lord of the Ascendant, he will die by iron <note>original: "ferro"; usually implying a sword, knife, or tool.</note> guided by a man’s hand. But if it is in a sign of a fiery nature, such as those under the light of the **Sun**, he will die by fire. If it is in a house of a watery nature, his death will be from hot water, or perhaps from hot medicine. If it is in a sign of an earthy nature, he will die by decay or burial <note>original: "pētu"; likely *putredine* or referring to being crushed by earth.</note>. 

If **Saturn** is in any angle of the sign of the Ascendant and is the Lord of the Eighth House in the Seventh <note>original: "A"; the Seventh House.</note> or the Eighth, and is in a watery sign, he will die in water. If, however, he is in a fiery sign, he will die from solitude. If he is of the nature of air, he will die from a fall from a height or from heart palpitations; or truly, a wall will collapse upon him. If he is the Lord of the Eighth House, he will die in infirmity. 

Similarly, if **Jupiter** is the Lord of the Eighth House and **Mars** aspects him; if he aspects from an opposition <term>Opposition; an aspect of 180 degrees, usually indicating conflict.</term>, he will die by a royal hand <note>By decree of a king or by execution.</note>. Likewise, the **Sun** and **Venus** are often found together; when **Venus** is the Lord of the Eighth House, it signifies a bad death. But if **Venus** is in her own proper position, death is delayed. If she is in another sign, death comes from pain in the neck <note>original: "cerui"; likely *cervix*.</note>. 

If the **Sun** and **Mercury** are found together, and **Mercury** is the Lord of the Eighth House, he will die an evil death. If in a sign of human likeness, by a man; if in a sign of a beast, by a beast; if in a sign of a water animal, by the same. Thus it is said: when **Saturn** or **Mars** is in Gemini or Pisces and is then in opposition to the **Sun**—whether by day or by night—and if it is in the angle of the Ascendant, he will die by hanging. Because if the Lord of the Eighth House is in the Eighth House and aspects him, his death will be in that place; but if he is in another house, he will die outside his own country <note>Dying in a foreign land.</note> which does not aspect it, because you ought to look at the highest point. 

For if it is in the body of a man as the **Sun**, it has great power. If the **Moon** is [aspected] by **Mars** in the Eighth or if it aspects him by a square <term>Square; an aspect of 90 degrees, considered difficult or "hard".</term>, he will die by the sword. Likewise **Mercury** in a sign of human likeness. If **Saturn** or **Mars** is the Lord of the Seventh House and is in opposition or square to the Ascendant or its Lord, death will be from a fall from a height or from drowning in the deep. And if the **Moon** so aspects the Ascendant, he will kill himself. 

Similarly, if **Saturn** is the Lord of the Fourth House and is in the Eighth House with the Lord of the Ascendant, he will be killed from on high. If the **Sun** is in the house of the [Lord] and is himself the Lord of the Ascendant, look to the nature of the sign: if it is watery, he will die in water. If the sign is of human likeness, a man causes it. If the sign of the Ascendant is a bird or Libra, and their Lords are fortunate, he will die from much thinking; if they are unfortunate, he will die because of a word he speaks, or perhaps through eating. Edm... <note>Illegible name, possibly an authority like "Edmundus" or a similar Latinized name.</note> says that when the Lord of death is in the Seventh House and is unfortunate, [he dies] from extreme excess. Because if the **Moon** is in the house of Scorpio and no one rules this in the Eighth House, and **Saturn** is direct in his path and in a high place of the small circle, he will die weary from constriction <note>original: "astactoe faessus"; likely *astrictione fessus*.</note>. If however...

->**The Gifts of the Ninth House**<-

The Ninth House <margin>9</margin> pertains to reverence, long journeys, wisdom, and philosophy. If the Lord of the Ascendant is in the ascending sign, it causes the child to be forced to make long journeys. If the Lord of the 9th house is strong, it will be good; if the Lord of the Ascendant is in the 9th house, he will go on a great journey of his own accord. If Aquarius is in the 9th house, thieves will appear on the road. If it is indeed in the 9th house at a birth by day or by night, let it be seen whether it is good or not. Wisdom is found through the 9th house, specifically through its distinction. Saturn governs geometry. Jupiter governs faith. Mars governs physics <note>original: "physicam"; in the medieval curriculum, this referred to "natural philosophy" or medicine.</note>. The Sun governs astronomy. Venus governs music. Mercury governs grammar and dialectic, and Mercury, the Lord of vigor, grants a sign of the Lord’s knowledge of physics. And of the minor planets, the Moon: hers is the reporting of what is heard or seen. And whenever Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are the Lords of these and of the Ascendant—as Mars will be for physics—it will be clear, especially if one of them is in any ascending sign.

->**The Tenth House**<-

Everything in the 10th <margin>10</margin> pertains to the mother and the arc of power. If it is a daytime birth, look at the place of Venus, which presides in the 10th house. If it is in any [unclear] and the Lord of its house does not regard it as it appears, and it is under the light of the sun, seek another life. And if the Moon is in any angle or house which is after the angles, and it appears towards the Ascendant and the Lord of that place regards it, you should take the motion from the years of the Lord in whose sign the Moon is, and lead Venus by day and the Moon by night to the place of the parents—that is, the mother. In this way, one ought to lead the degrees of the 8th and 10th houses and the "Part of the Mother" <term>Part of the Mother; a specific mathematical point in a chart calculated from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Venus.</term>, which is above Venus to the Moon by day and night, and <unclear>Angers</unclear> and it hastens the path of both degrees of the Ascendant. ### The Twelfth House

->Concerning the performance of bloodletting<-

**W**hen you wish to choose an hour for bloodletting <note>original: "sanguis minuendi"; the common medieval medical practice of withdrawing blood to balance the body's humors</note>, take care to see that the **Moon** is not in **Gemini** <note>In medical astrology, Gemini rules the arms and shoulders; it was considered dangerous to bleed a part of the body when the Moon was in the sign governing that part</note>. But ensure it is in a **sextile** <note>original: ".3."; an aspect of 60 degrees, usually considered harmonious</note> or **trine** <note>original: ".tr."; an aspect of 120 degrees, considered very favorable</note> aspect with **Mars**. However, let it not be in **conjunction** <note>original: "coniūcta"; occupying the same degree of the zodiac</note> with him by any of the aforementioned connections, nor even in a trine or **square** <note>original: "quadrato"; a 90-degree aspect, usually considered difficult or stressful</note> aspect. You should place the Moon in a sign compatible with the nature of the person being bled. If it is necessary to bleed in the <unclear>fappla</unclear> <note>likely referring to a specific vein or vessel</note> ... blood should not be let from a limb while the Moon is in the sign that governs those specific parts of the body, as assigned in the *Isagoge* <note>original: "ysagogis"; a reference to an introductory textbook on astrology, most likely the one by the 10th-century astrologer Al-Qabisi</note>. Likewise, when the Moon is in **Leo**, new clothing should not be worn. One wishing to give <term>electuaries</term> <note>medicinal pastes or syrups mixed with honey or sugar</note> should ensure the Moon is not in aspect with **Venus** or her companions... but an aspect with **Mars** harms little. But it is better in that part which is in aspect... it is better through the aforementioned sextile than in **Scorpio**; or let it be in **Cancer** or **Pisces**. See that it does not give the Lord of the part... as it will be above the earth. Nor should you wait for the sign... when the Moon is below the earth from the part of the **Ascendant** <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon</note>. But one wishing to choose a house to live in should ensure the Moon is in the house of **Saturn** or **Mercury**, with a sextile or other aspect of Mercury... provided that Mercury is not **retrograde** <note>appearing to move backward in the sky, which was thought to weaken a planet's influence</note>, nor in the <unclear>forz</unclear>, nor with the **Sun**, as a fortunate planet is better. It is better if the Ascendant is one of the houses of Mercury... or better yet that it appears as a canine <note>likely a reference to the dog-star, Sirius, or a specific constellation</note>.

->Concerning purchasing and profits<-

**O**ne wishing to buy something for <unclear>profit</unclear> should buy when the **Moon** is in the great part of the <term>triplicity</term> <note>original: "treaci"; a group of four sets of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water)</note> which extends from the head of **Aries** to the end of **Sagittarius**. It is better to have an aspect with the **Part of Fortune** <note>original: "pte for."; a mathematical point in a chart representing success and prosperity</note>, or a sextile or trine aspect with the **Sun**. Beware that it is not "under the rays" of the Sun <note>original: "sub lucē solis"; a planet is considered weakened or 'combust' when it is too close to the Sun's light</note>. It is better that the **Lord of the Ascendant** gives conjunction to a planet that is in the **10th house** <note>The house of career and public standing</note>... nor should it be received if it is retrograde. Let there be a planet in the Ascendant, or in the 11th or 2nd house, which are good. See where the Part of Fortune is in a good house... or better yet where the Lord of that part is in aspect with the Sun or Moon.

For wearing new clothes. A middling journey. A woman sleeping in this, though previously living or moving [well], will remain a widow. Buying slaves... which is increased in the space of bloodletting.

**Twenty-second**, called the Shepherd <note>Sa'd al-Dhabih, the Lucky One of the Slaughterer</note>. The <term>Indians</term> say it is good for medicine and sewing new clothes. Bloodletting is good. If one sleeps there or <unclear>sspsē</unclear>, they will not be recognized. If a messenger is sent, within three months he will die. The wife will be fiery. In this mansion, a fleeing slave will return to one's hands. Bad for buying slaves. A journey by fire <note>perhaps referring to heat or extreme speed</note>. Good for medicines. Captives will escape quickly. 22.

**Twenty-third**, [called] the Swallower <note>Sa'd al-Bula</note>. The <term>Indians</term> say it is good for medicine, sewing new clothes, and working iron. A good journey... Bad for the beginning of custody. A sleeper... regarding his wife... bad for buying slaves. Ships will be good. Good in [love/friendship]. The silent will quickly escape. 24.

**Twenty-fourth** [mansion, Sa'd al-Su'ud] says it is bad for buying, wearing new clothes, and taking a wife. Good for medicinal expenditures... sending [messengers]. A sleeper... of the father... ships will profit little. In bad causes... good for buying servants. There will be strong children. A captive will escape well. 25.

**Twenty-fifth**, [called] the Butterfly <note>Sa'd al-Akhbiya, the Lucky Star of the Tents</note>. The <term>Indians</term> say it is good for besieging cities... sending [messengers]... sewing, taking a wife, and sowing. A sleeper... good for buying slaves. There will be strong faith... sewing, a journey by sea... bad in lawsuits. A captive escapes slowly. 26.

**Twenty-sixth**, [called] the First Wall <note>Al-Fargh al-Muqdim, the Front Spout of the Bucket</note>. The <term>Indians</term> say it is bad for medicine, but good for a journey. A sleeper... soon to be deserted... good for buying slaves. There will be faith and investigation. Good in a cause for taking a ship, as they will not return late. In a bad cause, a captive does not escape. 27.

**Twenty-seventh**, [called] the Second Wall <note>Al-Fargh al-Thani, the Rear Spout</note>. The <term>Indians</term> say it is good for buying, stealing <note>perhaps meaning 'taking back' or 'raiding'</note>, and taking a wife. On a journey, it is only middling. Good for medicine... buying [slaves]... a sleeper [sees] that ships should be rebuilt. Bad in serving... captives escape slowly. 28.

**Twenty-eighth**, called the Tooth of the Fish <note>Al-Risha, the Cord, or Batn al-Hut, the Belly of the Fish</note>. The <term>Indians</term> say it is good for buying, making, and taking a wife. A sleeper's day is middling. Ships will be hindered... buying slaves. He will be in prison... falling at the end into evil. From prison they escape slowly.

**It is noted** from what has been said that it is necessary that the Moon should not be in the square <note>a 90-degree aspect, traditionally considered difficult</note> of the Sun... or opposite to it. Good for medicine... and buying slaves.

**The beginning** [of the mansions] is manifest... in the 12 houses <unclear>ap dī2</unclear>... in each mansion which is strong. ...the mansions according to the tables... in the circle of the straight [zodiac] in the 12 signs... in the time of **March 21, 1142**.

### In the name of the Lord, amen, the merciful and pious. Here begins the book of Messahalah on the astrolabe, containing 40 chapters. <note>Messahalah (Masha'allah ibn Athari, c. 740–815) was a Persian Jewish astronomer whose work on the astrolabe was the primary source for European knowledge on the subject for centuries.</note>

Chapter 1: On the purpose of the astrolabe and the names of the parts arranged upon it.
Chapter 2: On the equation of the sun, which is its position in the circle of the signs <note>the Zodiac</note>.

Chapter 4: On taking the altitude of the sun during the day and the altitude of the fixed stars at night.

Chapter 6: On the knowledge of the equal hours of the night and those stars which have passed, and the knowledge of the ascendant both by day and night.
Chapter 7: On the knowledge of the two hours [of twilight] preceding sunrise.
Chapter 8: On taking the arc of the day and night for any given degree.
Chapter 9: On the knowledge of the parts of these hours during the day and night.
Chapter 10: On taking the portion of the hour that has passed with certainty.
Chapter 11: To know how many equal hours there are in the day and night.
Chapter 12: To know how many equal hours have passed both in the day and the night.
Chapter 13: Concerning the conversion of unequal hours into equal ones, and equal into unequal.
Chapter 14: On the knowledge of the altitude of the sun at midday and the altitude of the fixed stars.
Chapter 15: Concerning the same.

Chapter 17: On the knowledge of an unknown day through the degree of the sun... <note>finding the calendar date from astronomical observations</note> in winter.
Chapter 18: To know at what hour any degree of the circle of signs rises or sets, or any of the stars placed on the <term>rete</term>, or when it will be on the line of the mid-heaven <note>the meridian</note>.
Chapter 19: On identifying stars which you do not know from the stars that are positioned on the astrolabe.
Chapter 20: To know which degree is in the mid-heaven for whichever star you wish, and with which degree it rises or sets.
Chapter 21: On the knowledge of the <term>azimuth</term> <note>compass direction</note> of the East or West, North or South, [as calculated for] Cordoba.

# Chapter One begins: On the Purpose of the Astrolabe and the marks existing upon it

The first of these is the ring <note>the suspension ring</note> upon which the **astrolabe** is suspended to take altitudes. After this is another rotating ring <note>a swivel or shackle</note> which is joined to the outer edge. Following this comes the <term>mater</term> <note>the "mother," the thick outer plate of the astrolabe</note>, which is the larger plate containing all the other plates within itself. In its circumference is the <term>limbus</term> <note>the rim or border</note>, which is divided into 360 <unclear>degrees</unclear> with Arabic letters written upon it designating the numbers, so that it may be used more easily and without labor.

Inside this are the plates; on each plate are circles [drawn] from the central point of the plate. The smaller one passes through [the tropics of] Capricorn and Cancer—this is called the equinoctial circle—and through the larger one passes the head of Capricorn <note>the Tropic of Capricorn</note>.

There are written the <term>almukantarat</term> <note>almucantars; circles of altitude</note>, which are circles like bows described on the part of the plate with the signs. Some Latins call these "parallels." The first of these is the horizon circle, which divides the upper part of the circles from the lower—the part <unclear>per medium</unclear> that is seen above from that which is beneath the earth and is not seen. The point in the middle of these circles is the zenith <note>original: "centauro hor", likely a corruption of "zenith" or "centrum horarum"</note>: that part of the sky which is directly above one's head.

After these are the azimuths, which are parts of the circles that intersect the <term>almukantarat</term>. Furthermore, there are lines set apart... hidden among the hours are five lines. One is established to designate a certain hour for <note>likely "fajr", the dawn prayer</note> after the midday, and two others for the two evening times, the first and second. Two others are placed in the upper part to show the rising of the dawn and the setting of the sun at night.

Then there is the line that circles the ring and passes through the middle point of the plate's center; its upper part, which is above the horizon, is called the midheaven <note>medium coelum</note> or the meridian line, where the midheaven ends. The part below the horizon is the line of the "angle of the earth" and is called the midnight line, which is similar to the western line.

Next follows the <term>Alhankabut</term> <note>the Rete; literally "the Spider"</note>, whose interpretation is "the spider." It is an openwork plate in which the signs and stars are placed. The northern signs among them are those above the center... [from] the sign of the Bear <note>Ursa Major</note> to the end of Virgo. The southern signs are those which move with the head of Capricorn.

After this is the *Al-muri* <note>original: "album", likely "Al-muri", the pointer</note>, called the "pointer" in the Arabic language, which some Latin calculators have called the "indicator." It is the little tooth placed at the head of Capricorn to identify the degrees.

Next, the <term>almahuar</term> is the hole in the middle of the rete in which the axis <note>the central pin</note> holds the plates, and the "horse" <note>a wedge shaped like a horse's head</note> which retains it. On the back of the astrolabe are certain circles...

...of the months, upon which the divisions of the circles are arranged according to the number of the days of the year. But on some astrolabes, they are divided simply; on others, they are divided by twos. And two are placed together after that which contains one space so that the days may be found more easily. Next follow the names of the **twelve signs** <note>original: "duodecim signorum"; the signs of the zodiac</note>, under which is written the number of degrees for each sign in groups of five. And above the written degrees of the circle, a line is marked out below which the number of degrees is written in the heart <note>likely referring to the center-line of the scale</note>, divided so that each part of the astrolabe may be observed, and so on. It should be known that this is for taking the altitude of the sun and so forth. After this is the fourth part of the altitude scale, which is on the side facing the sun when the astrolabe is suspended for taking a measurement. Then the quadrant on its lower side is divided into 12 parts; each of these is called an *isba* <note>original: "arabice ista"; a corruption of the Arabic "al-isba," meaning "finger"</note> in Arabic, and in Latin it is called a **digit** <note>original: "digitum"</note>, which we can also call "points." Next is the **alidade** <note>original: "allidada"; the revolving sighting rule on the back of the instrument</note>, which is moved over the back of the astrolabe. At the ends of this rule are two upright plates, and they are perforated; indeed, in each of them are two holes... for the rays of the sun to pass through to find its altitude, and afterwards for the large fixed stars at night.

## Chapter 2: On finding the Sun’s position in the circle of signs

If you wish to know in which sign the sun is and how many degrees of it the sun has traveled, count how many days have passed in the Latin month <note>the Roman/Julian calendar month</note>... place the rule over that day in the circle of months, and where the rule falls in the circle of signs will be the degree in which the sun is, and the sign it is in. You will also find the knowledge of the day by doing the reverse: by placing the rule over the degree of the sun in the sign it is in, it will show you the day you wish.

## Chapter 3: On knowing the degree of the sun and the nadir in the circle of signs for a given day in summer

The method for this is to equalize the point as you have learned. To find how many degrees it has traveled in the same sign, place the sign... in the circle of signs which is positioned on the rotation... as if you take the day and degree in the month of September. According to the point where the sun is in that sign, you then find the **nadir** <note>original: "nadir"; the point on the zodiac directly opposite the sun's current position, 180 degrees away</note>, which is the opposite point of the same sign. For this calculation, you count the sign in which the sun is and the subsequent signs until the seventh sign, which is the opposite. When you have done this, take the same number of degrees that the sun had in its sign and apply that number to the opposite sign; that will be the nadir of the sun's position.

## Chapter 4: On taking the altitude of the sun by day and the stars by night

When you wish to know the altitude of the sun, suspend the astrolabe from your hand by the **ring** <note>original: "armillam"</note> so it hangs freely. Turn the head of the rule toward the sun until the sun's rays enter through the holes of the upper plate and fall exactly upon the holes opposite them in the lower plate. When you have done this, look to see how many degrees the rule is raised on the quadrant scale. The number of degrees will be the altitude of the sun above the horizon. To find the altitude of the stars at night, suspend the astrolabe as described before and look at the star through the holes in the plates until you see it through both. When you have done this, the rule will show you its altitude just as it showed the altitude of the sun.

## Chapter 5: On the knowledge of unequal hours

If you wish to know this, take the altitude of the sun as described. Then move the **rete** <note>original: "reete"; the pierced star-map plate on the front of the astrolabe</note> until the point representing the sun's degree is placed upon the **almucantar** <note>original: "amilkantarāt"; lines of altitude engraved on the stationary plate beneath the rete</note> that matches the altitude you measured.

# Chapter 67: On the knowledge of the unequal hours of the night by the passage of the fixed stars through the signs.

When you wish to know how much of the night has passed in **unequal hours** <note>original: "horis inequalibus"; hours that vary in length based on the season, as opposed to fixed 60-minute clock hours</note> by the altitude of any of the **fixed stars** <note>original: "stelle fixxe"</note> positioned upon the **rete** <note>original: "rete"; the rotating star-map on the front of the astrolabe</note>, first identify the star. Afterward, move the rete until the point of the star falls upon the almucantars at the representation of its own altitude. If you took the altitude of the star in the west, place it specifically upon the western almucantars. If it was in the east, place it upon the eastern almucantars. However, if it was in the midheaven, leave it be and choose one of the stars that is currently in the west or the east. Specifically note where the degree of the sun falls upon the hour-lines; that will be the amount of the night that has passed in unequal hours. The **ascendant** will be whatever is upon the eastern horizon, and the **midheaven** will be whatever is upon the line of the midheaven... just as you did during the night, and at the rising of the **dawn** <note>original: "aurora"</note> in the morning.

# Chapter on the knowledge of the three hours in which the Saracens proceed after the midday of the day, etc.

You will then have the degree opposite the sun's degree. Place the hours upon its house and upon the lines established for this purpose... If you wish to know the same during the night or at the rising of the dawn, take the altitude of any fixed star placed upon the rete. If the **nadir** of the sun's degree falls upon the eastern almucantar established for this on the astrolabe, then it is **twilight** <note>original: "assafro"; likely from the Arabic *al-shafaq*</note>. This is that redness which is seen in the air after the setting of the sun; and this is certainly the hour of the morning of the night, if [the star is in the east].

## Chapter 8: Concerning the calculation of the arc of the day and night for any given degree

When you wish to determine the arc of the day and night, which are 360 degrees in the whole circle, 
place the degree of the sun in the sign in which it resides and place upon it the point which the makers 
intended to be the sun. For this purpose, as you find it, let it be supported by the eastern **horizon** <note>original: "emissij"; referring to the horizon line on the astrolabe</note> 
and see what is on the edge of the **rim** <note>original: "dūreto/mabre"; likely referring to the *limbus* or the graduated outer edge of the instrument</note>. Then, before you move the point from the horizon, mark it 
upon the rim. That is, place a mark upon it. After this, move the **rete** <note>the rotating star-map plate of the astrolabe</note> until the 
point of the sun's degree which you marked reaches the line of the western horizon. After this, 
look at the number which the **indicator** <note>original: "almut/almuri"; the small pointer on the rete</note> has traversed. From this movement of the point from the east to the west, 
whatever that number is, it will be the arc of the day. And whatever remains in the circle <note>the remaining degrees of the 360-degree rim</note> 
will be the arc of the night; and if you subtract one from the other, the larger number will be the length of that time. And if 
you wish to determine the arc of the night before the arc of the day, place the point of the sun's degree upon the line 
of the western horizon, and do just as you did for the arc of the day. And the number established for 
each individual part is the division of the space of the day and night. This division is 
360 degrees, according to the tradition of the philosophers. If one wishes to find the arc of the day for any 
possible position, just as the <term>taltabio</term> <note>original: "taltabio"; likely a corruption of *astrolabio* (astrolabe) or a specific reference to an astronomical table</note> establishes, and the arc of the night for it and its appearance above 
the earth, and you wish to know its setting, proceed just as you did for the degree of the sun.

## Chapter 9: Knowledge of the parts of one unequal hour from the hours of day and night

When you wish to know the hour, you must know the arc of the day and night. Divide whichever you wish by 
12, which is the number of unequal hours <note>the day and night were each divided into 12 hours regardless of season, meaning a "day hour" in summer was longer than in winter</note>, for both day and night. If you have divided the true arc, you will have the answer. If 
you have divided its arc, you will find the degrees of one hour of the day. Subtract them 
from 30, and whatever remains will be the number of degrees for one hour of the night. Do the same for the 
degrees of one hour of the night, and therefore they are subtracted from 30. Because the degrees of two hours—one of day 
and one of night—when collected together will be 30. This is the number of degrees for two 
equal hours. And if some of these unequal hours are subtracted from the equal hours, it is required 
in the other. And if you wish to reach the knowledge of the degrees of the hours without knowing the arcs of the hours, 
by placing the <term>nadir</term> <note>the point directly opposite the sun's position on the zodiac</note> of the sun's degree upon the line of whichever hour you wish. Then 
place a mark upon the location of the **indicator** <note>original: "almert/almuri"</note> on the rim. After this, you shall move the nadir until it falls 
upon the hour line. Then you will know how far the indicator has moved from where it was 
on the rim, to the place where it has then arrived. And whatever that distance is, it will be the 
degrees of one hour of that day. Do this by the nadir of the sun at night just as you did 
by the nadir during the day. And knowing this, you will find the degrees of one hour to be 30, and the 
remainder will be the degrees of the other hour, as was said before.

## Chapter 10: On finding the fractions of the hour that have passed during the day

When some part of any hour has passed and you wish to know how much of it has passed, 
place a mark upon the location of the **indicator** <note>original: "almutz/almuri"</note>. After this, turn your indicator to the beginning 
of the hour, and know how many degrees the indicator is distant from the mark. And know those degrees relative to the degrees of one 
hour of day or night, whichever it may be. Whatever it is, that will be the part which has passed.

### Chapter 11: To know how many hours and their parts have passed by the transit.

<margin>11</margin>
<margin>Vatican Apostolic Library</margin>
**W**hen you wish to know how many **equal hours** <note>hours of exactly 60 minutes, as opposed to seasonal "unequal" hours</note> there are of the day and night at whatever time you wish, divide all the minutes you wish by 15, and the result will be the number of degrees of one equal hour. And you will know how many there are in that part of the day. If, however, you wish to know the equal hours of the time of day or night thereafter, and to know their minutes, divide them by 15, and what remains will be the minutes of the hours. This is another method for itself.

### Chapter 12: To know how many hours have passed in the day and in the night

<margin>12</margin>
**W**hen you wish to know how many equal hours have passed of the day or the night, take the altitude of the sun. If it is during the day, find its degree and place it upon its corresponding **almucantar** <note>altitude line</note> on either the eastern or western side, as you know. After this, if the sign of the sun is set, mark the **almuri** <note>the indicator</note> on the **rim** <note>original: "limbo"; the graduated outer edge of the astrolabe</note>; then note the degree of the sun. Move the rete until you place it upon the line of the eastern horizon <note>original: "lineam emissis orientalis"</note> because that is the place of its rising in the middle of the day. After this, see how many degrees the *almuri* has moved across the degrees of the rim from its first position to its position on the eastern line. However many degrees the *almuri* has traveled from the hour of the sun's rising until the hour in which you took the altitude, divide that number by 15, and the result will be the equal hours that have passed in the day. Use the same method at night. You shall take the altitude of some star and place its point <note>the "head" or pointer for that star on the rete</note> upon its corresponding altitude in the **almucantars** <note>altitude circles</note>. If the location of the *almuri* is in the part where the degree of the sun meets the western horizon line, which is the place of its setting during the night—count all the degrees the *almuri* has traveled along the degrees of the rim and divide by 15; the result will be how many equal hours have passed. And if you wish to know at night how many equal hours have passed since the true dawn, take the altitude of a star as described above, place the star upon its altitude, and mark the position of the *almuri* on the rim. Afterwards, move the degree of the sun until it falls upon the **al-fajr** <note>original: "al feger"; from the Arabic for dawn, the start of morning twilight</note> almucantar, and know how much the *almuri* has moved across the degrees on the rim. Divide by 15, and the resulting hours will be the time between your current hour and the true dawn in equal degrees.

### Chapter 13: Concerning the calculation of unequal hours in terms of equal hours, and how many unequal hours there are.

<margin>13</margin>
**W**hen you wish to know the length of one **unequal hour** <note>also called "seasonal" hours; these divide daylight and darkness into 12 hours each, meaning they vary in length depending on the time of year</note> on any day you wish in terms of equal hours, know the degree of the sun on that same day. Then place the degree of the sun upon the line of the western hemisphere if it is an unequal hour of the day. Mark the position of the *almuri* on the rim and turn the degree of the sun to the end of the hours you wish to note. In this, it must be known and calculated how much the *almuri* moved across the degrees of the rim; divide this by 15, and the result will be the number of equal hours coming from the unequal hours of the night. If, however, there are unequal hours of the night, do everything as has been said, but using the **nadir** <note>the point 180 degrees opposite the sun’s current position</note>. Furthermore, if you wish to know equal hours from unequal ones, whether in the day or night, know the degree of the sun. If the daylight hours are sought, place the **nadir** of the sun upon the western horizon line, then mark the position of the *almuri* on the rim, and turn everything very carefully to the degree of the hour, multiplying the result by 15 to know what comes out.

### Chapter 12: On knowing the altitude of the sun at midday

When you wish to know the altitude of the sun at midday: Place the degree of the sun (calculated for that specific time) upon the line of the **midheaven** <note>original: "medij celi"; the meridian line representing the highest point in the sky</note>, and see upon which altitude the degree of the sun falls among the **almucantars** <note>original: "almuthantharat"; circles of altitude marked on the astrolabe plate</note>. This is its altitude at midday on that day. You will do the same for any calculation you wish to make, such as its highest altitude at the end of midday, by placing it upon the end point and observing the altitude where it falls among the **almucantars**; this will be the highest altitude possible in your region on that day.

### Chapter 13: On the same topic

Since the arcs of the signs are divided into two halves: one of which is taken as the winter solstice <note>original: "uernate," likely a scribal error for "hiemale" or "brumale" as it is paired with the summer solstice</note>. The beginning of **Cancer** is noted as the summer solstice. Every degree that is a shorter distance from either of the solstices [shares the same] declination. To the northern regions, as to the meridian, there will be a specific length of the day, and each of them will have an equal magnitude to the other, and similarly for the length of the night and the shadow of the movements. Thus, the altitude at midday will always be equal where the degree is the same, such as in **Capricorn** and the bottom of **Scorpio**. Similarly, if the degree of the sun is found in one of the signs and its distance from the solstice is equal, the signs will appear equal.

### Chapter 14: On knowing the degree of the sun on any given night

When you wish to know this, place a mark on the **almucantar** for the altitude of the middle of the night for the day you wish, holding it over the midday line <note>the meridian</note> according to that night's altitude, and move the **rete** <note>the rotating star-map of the astrolabe</note>. Then it must necessarily fall upon the mark at two degrees of the circle of signs, one of which will be from one of the solstices. Then you will see which one is in its course; and if you wish to know which quarter it is in, see if it is the vernal or the summer [quarter].

### Chapter 15: Concerning the day, the night, the degree of the sun, and the renewals of the signs

When you wish to know this, equate the sun to the known day and set the degree where it was. After this, look for the other degree whose distance from the solstice is the same as the distance of this degree of the night. And at midday, just as it was at the other midday. And to this end, you shall perform the calculation for the unknown part as it appears to you.

### Chapter 19: On identifying stars that you do not know, using known stars already placed on the astrolabe.

### Chapter 20: To know when a star you choose is in the midheaven, and at which degree it rises or sets.

### Chapter 21: To know the azimuth of the east or west, namely by the meridian of Córdoba.

Take, on the back of the instrument, the corresponding number of those degrees in the same quarter. It must follow that this is either the south-eastern, north-eastern, south-western, or north-western quarter, according to the movement of the different hemispheres in the four parts [of the world]. Do this by placing the tip of the **rule** <note>the sighting bar</note> over the number of those degrees from that same quarter. 
Then, place the opposite plate <note>the side of the astrolabe</note> that follows the tip of the rule upon one degree of the sun's ray, until the shadow is aligned upon the rule without it moving from its place. ### Chapter 21: Concerning the knowledge of the distance of each degree of the signs to be noted on the **equinoctial circle** <note>the celestial equator</note> through the movement of the first point of **Aries** and **Libra**.

When you wish to know this, place the [zodiacal] degree upon the **meridian line** <note>the line of mid-day</note> and know at what altitude it falls. Then know where the equinoctial circle is through the movement of the start of Aries and Libra from the altitude on the meridian line. Take the value that is between both altitudes; if the degree is <unclear>smaller</unclear> from the equinox of the day, as if the degree were from the northern signs, it will always be higher at mid-day than the equinoctial circle by the same amount that was between both of them. 

However, the degree of the southern signs will always be lower at mid-day than the equinoctial circle by that same amount that was between both of them. For Aries and Libra themselves serve as the <unclear>designation</unclear> because their movement does not deviate from the equinoctial circle. The greatest **declination** <note>the angular distance of a body north or south of the celestial equator</note> occurs at the beginning of **Cancer** and **Capricorn** <note>the solstices</note>. 

When you have found the declination of that same degree, and you wish to extract the position of any star, [move] the astrolabe by the part of the star's "head" over the meridian line and find its altitude there. Take that which is between its altitude and the altitude of the equinoctial circle, whether it be southern or northern.

### Chapter 24: To know the hour of the day by the azimuth which presents itself on the back

When you wish to know the hour, given the sun's altitude at midday of that day in that same region as previously established: after this, place the <term>rule<note>The 'rule' or alidade is the rotating sighting bar on the back of the astrolabe used to measure angles.</note></term> in the altitude quadrant upon its likeness. Suspend the astrolabe by its <term>ring<note>original: "armilla"; the ring at the top by which the instrument is held to hang vertically.</note></term> and show the upper plate to the sun, doing so for the recorded altitude. Move the astrolabe until the shadow of the plate falls downward onto the rule so that it does not exceed it, in the same manner you would do when taking the <term>azimuth<note>original: "azymut"; the horizontal direction of a celestial object, measured as an angle from the north or south.</note></term>. To whichever of the descending hour lines the shadow reaches, that shall be the hour of the day, if you took the reading before midday. If you took it after midday, subtract the resulting shadow from the hours of the day.

### Chapter 25: On longitude and azimuth

Know that <term>longitude<note>original: "longitudo"</note></term> is the distance between the midday of your region and the midday of another region, measured in degrees of the <term>equinoctial circle<note>original: "circuli equinoctialis"; the celestial equator.</note></term>. When you wish to know the longitude between two regions, it is necessary that you observe the middle of an <term>eclipse<note>original: "eclipis"</note></term> of the sun or moon. You must know the equation of the hour between the preceding midday and the hour the eclipse was recorded, so that you know it in both regions; and of those hours, you shall know how much time passes between the hour in one eclipse and the sum of those hours between midday in each of the regions, in equal hours. Convert that number into degrees as it is, multiply it by 15, and the resulting number will be the longitude between the two regions. 

**Ptolemy** <note>original: "Ptholomeus"</note> collected in this book, which is called the ***Almagest*** <note>original: "algeanastige"; a corruption of the Arabic "al-Majisti," referring to Ptolemy’s great astronomical work.</note>, the longitudes of known cities. He also provided their <term>latitude<note>original: "latitudo"</note></term>, how far their <term>zenith<note>original: "azimut capitu"; literally "azimuth of the head," referring to the point directly overhead.</note></term> is from the equinox in the northern region, and the longitudinal distances through the midday line of the regions.

### Chapter 26: To know the azimuth of the region you have asked about from your own region’s azimuth, and the longitude of its zenith:—

When you wish to know the azimuth of a region whose longitude and latitude are known relative to the region you are observing from: Know the latitude of the region you are asking about and place a mark on the plate of your region on the midday line, at its likeness in the northern part from the equinox. This shall be the latitude of the region you are asking about. When you have done this, move it until the mark falls upon the <unclear>noctam</unclear>. Then place a sign on the correct part which falls upon the mark. After this, move the mark to the opposite place <unclear>alhay</unclear> <note>These terms likely refer to specific markings or components on the astrolabe plate, such as the "almucantars" or specific coordinates.</note>. 

When you have done this, know what is upon the <unclear>flumem</unclear> between your region and the marked region, according to the longitude found in the book of ***Geography*** <note>original: "algearafie"; likely referring to a medieval Latin translation of a geographic text like that of Al-Khwarizmi or Ptolemy.</note>. If the longitude of the region is greater than your region’s longitude, it is undoubtedly to the East. Then move the <term>almucantars<note>original: "almencantharat"; the circles of equal altitude drawn on the astrolabe plate.</note></term> through the number of degrees in the borders from their place in the Eastern part, according to the difference between the two longitudes. If the longitude of the region is less than your region’s longitude, it is without doubt to the West. Then move the <term>almucantars</term> from their place in the Western part according to the number between both.

### Chapter 28: On the knowledge of shadows from altitude

Know that in the <term>quadrant<note>The "shadow square" usually found on the back of an astrolabe, used for surveying and height calculations.</note></term> which is placed on the back of the astrolabe, there are two divided sides, each of which is divided into twelve parts. One of these divisions is called what in Latin sounds like a <term>digit<note>original: "digitus"; literally "finger." A standard unit in medieval shadow calculations where a gnomon is assumed to be 12 digits high.</note></term>, and we can also call it a "point." Furthermore, the side that goes outward is the side of the <term>extended shadow<note>original: "umbre extense"; the horizontal shadow cast on the ground by an object.</note></term>. And the same side which is higher is the side of the <term>vertical shadow<note>original: "umbre verse"; the shadow cast on a vertical surface, like a wall.</note></term>. Therefore, when you wish to know how many points are in a shadow: Take the altitude of the sun, and if the altitude is 45 degrees, the extended shadow will be 12 points, and likewise for any similar thing. And if the altitude is more, the <term>rule<note>The alidade or sighting bar.</note></term> will fall upon and be smaller on the side of the extended shadow. If indeed it is less, the rule at 45 degrees will fall upon the side of the vertical shadow. Look and see upon how many points the rule falls, for that itself will be the vertical shadow. Therefore, if you wish to know the extended shadow of this altitude, divide 144 by the points which you have from the vertical shadow, and what results will be the number of points of the extended shadow for that same altitude. Likewise, if the altitude is more than 45 degrees and you wish to know the points of the vertical shadow, divide 144 by the points you have from the extended shadow, and what results is the number of points of the vertical shadow of that altitude. And likewise, divide 144 by the points of one shadow and the points of the other will result, because the multiplication of the points of the extended shadow of any altitude by the points of the vertical shadow of any altitude equals 144. And this is the number 144 because twelve multiplied by itself is 12 times 12, which is the number of points of the scales in themselves. When you wish to know how many <term>statures<note>original: "statux" (staturas); a unit of measure based on the height of a man.</note></term> are in a shadow, divide the points of the shadow you have by 12, and however many divisions result, that is how many statures are in it. And if the shadow is less than a stature, it shall be named by its parts. If it falls upon a fraction of a point and you wish to know that fraction, place a mark upon the place where the rule falls in the inner quadrant... after this, move the rule until it falls upon the beginning of the point, and place a mark at the tip of the rule, and look how many degrees are between both marks and save them. Then move the rule from the beginning of the point until it falls upon the end of it, and see upon how many degrees its tip falls... and what that is will be the fraction you wish to know, if God wills.

When wishing to know what the altitude of the sun is from the <term>extended shadow<note>original: "umbra extensa"; the horizontal shadow cast on a flat surface, usually measured when the sun is more than 45 degrees high.</note></term>, first find how many <term>points<note>original: "punctos"; the shadow square is typically divided into 12 units or "digits."</note></term> there are. If it is 12 points or fewer, place the <term>rule<note>original: "regulam"; the alidade or sighting arm on the back of the astrolabe.</note></term> over the number of points of the shadow in the "extended shadow" section. Then, look to see upon which degree of altitude the rule falls in the upper quadrant. Whatever that number is will be the altitude of the sun for that shadow. Through the altitude of the sun, you may know the hour, if you so desire. 

And if there are more than 12 points, divide them by 12; the result will be the number of points for the <term>versed shadow<note>original: "umbra versa"; the vertical shadow cast against a wall, measured when the sun is low.</note></term>. To find the altitude, then place the rule over the number of points on the side of the versed shadow. Whatever degree its tip falls upon in the altitude scale, that will be the altitude of the sun for that shadow.

If, however, it is the versed shadow and you wish to know the altitude, and the number of points is 12: place the rule over the number of points on the side which is the "versed shadow" side. And thus the rule will show you the altitude; because when you know this, you will know the hour if you wish. 

If there are more than 12 points, divide 149 <note>original: "cxlviiii"; this may be a scribal error for 144, which is 12 squared, a common constant in these calculations.</note> by them, and the result will be the points of the extended shadow. To find the altitude, place the rule over that number; the extended shadow will result. After this you will know the altitude. 

If the measurement is in points and fractions, and you wish to know the portion of the rule over the fraction in those points, it is necessary that you place the rule at the beginning of the point from which the fraction comes, and place a mark at its tip in the lower quadrant. Move the rule to the end of that point and take from those degrees a likeness of that same fraction. Hold the rule until you place it over the previous mark according to the quantity of the degrees of the fraction. And in this way, the rule will be set over the desired fraction of the points.

### Chapter 30: On the midday shadow, which is the truest shadow, and on the two hours that occur around midday in every day of the year.

When wishing to know the midday shadow for a given day, equate the sun for that same hour. Once you know its degree, find what the midday altitude of that degree is according to what was explained previously. Then find the shadow of that altitude; whatever it is will be the truest points of the midday shadow on that day. 

To find the start of the hour called <term>al-Asr<note>original: "alazare"; the Islamic afternoon prayer time.</note></term>—which is one of the two hours in which the <term>Saracens<note>original: "saracei"; a medieval European term for Muslims.</note></term> pray after midday—and for the end of those hours: you should add three points (which is a quarter of a "status" or the height of a man) to the midday shadow, which is the truest shadow, and that will be the shadow at the hour of <term>al-Zuhr<note>original: "ad dork"; likely a corruption of al-Zuhr, the midday prayer.</note></term>. You shall add 7 points to the midday shadow for the beginning of the *al-Asr* hour, and 19 points for the end of the hour. Then, calculate the points of the extended shadow for that hour and for *al-Asr*. Use the <term>nadir<note>original: "nadir"; the point on the zodiac directly opposite the sun's current position.</note></term> of the sun's degree to find the altitude in the <term>almucantars<note>original: "almukantarat"; the lines of altitude on the front of the astrolabe.</note></term>. Similarly, the altitude of the sun will be found for the start of the *al-Zuhr* hour, and through it the shadow points are known as best as they can be. You shall do the same for the start of the *al-Asr* hour and for the end of the hour by the altitude, because once the extended shadow is known, you will know the hours through them.

### Chapter 32: In these matters, how you may know the day you are in through only a known altitude and azimuth.

When you wish to know the position on the astrolabe, and the <term>azimuth<note>original: "azumut"; the horizontal direction of a celestial body measured clockwise from north.</note></term> is placed on it so that it matches your inquiry in the <term>almucantar<note>original: "alimukantarat"; the circles of altitude on the astrolabe plate.</note></term>. Move the azimuth correctly through this; here it is necessary that you arrange two known locations by means of the rising of the signs, the longitude of which will be one from the other—that is, further out. Know also the degree of each day on the days when this will be known and completed. ### Chapter 33: In these matters, concerning the height of towers and other things that rise above the earth.

When you wish to know the height of an object by using the <term>rule<note>original: "regulam"; the alidade or sighting arm on the back of the astrolabe.</note></term>: it should be graduated, and in this you will act so that it divides the <term>quadrant<note>original: "quadrantem"; the shadow square or the quarter-circle scale on the back of the instrument.</note></term> into two parts; suspend the astrolabe by this. Look through the sighting holes of the plates at the summit of the thing to be measured, moving toward it or receding from it until you see its summit through the holes. When you have done this, take the distance from the place where you stood to the base of the standing object, and add the height of your own stature <note>Because the observer is looking from eye-level, the height of the observer must be added to the distance measured on the ground to get the total height of the tower.</note>. Divide this by feet, or by palms, or inches; whatever number of feet, palms, or inches you collect in that space, you will undoubtedly find that same amount in the height of the object being measured.

If, however, you wish to know the height of an object without moving—so that you do not move from your place—move the rule. Take the altitude which is made according to the measurement of the height of the object. After this, see if the rule of the quadrant falls upon the side of the <term>extended shadow<note>original: "latus umbre extense"; the horizontal scale of the shadow square.</note></term>. Take the points upon which it falls and divide 12 by them. Whatever number of points results from this will be the fraction of the object's height relative to the length between you and it; save that result. Afterwards, measure that length and multiply it by the parts you saved; then add to that the result <note>original: "p"; likely an abbreviation for "partem" (part) or "pedes" (feet).</note> which was collected, which is from your eye to the ground. That result will be the height of the object.

If the rule falls upon the side of the <term>versed shadow<note>original: "latus umbre verse"; the vertical scale of the shadow square.</note></term>, know how many points the rule falls upon out of 12. Whatever that fraction of 12 is, it will be the part of the object's height from the length; again, keep that. After this, measure that length and take from it that part which you saved, and add what was measured from your eye to the ground, according to what was done before. Whatever is collected will be the height of the object. 

And know that when the rule falls upon the diagonal <note>original: "diametron"; the 45-degree line of the shadow square.</note> of the quadrant, the height of the object is equal to the length from you to it, plus your stature. If it falls upon the side of the versed shadow, the height of the object is less than the length, and therefore the stature must be added to the measurement and the multipliers. Just as you took the altitude while standing, if you take it while sitting, add the distance from your eye to the ground.

And if you wish to know the elevation of an object from one place up to its highest point, measure and know the height of the object. Then, however much it was from the place again, take the surplus that was between both heights. This will be the result <note>original: "p"</note> to be tested from the place you wished toward its summit. After this, you will perform the work with the instrument suspended so that it does not touch the ground. When you wish to know the length from the place of suspension and the rest that preceded: but if you wish to know the height of an object whose base you cannot reach because of the steepness of some thing—such as a cliff or something similar—take its altitude from some place, and know the points upon which the rule falls and which side it is on; let that be A.

### Chapter 23: On the knowledge of obtaining the latitude of any region:

<margin>
Rule. <note>original: "Ra." (likely for Radix or Ratio)</note>
Mark this sign.
</margin>

When you are in any region whose <term>latitude<note>The angular distance north or south of the Earth's equator.</note></term> you do not know, and you wish to find its latitude, observe the <term>altitude of the sun<note>The height of the sun above the horizon, measured in degrees.</note></term> at midday until the sun is in the <term>meridian<note>original: "medio celi"; literally "the middle of the sky," the highest point the sun reaches during the day.</note></term>. If it is as high as it can possibly be, as happens when the sun is at the beginning of <term>Aries<note>The first sign of the Zodiac; the sun enters Aries at the spring equinox.</note></term> or <term>Libra<note>The seventh sign of the Zodiac; the sun enters Libra at the autumn equinox.</note></term>—which occurs on the day of the <term>equinox<note>original: "die equo"; the two days a year when day and night are of equal length.</note></term> twice a year—subtract the altitude you measured from 90. What remains will be the latitude of the region.

But if the sun is not at the beginning of Aries or Libra, take the <term>declination<note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note></term> of that same sun which you have obtained from the equinoctial circle. If the declination is northern, subtract it from the altitude you measured; what remains will be the altitude of the start of Libra or Aries <note>The altitude of the celestial equator</note> in that region. Then, subtract that figure from 90; what remains will be the latitude of the region. If the declination is southern, add it to the altitude, which will result in the altitude of the equinoctial circle and the altitude of the start of Libra and Aries in that same region. Subtract this from 90, and what remains will be the latitude of that region. 

And if you wish, take the altitude of any star when it is in the meridian—that is, as high as it can be—and knowing its declination, proceed as you did with the sun. Advancing also to the knowledge of the aforementioned latitude of a region using a star near the North Pole which does not set in that region <note>A circumpolar star, which circles the pole without dropping below the horizon.</note>, take the altitude of one of these stars when it is as high as possible in the meridian. Then take its altitude when it is as low as possible in the meridian likewise; add both altitudes together and divide the total by two. What results will be the latitude of the region as desired.

### Chapter 24: On the knowledge of obtaining the hours in a region whose latitude is not found in the tables contained in the mother, through which knowledge is gained from latitudes.

When you are in any region whose latitude is not found in the <term>latitude tables<note>Pre-calculated tables on the astrolabe's "mother" (the main frame) or plates for specific locations.</note></term>, take two latitudes from the tables, one of which is greater than your region's latitude and the other less. Find the difference between your region's latitude and the two latitudes you selected—noting how much closer it is to one or the other—and keep this proportion in mind for what follows. 

Whenever you wish to know how many hours of the day have passed in your region: measure the altitude, and find through it how many hours have passed according to the table whose latitude is closer to your region's latitude. Keep those hours. If there is a fractional part, then find by the same altitude how much of the day has passed in the other table you chose. Find the difference between the hours obtained from both latitudes. Take from that same difference a proportion similar to the one you noted before, and keep that as the fraction of the hour. 

If the value for the closer latitude is less than the other, add the fraction to the hours of the closer latitude; if it is more, subtract it. The result after addition or subtraction will be the correct hours of the day passed in your region for the altitude you measured. Do the same for knowing the hours of the night by the stars, and for finding the <term>arc of the day<note>The total time or degree-span the sun or a star stays above the horizon.</note></term> or night for your region, by taking the arc in both tables.

<meta>This page continues the practical instructions for using an astrolabe, moving from celestial observations (latitude) to terrestrial surveying. It explains how to use the "shadow square" on the back of the instrument to calculate heights and distances.</meta>

☩ Let this be the ratio of the length and the height of an object. If the <term>ruler<note>original: "regula"; the alidade or sighting arm on the back of the astrolabe.</note></term> falls upon the side of the **horizontal shadow** <note>original: "umbra recta"; the horizontal scale of the shadow square used when the angle of elevation is less than 45 degrees.</note>, count those points upon which it falls and whatever the value is; that will be the ratio of the length and height of the object. But if the ruler falls upon the side of the **vertical shadow** <note>original: "umbra versa"; the vertical scale used for angles of elevation greater than 45 degrees.</note>, divide 12 by the number of points, and the result will be the ratio of the length and height of the object. 

Keep this ratio in mind. After this, move from your position toward the elevated object as you wish, or move backward from it, and again take its height from the place where you are. Calculate what the ratio of the length or elevation is from that second position, just as you did before. Then, take the difference <note>original: "supfluum"; literally the "superfluity" or remainder.</note> between the two ratios and keep that value. After this, measure the distance between your first and second stations. Divide the number of <term>cubits<note>A traditional unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note></term> you measured by the difference you kept from the two ratios. The result will be the height of the object, excluding your own **height** <note>original: "status"; the height of the observer from the ground to their eyes.</note>. Therefore, add your height to it, and the sum will be the total height of the object. 

Conversely, if you wish to know the length of the space between yourself and the base of the elevated object from any place you choose: take the height of the object—which was known before adding your own height—and multiply it by the ratio you kept for that location where you wished to know the distance. The result will be the length between the two points.

### Chapter 34: On lengths when the locations are level:

**I**f you wish to know the distance between two places that are level, such as on a flat plain: suspend the astrolabe as you usually do so that the ruler falls upon the <term>quadrant<note>The 90-degree arc used for measuring angles.</note></term>. This cannot be done unless there are two quadrants on the astrolabe. Then, suspend it from your right hand. After this, look through the sighting holes of the plates until you see the location. When you have done this, look at the ruler. If it falls upon the side of the horizontal shadow, take the points it occupies out of 12; this value represents the ratio of the space between the two elevated locations, just as the ratio dictates, such as a fourth and so on. 

If the ruler falls upon the side of the vertical shadow, divide 12 by the number of points, if there are any. The result will be the distance between the two places based on the ratio of your own height. To find how many cubits are in that space, multiply the ratio of your height by the number of cubits in the distance. 

Furthermore, if you wish to know how much one place is elevated above another, take a reed or a rod and set it up to match your height. Mark the spot on it that is level with your eyes. Then stand in one of the locations and set the rod in the other location; ensure it is not tilted but standing perfectly upright. Suspend the astrolabe from your hand by the ring, directly over the surface of the earth. After this, look through the sighting holes of the plates without moving the ruler. If your sight falls upon the mark, the locations are at equal height. If it falls above the mark, your location is higher than the location of the rod by that specific quantity on the rod between the point of your sight and the mark. 

Through this work, water may be led from place to place. You will know the distance between both locations, and you will know how much the height of the place is—that is, the water above the place to which it flows—by calculating it in cubits. Divide this by the total length, and you will see how much the elevation drops for each cubit of length. If the slope is light, such as one cubit for every hundred cubits of length, the flow will be steady until the end of the distance. If you wish to know how much the elevation is from the world's gift <note>This likely refers to a specific landmark or a local reference point for "ground level."</note> to a certain place, place the ruler on the diameter of the astrolabe which hangs from the ring...

**Chapter 33: To find by how many degrees a sign rises from the degrees of the equinoctial circle in the direct circle, and likewise its ascension on the meridian line**

If you wish to know this, place the beginning of the <term>sign<note>A sign of the zodiac.</note></term> upon the **meridian line** and put a mark over its location on the <term>limb<note>original: "limbo"; the outer graduated rim of the astrolabe.</note></term>. Afterwards, move it precisely until the end of the sign falls upon the aforementioned line; however much the limb moves in degrees, those are the degrees of the **ascensions** of that same sign in the <term>direct circle<note>original: "circulo directo"; also known as the "right sphere," referring to the celestial equator's perspective where the North Pole is on the horizon.</note></term>. You shall do the same if you wish to know the ascensions of a half or a third of the signs, or whichever you wish. Let us stand at the part of the degrees of one sign: place the beginning of the degrees upon the meridian line. After this, move it precisely until the end of it falls upon the aforementioned [line]. That which the <term>indicator<note>original: "almeer"; the small pointer or "tooth" on the rotating star-map (rete) used to point to the degrees on the outer rim.</note></term> moved in degrees on the limb is what you wish to know. And if you did not take it on the meridian line, the <term>equinoctial circle<note>original: "circulus equans diem"; the celestial equator.</note></term> on the astrolabe is in a straight line just like the meridian line.

**Chapter 36: To find if a degree rises from the degrees of the equinoctial circle in whatever region you wish.**

If you wish to know this, take the <term>plate<note>original: "tabulam"; one of the interchangeable discs inside the astrolabe engraved for a specific latitude.</note></term> for that specific latitude and place it under the <term>rete<note>original: "rete"; the rotating star-map of the astrolabe.</note></term>. Afterwards, if you can, find that sign upon the line of the **eastern horizon** and put a mark over its location on the limb. Then move it precisely until the end of the sign falls upon the aforementioned horizon line. However much the <term>indicator<note>original: "almuir"; another variant for the pointer on the rim.</note></term> moved in degrees, that will be the ascension of that same sign in that region. You shall do the same if it is more or less, according to what was in the preceding chapter. But if you wish to know by how many degrees that sign sets in the same region, do the same on the **western horizon** as you did on the eastern horizon.

**Chapter 37: To know the location of the planets in the signs and other things by the fixed stars.**

If you wish to know the location of the planets, take its altitude and save it. After this, at the same hour, look at the altitude of some **fixed star** present on the rete. Place it on the <term>almucantar<note>original: "almuchantarat"; the lines of altitude engraved on the astrolabe's plate.</note></term> at the mark of its altitude. After this, know the degree of the day from the degrees of the signs; it will fall on the almucantar at the mark of its altitude in the part in which it was, whether it was in the east or the west, and that will be the degree in the same. 

If you wish to know its location during the day and it appears to you, take the altitude of the **sun** and the altitude of the **moon**, and work with both altitudes as you did at night with the planets and the fixed stars. If at the same hour you wish to know whether it is **retrograde** or **direct** <note>A planet is "direct" when it moves forward through the zodiac and "retrograde" when it appears to move backward.</note>, take its altitude and save it, and at the same hour know the altitude of some fixed star and save it. When the work is done after two or three nights—according to when the decrease or increase can appear to you—then observe the aforementioned fixed star until it is at the same altitude you saved, in the part where you took its altitude. After this, at the same hour, take the altitude of the existing planet. If it is further east and you find its altitude gives a smaller [value], it will be direct. But if it is greater, it will be retrograde. And if the planet is in the west, it is the reverse: if it adds, it will be direct, and if it diminishes, it will be retrograde.

If you wish to know [the division of the houses], take the **ascending degree** which is in the middle of the first <term>house<note>In astrology, the sky is divided into twelve "houses" that govern different areas of life. Then, observe which degree from the <term>signs<note>The zodiac signs.</note></term> emerges upon the line of the angle of the earth, and that will be the middle of the **second house**. After this, move it precisely in the same way for two hours <unclear>likewise</unclear> until the ascending degree falls upon the end of the 10th hour; and observe which degree from the signs falls upon the line of the angle of the earth, and that will be in the middle of the **third house**. Again, move it precisely until the ascending degree falls upon the line of the **eastern hemisphere** <note>The horizon line.</note> and the <term>nadir<note>original: "nadir"; the point exactly 180 degrees opposite the given degree.</note></term> is upon the line of the angle of the earth; and this shall be the middle of the **fourth house**. After this, move it precisely for two hours until the nadir of the ascending degree falls upon the end of the second hour; and observe which degree emerges upon the line of the angle of the earth, and that will be the middle of the **fifth house**. Then move it precisely for two hours until the nadir of the ascending degree falls upon the end of the fourth hour; and observe which degree falls upon the line of the angle of the earth, and this will be the middle of the **sixth house**. Again, move it precisely for two hours until the end of the sixth hour, which is the line of the angle of the earth; the nadir of the ascending degree falls upon it, which is the middle of the **seventh house**. And it should be known that there remains the completion of the houses from what we have said of them, because the eighth <insert>house</insert> is the nadir of the second, and the ninth is the nadir of the third, and the tenth is the nadir of the fourth. The twelfth, moreover, is the nadir of the sixth. The middles of the houses have been equalized, by the praise of God and His help.

## Chapter 3: On the revolution of the years of the world and of nativities

When you wish to know the **revolutions** of the ascendant for the years of the world <note>The "revolution of the year of the world" refers to the calculation of the chart for the moment the Sun enters Aries, used in mundane astrology to predict events for the coming year.</note>, take the degree of the past year and place it upon the line of the eastern hemisphere. Place a mark upon the location of the <term>almuri<note>The "almuri" or "ostensor" is a small pointer or tooth on the edge of the astrolabe's rete (the star-map) used to track degrees on the outer rim (the limb).</note></term> on the edges. Then, find the years for which you wish to revolve the ascendant—whether it is the first after the [base] year or a new ascendant. Move the pointer from the location of the mark by 57 degrees. If it is the second year, you shall move the pointer according to the same number; that is, you shall move it from the location of the mark 57 degrees for every year. And if there are many years, you shall multiply their number by 57 degrees; and let whatever remains of the sum after 360 degrees be less than 360. After this, move the almuri from the location of the mark to that [result]; and whatever then falls upon the line of the eastern hemisphere from the degrees of the signs, that will be the **ascending degree** for that same year.

## Chapter 4: To determine the beginning of the years of the Franks and their months

When you wish to know on which day **January** begins in whichever year you wish, find that entrance [year] as it is from the [birth] of Christ. Cast away whole groups of 28 years <note>The solar cycle of 28 years, after which the days of the week and the calendar dates of the Julian year repeat.</note>, and the remainder will be less than 28. Seek the same number in the upper table provided for this purpose, and take what is under it in the second table and in the inner circle under January, and keep it. After this, take the number for the Lord’s Day [Sunday], giving one to each day. On whichever day the number is finished, on that same day January shall enter in the year you desire. And if you wish to know the beginning of the other months of that same year, take the "note" of the month you wish to know; the number written under the months is added to the day January started on, and give one to each day until the number you have is finished. On whatever day it is finished, that is the day of the beginning of the month you desire from your year. And you should know the year is a **leap year** <note>original: "bissextile".</note> when "leap year" <note>original: "bissextus".</note> is written under the year in the third circle. Then know that December, which is the last of the months of the year, will be in that same year of 27 days <note>This likely refers to a specific calculation or is a transcription error for 31.</note>. And know that the January which will be in the following year will enter in the beginning of the 1016th year of Christ, and the year that enters is the 17th from the years of Christ <note>These specific dates likely serve as a calculation example for the reader.</note>.
