Let it be equated <note>Calculated or adjusted for accuracy.</note> for five days; then for 10; then for 15; then for 20; then for 24; and from there to 30, if it is a lunar month of 30 days; or to 29 days if it is a month of 29 days. Then, the difference should be taken between the position of the day in the present [calculated] state and the position of the following month's day. That difference ought to be divided by 31, if possible. If, however, that difference is seen in **minutes** <note>Units of 1/60th of a degree.</note>, let those 431 be divided by 31; and whatever results in degrees and minutes should be added to the **root** <note>original: "radici"; the base value or starting point of a calculation.</note> previously found, proceeding in that addition up to 31 days. What results will be similar to the calculation of the previous day; otherwise, the mass was a partition or an addition.

Then, take the difference from the fifth day to the 10th day, then to the 15th, and so on for the others, just as you did from the root to the 31st day. If any minutes remain after the addition made by 31, those minutes are distributed at the end of the days for as long as it has been since the beginning until that point. And let those minutes be distributed in the greater part of the days during the time the Sun is from the beginning of **Capricorn** <note>The winter solstice point.</note> until the end of **Gemini** <note>The summer solstice point.</note>.

The **Sun, Mercury, and Mars**—each of these should be equated every 5 days. **Saturn and Jupiter** every 10 days, or every 14 if it is a month of 29 days. This rule is to be reserved for these three aforementioned: if they are with the Sun in the same degree, and any minutes remain from the addition by 4, or 14, those minutes must be distributed in the greater part of the days. This continues until it arrives at its **first station** <note>original: "stacione p[rim]ã"; the point where a planet appears to stop before moving backward.</note>, and then its own **retrograde** <note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky.</note> motion begins. Then, the minutes that remain ought to be distributed at the end of the days until it is in opposition to the Sun; and then the minutes that remain from the additions made should be distributed in the greater part of the days until it arrives at its **second station** <note>The point where a planet stops before moving forward again.</note>. Then it is taken and its own motion is directed [forward]. The minutes that remain from the additions ought to be distributed at the end of the days until its motion returns to the same [position] present to us. The minutes that result from the additions made ought to be added to the places found or equated as long as the motion is direct; and as long as the motion is retrograde, the other minutes must be subtracted.

The **Moon** is equated every two days, or at 31 if the difference is taken from one day to the other and that difference is divided by two. If it is a set of four for 2 days, or by 31 if it is the same day. If one subtracts the equated place as was said above, and if any minutes remain from the subtractions made, let them be added in the middle of the day, as long as the Moon diminishes its course. Conversely, it increases its course toward the addition of days. The **Head of the Dragon** <note>original: "Caput draconis"; the North Node of the Moon, where its orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> is equated every 30 days, or 29 at the end of every month. # Here begins Hermes on the 15 stars, 15 stones, 15 herbs, and 15 images.

There are, however, only seventeen things of which the fourth of the book says he wished to determine these: namely concerning 15 stars, 15 proper stones, 15 herbs, and 15 figures <note>Magical sigils or symbols believed to capture the power of the stars.</note> to be carved in these stones. In the herbs they are as they appear, therefore they are correctly fitted under the stones. Of which stars it is said to be true that it was the greater and first. That is, of the first stars, Aldebaran. The proper star of the "branch" is that which is called Aldebaran, and it is placed in the 20th degree of Taurus and it is large, red, and shining. And it is of two natures and the complexion of Venus. And as much more as Aldebaran is: then it becomes avaricious by the virtue of Venus indeed. And since Venus is thus in one degree because Aldebaran is here, the virtue is such as if of Venus, which arts would be in one degree. Because the Moon is Aldebaran and the Sun or Venus should look back at them with a good aspect, or let Mars from the opposite or in whatever part it falls, it becomes of the same virtue. If it were from Mars in one degree, because the Moon and Aldebaran look back at it, it comes or is above, or the Sun will fall with a good aspect in virtue, this as if it were from Venus in one degree. When Aldebaran is in the ascendant or in the mid-heaven, Mars ends and let him know the figure of the way and that, but what he perfects he does not perfect. Because from Venus the separation is made on earth, but more by the heat of Mars than Venus. Let us therefore place a stone similar to it in nature, color, and virtue. Hermes speaks of the stars and their inherent natures and virtues. Indeed, at the end of the tail of the ox <note>original: "caude bouis." This likely refers to the constellation Taurus or a specific star within it, though the text later blends these with the "Behenian" stars.</note> carrying with it *han* <note>possibly a corrupted Arabic name for a star</note>, and it is one of the stars that act by the motion of the **First Mover** <note original: "motu p^i" (primum mobile). In medieval cosmology, the outermost sphere that moves all others.</note> and more specifically to the same as they are in one part of the wise man. Just as one takes the hour in the height of the year at night, so one should take the ides and the sun in the part which the **First Mover** <note>original: "p^i"</note> makes. After taking the hour in the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> of the remote according to the sign, when they protect much. Thus the **First Mover** <note>original: "p^i"</note> will be well-omened. Some show the orb and stand for a long time in the northern part, and that stone of many names makes it so. The guardians of the science [take] the hour of the day, four <unclear>trefoils</unclear>. Hermes says of the constellation that they are in the beginning given for helping; it will make men very learned and wise. Hermes speaks of what is called *Circeas* <note>likely a corruption of a star name</note> when they are not turned toward the "Benays" <note>The Behenian fixed stars.</note> and after the inspection, he wished to be made more certain of the part of the **First Mover** <note>original: "p^i"</note>. Thus Hermes [gives] the hour of the day and the lady of Venus, and it is called *Alhaith* <note>Alkaid, the star at the end of the Great Bear's tail.</note> and Mercury, from which come many bright herbs in the star which is in the "Benays" trefoil.

### Here begins the instruction for making an astrolabe, which teaches [the art]

**S**ince John of <unclear>Bologna</unclear> <note original: "Iohannes de Bononia"> wishes to make an astrolabe, take the finest brass <note original: "auricalcum" - a copper-alloy like brass or orichalcum</note>, because it is more useful for this work than other elements, being both strong and beautiful. From it, make plates according to the number and size you wish; let the plates be very flat and shiny. And if there are many, let two of them be thicker than the others. From these two, we take one to be the **mater** <note>The "mother," or the main hollowed-out body of the astrolabe that holds the other plates.</note>, in which the others are carried. And we shall leave a certain extra part on it: which will be the **armilla** <note>The ring at the top of the instrument by which it is suspended to hang vertically.</note> through which it is suspended. You should also leave a space around the circumference which will be the **limbus** <note>The rim or border of the "mother."</note>, of such a width that degrees can be marked on it, along with their circles and the letters containing the numbers of those degrees. This being done, you should make a circle by means of two diameters. One of which should be in line with that extra part and directed as if through the aforementioned ring. Let this diameter be drawn from South to North, and the other from West to East, intersecting at the center point. And thus you divide the aforementioned circle into four equal parts: and take care that all are equal. 

But so that you may obtain certainty in this work, let us teach you another way. Let us therefore make this figure on <unclear>parchment</unclear>. Let us make a circle which will be the circle of Capricorn <note>In astrolabe construction, the outermost circle usually represents the Tropic of Capricorn.</note>, which we square with two diameters, and we shall write letters upon the ends of the diameter. Therefore, we shall place at the top of that diameter which is in line with the aforementioned extra part point **.a.**, the meridian point which we call the Midheaven **.a.** <note original: "medium celi">. At the bottom part, point **.c.**, the meridian point opposite **.a.**. And at the eastern point, **.b.**; and at the western point, **.d.**. 

Let us therefore divide that quarter which is **.a.b.** into 90 equal parts. And let there be a <term>dyo</term> <note>A term here referring to a specific angular division or unit of measure used in the construction.</note>; in this way we divide that quarter into three equal parts, and each third contains 30 [degrees] towards **.a.**. Let us divide the remaining third into 2 equal parts, and each contains the space of the dimension—let us take two towards **.a.**, that is, we mark the second division. Placing a straight rule upon this, let us draw it to the western point which is point **.d.**, and where the rule cuts the diameter, we shall place a mark. Let us take a compass and place one of its ends on the point of the circle which is point **.c.**, and the other upon the aforementioned mark, and let us make a circle which is the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note>, upon which the "head" [start] of Aries and Libra move. 

But so that the prudent reader may understand what we have done, for the sake of example, let us repeat the aforementioned work. For we said above that we should divide the aforementioned quarter into 90 equal parts. But so that we do not take away the labor of the divisions, we will divide the quarter into three equal parts. Therefore, from two divisions we were content with a third, in which there would be 30 divisions; we added by the same division into three parts, and there were 10 in each <term>dione</term>. Of which we said two towards **.a.** for 20, and the third we join by 3. Therefore we took two parts because the division was double. And thus we have 24 divisions, which is one-fifteenth of the circle; and if I were to divide into 90 and we took [the measurement] as above, it is the same place. But it is faster and <unclear>easier</unclear> to measure it this way. And if we divided that third into 30—this we said by 2—and we took 2 from them, and besides that 1, they would become 24 together; and it is a fine <term>dyo</term>. Having made the equinoctial circle, let us mark this again with letters, placing **.f.** upon the western point and upon the meridian...

...we should have placed the mark **a** over the western point, **h** over the southern point, and **k** over the northern point. And let us divide the arc that runs from **h** into 90 parts, as described above, from which we shall take 24 parts starting from point **o** <note>Point 'o' represents the Meridian or South point in this geometric construction</note>. We then place a ruler upon this division, drawing it through point **f**. Where it intersects the diameter, let us place the mark **l**. Then, let us place one tip of the compass on point **z** and the other tip on the marked point **l**. We shall draw a circle inside the **equinoctial circle** <note original: "circulus equinoctialis">, which shall be the **Circle of the Head of Cancer** <note>The Tropic of Cancer</note>. 

If we wish to derive these circles from one another—that is, if we wish to derive the equinoctial circle from the circle of Cancer and the circle of Capricorn—or the equinoctial circle from the beginning of the circle of Cancer, we divide one fourth of it into 90 parts, as is common practice. Suppose we wished to divide the meridian quarter which is from the southern point **o** to **h** into 90 parts. We placed [the marks] at **a** and **f**, and **h** at the point of the west, where we placed **h** into 90 parts as above. We take the aforementioned 24 parts from the side of **l**, and we shall extend the diameter outside the circle. We would place the ruler on point **h**, extending it through the aforementioned 24th division until it reaches the diameter extended outside the circle. Where it intersects the diameter, we shall place a mark upon which we would place one tip of the compass, and the other upon point **e**. This would create a circle that is undoubtedly the equinoctial circle, since the [inner] circle is the Circle of the Head of Cancer. And in the same way, we can derive the circle of Capricorn from the Arctic circle, or the Arctic circle from the circle of Cancer. And again, we could derive the circle of Cancer... just as we derived the Arctic circle from the circle of Capricorn. 

Now, look here regarding the master. We have accepted this division of 24 parts because among astronomers, the **declination** <note original: "declinatio" — the angle between the celestial equator and the ecliptic, or the 'tilt' of the sun's path</note> is considered smaller by some. Lest I create any opposition of opinion, a response must be given to the prudent reader: the declination according to **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> is 23 degrees and 51 minutes. Among many philosophers, it is 23 degrees and 33 minutes. Among the **Jews** <note>Likely referring to Hebrew astronomical tables or scholars like Abraham Ibn Ezra</note>, however, it is 24 degrees. This diversity is not to be wondered at, for it is quite small. This happens, as some say, because of the variety of instruments used. Others say that the observation is the same, but the declination varies in magnitude or brevity. For if it is measured with a small instrument or a large one, the result may vary. 

However, some of those who are expert in the figures of the circles and all the movements of the heavens have contemplated the matter carefully. They say that the declination moves gradually through the **access and recess of the heavens** <note original: "accessiōem et quē recessiōem" — a reference to the Theory of Trepidation, an obsolete model explaining the precession of the equinoxes</note> and reaches up to 24 degrees, which the Indian authors affirmed in their greatness. For a long time, it has been less, such as 23 degrees and 33 minutes. But it should be known that there is a **fixed declination** related to the **ninth circle** <note>The 'Primum Mobile' or the outermost sphere that moves all others</note>, which is called the sloping circle because it slopes toward the north and south from the equinoctial circle. And beneath this sphere of the fixed stars, there is another **sloping circle** whose declination moves gradually beneath the aforementioned fixed declination, toward the north and south, and it proceeds to the **eighth circle** <note>The sphere containing the fixed stars and the constellations of the Zodiac</note>. We do not wish to narrate more of these matters in this book, as we intend to move on to other things. We have said this so that we might avoid the objections of critics regarding what follows. Although the difference is almost... it is imperceptible, and it cannot hinder the work if the **astrolabe** is made according to different values. If anyone wishes to establish this division according to the aforementioned fixed declination, it will be appropriate. 

But let us return to the work. Having made the aforementioned circles, let us make the **limbus** <note>The outer rim or border of the astrolabe's 'mother'</note>, which shall be of such a width that the degrees and arcs can be described upon it. It shall be perfectly round, flat, and polished...

## After this limb has been finished with God's help

...concerning the <term>almucanthurat</term> <note>Altitude circles drawn on the astrolabe plates to measure how high a star is above the horizon</note>, which in Latin we can call circles of altitudes. Some of these are usually called parallels of latitude... through 90 degrees. We should assert that we would not have set out to describe them earlier in this book, but so that it might appear more clearly and obviously to the reader's intellect, we decided to demonstrate them on some plate under a diagram. But first it ought to be explained that for the book itself, we must take plates according to the number and quantity that the prudent reader who is about to do this work intends. For **astrolabes** <note>A complex medieval computer used for navigation and astronomy</note> are diverse in their construction and measurement. Specifically, there are diverse latitudes of regions according to various differences, so that some are called "universal," some "proper," and some "halves," some "thirds," and some "sixths" <note>This refers to the density of altitude lines: "halves" have lines every 2 degrees, "thirds" every 3, etc.</note> according to their number, magnitude, and brevity. Some of these are for the seven <term>climata</term> <note>The seven traditional geographic zones of the inhabited world</note>, while others are for other regions placed within the spaces of one climate. Others are for the whole world universally. In some astrolabes, 7 plates are placed; in some three; in some two; and in some none at all because of the <term>matre</term> <note>The "mother" or case of the astrolabe often had a latitude plate engraved directly into its interior surface</note>, which is correct. For I say that for the 7 climates, three plates along with the **mother** are sufficient, whereas for the whole world...

### On the preparation of the plates

One should prepare the plates and let them be of such thickness and size—matching the size of the **circle of Capricorn**—that they can fit inside the **mother**. But let it have this moderate surface in the manner of the aforementioned small wheel. And thus it will be on the surface of the **mother**, in which the **ring** <note>original: "armilla"; the suspension ring at the top</note> must be placed, joined at the upper **diameter** of the prepared shape, into which a small **tooth** <note>original: "denticulus"; a lug or notch that keeps the plate from rotating</note> of the wall should enter so that it holds the plate firmly, lest an error be caused by its movement.

Let the aforementioned shape be of such height and width that it can firmly contain the interior of all the plates, so that the plate does not move; when it has been thus finished, let it be placed on a flat wooden board in the place prepared for it, so that the upper face of the metal plate is level with the surface of the wooden board; let them naturally be perfectly flat lest they generate an error in measurement. And let it be marked on both surfaces...

Let them take the compass, placing one tip in the middle of the plate and the other equidistant along the margin of the board. Let us make a circle to the size of the **circle of Capricorn** which we made in the **mother**, which is divided into a square by two diameters as we said above regarding the **mother**. One of these diameters should pass through the middle of the **tooth**, so that the diameter itself is in line with the diameter of the **mother**, by which it is distinguished on the surface of the **mother** where the **ring** must be placed. Let us watch carefully so that there is no error in the diameters of the square. And let us write upon the surface the letters of the diameters as we did in the mother.

Furthermore, wishing to make the **almucantars** <note>original: "alim lammuth"; the circles of altitude above the horizon</note>, it is necessary for us first to establish the circle of some **climate** or region which we want on the plate. The practice of which will be thus: let us take the **latitude** of the region we want on the **equinoctial circle**, starting from point **h** and extending the arc toward **l**, so that it becomes manifest. Let us introduce the latitude of some region, for example: let us suppose that we wish to work at a latitude of 30 degrees. [Divide] the quarter of the **equinoctial circle** which is from **h** to **l** into [90] parts and take 30 of them from the side of **h** along the arc.

Placing one tip of the compass on point **h** and the other on the thirtieth division, let us mark it, which will be named the "first latitude." And taking a straight **rule**, we place it over the marked division and over point **f** in the same circle; and where it intersects the diameter, we place a mark, because that will be the intersection of the circle with the next line. Then let us return to point **f**, and place the tip of the compass upon it, and let it be placed in the same quarter of the third circle which is from **f** to **l** at a similarity of the parts of the latitude which we took above by the arc, and let us note the place. Then let us place the rule over that mark and lead it to the mark of the other latitude...

If we have established the point and it passes through the center <note>original: "cuspidem"</note> of the plate as it is drawn, we shall learn the process well. If, however, we deviate from this, we will fall into error. But if the path is clear, we will succeed. 

Extend the end of the diameter located at point **a** using a **rule** <note>original: "regulam"; a straightedge used for drawing precise lines</note> placed in a straight line extending beyond the edge of the plate. Then, taking a **compass** <note>original: "circinum"</note>, find the midpoint of the segment on that diameter between the mark you just made and the point where the **Circle of Capricorn** <note>original: "circulus capricorni"; the outermost boundary circle of the astrolabe's projection</note> intersects the same diameter. Mark this midpoint. This point will serve as the center upon which you will place the foot of the compass to draw a circle. We should draw this arc from the center toward the Circle of Capricorn, but no further. If the line passes through these three locations including **p**, you will know the work is correct; if not, know that there was an error in the other steps.

### On the Construction of the Altitude Lines

Likewise, once the primary circle is found, when we wish to create the remaining **almucantars** <note>original: "almucantharath"; these are the circles on an astrolabe that represent degrees of altitude above the horizon</note>, we must divide that part of the arc of the **equinoctial circle** <note>the celestial equator</note>. 

The method of division is as follows:
* If we wish to draw them degree by degree, we divide the circle by 180 points, as this is the maximum precision.
* If we wish to represent them every three degrees, we divide by 120.
* If we wish to make a "standard" <note>original: "fertile"; likely referring to a common or complete instrument</note> astrolabe where each almucantar represents five degrees, we divide by 36.

These divisions are used because they are the most common ways to graduate **astrolabes** <note>original: "astrolabii"</note>, although some may be found divided by two degrees. <unclear>How</unclear> this is noted here is a matter of <unclear>gratitude</unclear>. Alternatively, if the division is to be by 30 for a standard astrolabe, we divide the aforementioned circuit by 30, using the midpoints of the arcs for the divisions.

If we wish to create the almucantars by another rule upon the diameter, the division follows because we find it through the latitude. Lead the rule to point **f**, and where it cuts the diameter, place a mark. Then place the rule over point **f** through the division following the second latitude, extending it to the diameter line outside the plate. Where it cuts the diameter, place a mark. 

Find the midpoint of the diameter space between these two marks; this midpoint will be your center <note>original: "cuspidem"</note>. Draw an arc from one side of the Circle of Capricorn to the other side of the same circle, passing through the previously marked point. 

Again, place the rule upon the third division from the first point, which we lead to point **f**, marking the point of intersection on the diameter. Likewise, place the rule on point **f** and lead it through the third division from the second latitude to the diameter extended outside the plate. Where it cuts the diameter, place a mark and find the midpoint of that diameter space. Using that midpoint as the center, draw a circle from the Circle of Capricorn to the other side of the same circle, passing through the diameter mark. 

In this manner, we shall create the remaining almucantars. It should be understood that while the almucantar circles are large, they cannot be drawn completely within the Circle of Capricorn. They will not be perfect circles but will be partial arcs. It is necessary to draw these arcs from the Circle of Capricorn to its other side, as they do not need to cross outside that circle. However, when they fall entirely within the Circle of Capricorn, they will be complete and round circles.

We shall describe all the almucantar circles until the very last one, the smallest of all, at the center of which is drawn the **zenith** <note>original: "cenit capitis"; the point in the sky directly above the observer</note>. But to know whether I have discerned the placement well or not, it is necessary that...

Afterward, let us extract the point of the **zenith** <note>original: "cemith capiti"; literally 'the zenith of the head,' the point directly above the observer</note>. If it falls as was said above in the middle of the circle, we have found it.

Having completed with God's help the work on the **almucantars** <note>original: <term>almucantharath</term>; circles on the astrolabe that measure altitude above the horizon</note>, we shall speak of the **azimuths** <note>original: <term>azimuth</term>; vertical circles that intersect at the zenith and measure horizontal direction</note>. These are written in order, or should be placed on one table. But lest the diversity of the work obscure the understanding of the viewer, we have decided to mark them in another figure so that the prudent reader might more easily grasp the work. It is our intention to observe that which the purpose of this work does not exclude. As for what an azimuth is—the singular of which is **assmith** <note>original: "assmith"; from the Arabic *al-sumūt*</note>—since this name is unknown to the Latins, we strive to make its function manifest by explaining it. Although, as I believe, it could be called by others the "placed center" or **pazumuth** <note>original: <term>pazumuth</term></note>, understood as "straightness." There are certain parts placed on the **astrolabe** <note>original: <term>astrolabio</term></note> to discern the directions of regions; for if anyone wishes to know about a certain region or city in which part of the world it lies from his own city—whether it be in the east or west or other parts—he will easily be able to do so through these lines which are described on the astrolabe, corresponding to both celestial and terrestrial parts. We shall perform their work as we have begun, through figures and demonstration.

Upon the **Circle of Capricorn** <note>original: <term>capicorny</term></note>, as above, let us extract the other circles from it. Dividing them through the diameter into quadrants by measurement, let us extract the aid of the hemisphere, which is the previous circle of the almucantars for the latitude of the region as we defined above. Once this is done, we extract the **zenith** <note>original: <term>cemith capiti</term></note> by placing the compass on point **b** of the Circle of Aries, which is the top of the midheaven. Taking the aforementioned latitude from sight **h**, let us place the rule upon it and lead it to point **f**; where it intersects the diameter, let us place a mark, for there will be the zenith. Let us write **ay** in that same place. Then let us place the arc upon point **k** and take the aforementioned latitude in the same circle of sight **f**. Then we extend the diameter **a. c.** from the circle led out, and place the rule upon point **f** in the Circle of Aries and extend it to the diameter which we extended into the circle, leading it by the latitude we took **a. k.** into **f**. And where it intersects the extended diameter, let us place a mark and write **n**, which we divide between **ay** and **n** in that circle by measurement. This will be the point upon which, placing the compass, we shall make a circle that will necessarily pass through point **h** and through point **ay**, and will return to point **f**. That portion of the circle will be manifest; the remaining part, however, will be hidden, because the preparation of the azimuth circle will not be necessary. Let us divide these arcs through the middle on both sides, writing **z** and **s** in the places of the divisions. Now, by the division of the points, placing the rule, let us make a line passing through point **p**. Let us extend this toward the circle on both sides like **az** in this figure. We have found the centers <note>original: "cuspides"</note> of the azimuth circles. If we should wish to prove whether...

Between both centers there will be one [division]... and between both circles at the top they shall be as one, so they do not join <note>This refers to the "eccentric" calendar ring, which is slightly off-center to account for the sun's varying speed through the year</note>.

Then let us make below this circle another circle in which we shall write the number of the days of the **Latin months**. Similarly, we shall write another circle in which we write the names of the **Latin months**. After these things, we shall place the rule over the 15th degree of the sign of **Sagittarius**, and we shall lead it to the center of the circle of signs, and we shall mark the locations of the months. And it shall be as if it were joined from the eccentric [center]. Let it be from this place at point **.c.**, which is in the north in the aforementioned [instruction]. There will remain for this small part... for the 12th day of **December**, 370 days <note>The scribe's math or transcription here regarding "370" is unclear, as it exceeds the solar year</note> upon which you divide the remainder of the circle. This was done in Gemini because 365 is not a multiplication... Know through the sun...

<meta>This page transitions from the practical construction of the astrolabe's star-map (the rete) to a theoretical treatise on the nature of the cosmos, defining the "sphere" and the hierarchical arrangement of the nine celestial bodies.</meta>

**All** material of doctrine is now divided into three parts: namely, the animated and the inanimate body. Once these three have been sufficiently treated, this science will be perfect.

**The body**, therefore, which is the subject of our material, is divided into nine parts, each of which is called a **sphere** <note>original: "speram"; here meaning a celestial shell or orb</note> or a cell. Let us see what a sphere is. A sphere is a round body [bounded] on all sides by a line according to its surface, whose width and length are equal. And in the middle is a point called the **center**, from which all extreme parts are equally distant in every direction. There are, therefore, nine spheres, the first of which is the outermost, enclosing all others; it is not "starred" <note>original: "stelata"; referring to the absence of visible fixed stars in the highest heaven</note> because nothing is easily contained in it, and it is called the **ninth sphere** <note>often identified as the Primum Mobile or "First Mover" in medieval cosmology</note>. The second is called the starred sphere, containing within itself the **firmament**—namely, the 12 signs of the zodiac and the 48 images <note>original: "vmagines"; the classical constellations</note>. The third is the sphere of **Saturn**. The fourth of **Jupiter**. The fifth of **Mars**. The sixth of the **Sun**. The seventh of **Venus**. The eighth of **Mercury**. The ninth of the **Moon**. All of these and all their spheres are treated here.

First, we speak of the higher and outer spheres. They are called spheres because of their nature: the closer they are [to the center], such as the starred spheres, the smaller their diameters and the thicker and more "corporeal" <note>heavy or dense</note> they are. The further they are removed, the more subtle, prior, lighter, and less corporeal they are. This reaches such a point that the outermost part can be called neither corporeal nor incorporeal, but possesses something of both. An Arabic philosopher proves this, saying: **Nature**—that is, the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "aiā mundi"; the *Anima Mundi*, a philosophical concept of an intrinsic force that animates the universe</note>—moves the outer sphere and expands it. But nothing purely incorporeal can expand something purely corporeal unless there is a mediator that possesses properties common to both. But there is no medium between those two that possesses a common property, except that which is not perfectly corporeal, such that the sphere has that common property which is neither [fully] corporeal nor incorporeal.

**Regarding** these first spheres, we have seen them; now let us look at the second ones, namely the eighth sphere. In this sphere of the whole world, we see circles, some of which are greatest, some smaller, and some middle-sized. The **greatest circles** are all equal to each other and share the same center, dividing the sphere into two equal halves. One of these, passing through both poles, divides the sphere equally into 12 equal sections <note>likely referring to the colures or meridians used to mark the zodiacal houses</note>. Another circle divides the sphere crosswise into two equal halves, so that one pole remains on one side and the other on the opposite side; this is called the **equator of days**. Another similarly divides the sphere crosswise and intersects the equator at two points, such that one part of that circle declines toward the south and the other toward the north, with one point at the **head of Aries** and the other at the **head of Libra**.

From this, it clearly appears that there are 12 equal sections of the sphere created by 6 greatest circles. Each of these creates two sections called **degrees**. The closer they are to the pole, the narrower and shorter they are; the further away, the larger and wider, so that the greatest width is 30 degrees. There are also two other greatest circles, namely the equator and the **zodiac**, which divide the sphere crosswise into two equal parts; the further they are from the points of intersection, the larger they become, so that the greatest latitude is 23 degrees, 33 minutes, and 8 seconds <note>the medieval measurement of the obliquity of the ecliptic, the angle between the equator and the sun's path</note>. The space of one degree is one thousand, one hundred, and forty-one... once a thousand... one hundred and sixty-two miles <note>The text provides a complex numerical string for the earth's measurement; in medieval miles, a degree was often calculated as approx. 56.6 miles, making the total circumference approx. 20,400 miles</note>. Once the quantity of one degree is confirmed, the quantity of the whole world-orb is confirmed, if the miles of one degree are multiplied by the 360 degrees into which the whole sphere is divided. There are two other circles called "middle" circles, equidistant from the equator; one passes through the southern latitude at the **head of Capricorn**, and the other through the northern latitude at the **head of Cancer** <note>these are the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</note>. All others that can be imagined in this quantity are called middle or equidistant circles. 

This concludes the definitions of the circles of the greater, middle, and smaller spheres. Concerning the method...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial bodies, moving from the nine spheres mentioned on the previous page to a detailed catalog of the zodiac signs and the 48 classical constellations. It also introduces the concept of stellar magnitudes (the brightness and size of stars).</meta>

### Concerning the Signs

Let us treat the **signs** <note>original: "signis"; the twelve constellations of the zodiac</note> according to their number, figure or form, and their aspects. By number, there are **12 equal parts** of the zodiac, each of which contains **30 degrees**. These 12 signs are arranged along the circle. Each sign consists of 30 degrees. Their beginning is at the intersection of the zodiac and the equator of the day <note>the vernal equinox</note>, and they are as follows:
->**Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces.**<-

**The Divisions.** Although there are 12 signs in the zodiac, there are many other images <note>constellations</note> existing with them, both to the south and to the north. While their number is technically limited and finite, they are not fully known by philosophers and wise men because of their vast multitude. For just as there are many species of things on earth, there are many celestial images similar to these things, possessing a private virtue, utility, and power over generated things. This is according to what **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose work "The Almagest" defined medieval astronomy</note> says in his book of aphorisms: "The faces of this world are subject to the celestial faces." Similarly, elsewhere it is said that the works of this world obey the celestial images: for example, the earthly lion obeys the celestial **Leo**, the fish of the water obey the celestial **Pisces**, and the birds of this world obey the celestial **Birds** <note>referring to constellations like Cygnus or Aquila</note>. From this great principle, philosophers have identified **48 images** <note>the standard 48 constellations of the Ptolemaic system</note> besides the 12 principal signs, in which they found greater efficacy, virtue, power, and significance over the elements and generated things. Some of these decline from the zodiac toward the north, and some from the zodiac toward the south.

First, I will speak of those that decline toward the **North**:
These are the **Greater Bear** and the **Lesser Bear** <note>Ursa Major and Ursa Minor</note>, which are the two "wagons" <note>original: "plaustra"; a common medieval name for the Big and Little Dipper</note>. At the end of the tail of the Lesser Bear is the fixed and immobile pole. There are also two vultures, one flying and the other falling <note>original: "vulteriores unus volans & alter cadens"; these are the stars Vega and Altair, often depicted as vultures in medieval Arabic-Latin astronomy</note>. There is the **Eagle** (Aquila), the **River**, the **Tortoise** (Lyra), the **Serpent**, and the **Serpent-Bearer** <note>Ophiuchus</note>. There is the man holding a sword in his right hand and a head in his left by the hair: this is **Perseus**, and the head is **Algol**, shining with a devilish form <note>the "Demon Star," representing Medusa's head</note>. There is the man having a serpent upon his shoulders, and the man holding a book in his hand. There is the **Charioteer** (Auriga), the man holding a rewarding and uplifted palm. There is **Algethi** <note>Hercules</note>, the kneeler. There is **Capella** <note>original: "Alaicc"</note>, holding the reins. There is the **Serpent-Bearer** and the serpent in his hands. There is the **Hen** <note>original: "Gallina"; the Swan or Cygnus</note>, the **Dolphin** (which is a fish of the sea), the **First Horse** and the **Second Horse** <note>Pegasus and Equuleus</note>. There is **Andromeda**, the "chained woman" who is said to have never seen a man. There is the boy in the lap of **Venus**, who is called Jesus <note>a curious medieval Christian interpretation of a celestial figure</note>.

There are other images that decline toward the **South**, and they are these:
The **Ship** <note>Argo Navis</note> with its necessary parts; then **Sirius** <note>original: "venus bello" - likely a corruption of "Canis Alba" or similar</note>, which is a very bright star in the width of the lower oar, called the **Dog Star**. There is the man holding a torch in his hand <note>Orion</note>, and another holding a pig by the hind foot. There is the **Hare** (Lepus) and two dogs: one called the "toiler" and the other "submerged." Below the aforementioned ship is the great fish called the **Whale** (Cetus). There is the **Hydra** (the water-serpent), the **Cup** (Crater), the **Crow** (Corvus), and the **Centaur** (half man and half horse). There is the **Southern Crown** and the **Bow of Sagittarius**. Some of these northern and southern images occupy two signs, and some three, expanding their hands and limbs to various places, so it is difficult to assign a single location to each.

**Concerning the magnitude of the stars.** Not all stars are equal. I will speak of the magnitudes of the fixed stars.
*   In the **1st magnitude**: 15 stars.
*   In the **2nd magnitude**: 44 stars.
*   In the **3rd magnitude**: 208 stars.
*   In the **4th magnitude**: 484 stars.
*   In the **5th magnitude**: 214 stars.
*   In the **6th magnitude**: 36 stars.

Any star of the first magnitude is 106 <note>a standard medieval calculation</note> times larger than the Earth. The first of the stars...

### Concerning the Aspects and Proportions of the Planets

There follows the **aspect** <note>The angular distance between celestial bodies that determines their astrological influence</note> and proportion of the planets and other images. There are four aspects: **Sextile, Quartile, Trine, and Opposite.**

*   **Sextile** is that which is through the sixth part of the whole sphere; that is, through 60 degrees from either side. 
*   **Quartile** <note>original: "Quartus"</note> is that which is through the fourth part; that is, through 90 degrees from either side. 
*   **Trine** is through the third part of the whole sphere; that is, through 120 degrees from either side. 
*   **Opposite** is through opposition across the diameter; that is, through the semi-diameter of the whole sphere. 

Wherever any of the planets may be, for example in the first degree of **Aries**, it looks upon <note>original: "aspectat"</note> that which is in the beginning of the sixth degree of the second sign in the second aspect, and so it is for the other aspects.

Of the **Signs**, three are **hot and dry**, such as **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius** <note>The Fire signs</note>. Three are **cold and dry**, such as **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn** <note>The Earth signs</note>. Three are **hot and moist**, such as **Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius** <note>The Air signs</note>. Three are **cold and moist**, such as **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces** <note>The Water signs</note>. If signs are of the same **complexion** <note>The elemental nature or temperament</note>, as they are in the space of a **Trine** or **Sextile** aspect, it will be a good and suitable aspect; but otherwise, the aspect will be bad. Indeed, it will be best if they are in an aspect of the same complexion; but if they are in a **Quartile** aspect, the complexion will be most unfavorable <note>original: "passimus"</note>.

Note that the distance of the sphere of the stars, and of any fixed star, from the surface of the Earth is [the distance previously mentioned]. But that same distance is the minimum distance of the sphere of **Saturn**, which is **46,816,250 miles** <note>original: "quadragies sexcentis millies mille octies centies sexdecies mille ducente quinquagita"</note>. Between the maximum and minimum distance is the space which is the **Sphere of Saturn**, in which there is a circle called the **eccentric** <note>term: eccentric — a circular path whose center is not the Earth, used to explain why planets seem closer or further at different times</note>, because one part comes closer to the Earth than the others. There is also a circle within it called the **epicycle** <note>term: epicycle — a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note>, the center of which moves along the eccentric, and by which the body of **Saturn** is moved. And it is [described by] its own degrees. 

The minimum distance of the sphere of **Saturn** is the maximum distance of the sphere of **Jupiter**. But the minimum distance of the sphere of **Jupiter** is **28,000,867,000 miles** <note>This number is likely corrupted or follows a different scale in the manuscript: "vigities octogies ni'l millies mille octies centies sexadraginta septe mille"</note>. Between the maximum and minimum distance is the space of the sphere of **Jupiter**, in which is the circle called the **eccentric**, which is closer to the Earth on one side than on the other. In this eccentric is another circle called the **epicycle**, the center of which moves along the eccentric, and by which the body of **Jupiter** is moved. 

The minimum distance of **Jupiter** is the same as the maximum distance of the sphere of **Mars**. But the minimum distance of the sphere of **Mars** is **3,090,065 miles** <note>original: "ter millies mille nonaginta millia sexaginta quoque"</note>. Between the maximum and minimum distance is the sphere of **Mars**, in which are the **eccentric** and **epicycle** in the same manner as mentioned before, containing the body of Mars. 

The minimum distance of the sphere of **Mars** is the same as the maximum distance of the sphere of the **Sun**. But the minimum distance of the sphere of the **Sun** is **3,640,000 miles** <note>original: "ter mille mille millia sexcenta millia quadraginta milles"</note>. Between the maximum and minimum distance is the sphere of the **Sun**, in which is the **eccentric**—that is, the Sun itself—and it is without an **epicycle**. And the body of the Sun is one hundred times...

Next follows the motion of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which medieval astronomers believed moved very slowly due to the precession of the equinoxes</note>, which motion is not a simple matter. The motion of the signs is twofold; it is the motion of the orb, and every first motion goes from North to South. This moves by one degree in 100 years; **Ptolemy** approved this, others say 50 years, others 60. But the principal motion is knowing that a certain sign begins to appear over the horizon and, by turning, arrives back at the same point; and this happens in one natural day. A natural motion is when it stands from any point back to the same point in 24 equal hours, each of which accounts for 15 degrees, so that 360 degrees are divided by 24 parts... and these hours are called **natural**. Furthermore, there are others called **accidental** <note>Also known as "unequal hours," where the day and night are each divided into 12 hours regardless of the season, meaning an hour in summer is longer than an hour in winter</note>, which are equal to each other but longer or shorter depending on whether the arc which the sun makes over the earth is larger or smaller. Furthermore, there are certain signs which are greater in number during their rising or setting because others are more or less distant from the **equator of the day**. Since there are 12 signs, each of which completes a natural day divided into 24 hours, it seems that each sign should have two hours. Indeed, this inequality occurs through the distance of the signs from the equator of the day. The further they are from the signs [of the equator], the less time they spend in rising and setting. If one sign lasts for two hours, neither more nor less, then the opposite sign lasts just as long. But if one sign lasts for less than two hours, its opposite lasts longer. In a flat representation of the signs, if they were to have 4 hours, this inequality happens from the distance or proximity of the signs to the equator, and the arcs which the sun makes over the earth. And the earth itself varies similarly based on the distance or proximity of the arc where the sun is, as it is in the first point of **Capricorn**.

### Concerning the Motion of the Planets

Having spoken of the motion of the diverse signs, let us now look at the motion of the **planets**. For the understanding of these, certain rules must first be noted, one of which is this: Whichever planet, whether superior or inferior, rises or turns before the sun in a portion less than half of the whole sphere, will be "oriental" <note>appearing in the east before sunrise</note> from the sun. 

Now, the motion of the planets is of different types: one is the **mean motion**, another is the **local** (true) motion, and another is the mean motion that occurs as the center of the **epicycle** <note>term: epicycle; a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the eccentric), used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets</note> moves upon the **eccentric**. Likewise, the mean motion is that which is between the motion of **retrogradation** and **direction** <note>term: retrograde; the optical illusion where a planet appears to move backward in the sky; "direction" or "direct motion" is its normal forward path</note>. The third, the local motion, is the degree in which the planet is said to be in a straight line [from the observer]. And to the planet is given that uniform motion which the planet makes upon the epicycle; it will be in the second <unclear>senade</unclear> and will ascend so that when it reaches the middle of its leading path, it is said to approach its **apogee** <note>term: apogee (auge); the point in an orbit where a planet is farthest from the Earth</note>. And when it is there, it is said to be in apogee until it reaches its first **station**. Following the manner of retrogradation, it reaches the **perigee** <note>original: "ima"; the lowest point or point closest to Earth</note>, and when it begins to move away, it is said to reach the second station.

Likewise, whenever it is in the same opposition from the sphere as was described before, it occurs when one planet is beneath the sphere of another; this can occur at a minimum of 12 degrees and it is between the <unclear>higher and lower</unclear>. 

#### Orbital Periods of the Planets

The following are the periods of the superior planets:
*   The sphere of **Saturn** completes its circuit in 30 years.
*   That of **Jupiter** in 12 years.
*   **Mars** in one year and a half, that is, 15 months. <note>The author provides a shorter period here than the standard 687 days</note>
*   The **Sun** in 12 months, running its solar course.

Again, for the center of the epicycle upon the eccentric, [Saturn moves] 30 [degrees] in a year, and if that is halved, it is 15. Through one year, it happens that for any part there is half a year. If that is halved again, one degree falls to each month. 

The motion of **Saturn**, which is its uniform course, is equal to the motion of the sun. Thus, if the sun begins in some degree with Saturn and the sun is then in opposition, Saturn will be in its first station and will be retrograde. 

The mean motion of **Jupiter** is 12 years. Its mean motion is equal to the motion of the sun as if received by part. 

The motion of **Mars** occurs in one year and a half, or 15 months, and its motion and mean motion are equal to the motion of the sun. If the sun and Mars start in another degree as was said above, whenever it is in opposition to the superior planets, they always begin to move backward or are retrograde. 

The motion of the **Sun** and the mean courses of **Venus** and **Mercury** are equal, occurring at a rate of 49 minutes and 8 seconds per day. <note>Standard medieval tables usually give 59 minutes and 8 seconds for the mean daily motion of the Sun</note> 

The direct motion of **Venus** occurs in a day, sometimes by 12 degrees, sometimes by 7 and a half, sometimes equal. It can be distant from the sun by no more than 48 degrees. 

The motion of **Mercury** occurs sometimes by 13 degrees, sometimes by 2; and it cannot be further from the sun than 24 degrees. 

The mean motion of the **Moon** occurs in 28 days and 8 hours. Its true motion <note>The synodic month, from new moon to new moon</note> occurs in 29 days, and sometimes in 30; and thus in every [cycle], it is 29 in one and 30 in the other, forever.

### Concerning the Significance of the Bodies

It follows concerning the last part of our subject matter: namely, concerning **significance** <note>meaning the astrological influence or meaning of the planets</note>. But it must be known that one significance is the nature of the body, and another is its figurative power. Of these, one is principal and the other secondary. The **principal** [significance] is the natural **complexion** <note>The "complexion" or temperament was the specific balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness in a body</note> of each body based on the innate [quality] regarding the spirit to be generated within it. The **secondary** [significance] is the scent or the reaching out, or the agreement or disagreement of the planets and the signs, which proceeds from their **aspects** <note>the geometric angles between planets</note>, such as all planets to the signs, the signs to the planets, or the planets on the earth, or the signs among themselves, according to their shifting and variable powers. 

There is also a principal and a secondary **figurative power**. The **principal** and visible power is that which the superior bodies have distributed to them according to the various dispositions of different times, such as ages, years, months, weeks, days, and hours. 

In the beginning of the world’s creation:
- **Aries** with **Mars**, its lord, ruled for 12,000 years. 
- Then **Taurus** with **Venus** for 11,000 years. 
- Then **Gemini** with **Mercury** for 10,000 years. 
- Then **Cancer** with the **Moon** for 9,000 years. 
- Then **Leo** with the **Sun** for 8,000 years. 

In our age—namely, beginning from the first flower—starts the lordship of **Virgo** with **Mercury**, and because it has a human form, therefore [many] men are born [during this time]. It will rule for 7,000 years, and when that space of time is perfected, the lordship of Virgo shall cease, and **Libra** will begin to rule and will continue until the **Judgment**, and it will place all things in its equality <note>referring to the Scales of Libra as a symbol of final justice</note>. That age shall endure according to certain [reckonings]. There are other dispositions that were in the beginning of years and births, and at the start of works and their completion; for as often as it is disposed, it remains so as long as that period lasts.

### The Triplicities of the Signs

This is according to the principal figurative power. The **secondary** figurative power is a particular, accidental, and variable power which the superior bodies have due to their various positions in different **houses** <note>astrological divisions of the sky</note>. For a planet signifies something in its own houses and dignities, and something else in another's. It signifies one thing in the first house and another in the second. 

To make this clearer, let us learn each part by opening our [study] of the **Triplicities** <note>original: "triplicitate"; a group of three zodiac signs that share the same elemental nature</note>, beginning with **Aries**:
1. The principal nature of **Aries** is hot and dry—and three are in this complexion: **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius**. <note>The Fire signs</note>
2. **Taurus** is cold and dry, and three are in this complexion: **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn**. <note>The Earth signs</note>
3. The nature of **Gemini** is hot and moist, and three are in this complexion: **Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius**. <note>The Air signs</note>
4. The nature of **Cancer** is cold and moist, and three are in this complexion: **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces**. <note>The Water signs</note>

<margin>X</margin> From this nature arise two **dignities**: the dignity of **sex** and the dignity of **time**. Some of these are masculine, others feminine; some are diurnal [of the day], others nocturnal [of the night].

Likewise, among the signs, some are **rational** <note>Signs with human forms</note> such as **Gemini, Virgo, Libra, Aquarius,** and half of **Sagittarius**. Also, some have **loud voices**, such as **Aries, Taurus, Leo, Sagittarius,** and **Capricorn**. Some have almost no voice, such as **Cancer, Scorpio,** and **Pisces**. 

From all this principal significance, it follows that some of the signs are [signs] of **many children** <note>fertile signs</note>, such as **Cancer, Scorpio,** and **Pisces**; others have few, which are called **sterile**, such as **Leo, Virgo,** and **Capricorn**; others are called **mediocre**. Those which signify many children signify a multitude of people. Those that are mediocre signify an average number of humans. Those that are sterile note a scarcity of men. 

Likewise, from this principal significance, it follows that certain signs operate in certain **members of the body**:
- **Aries** rules the head, ears, and the face and its parts.
- **Taurus** has the neck, throat, and gullet.
- **Gemini** the shoulders, arms, and hands.
- **Cancer** the chest and rules the thorax.
- **Leo** the stomach and kidneys.
- **Virgo** the intestines and the belly.
- **Libra** the vulva, the penis, the testicles, and the feminine vessels.
- **Scorpio** the buttocks and the anus.
- **Sagittarius** the hips and thighs.
- **Capricorn** the knees.
- **Aquarius** the legs and shins.
- **Pisces** the feet and the soles.

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of the zodiac signs, moving from their elemental qualities to their specific influences on the human body, their geometric relationships (aspects), and their effects on the character and fate of individuals born under certain degrees.</meta>

Although by divine grace any sign operates principally in its [assigned] limb <note>This refers to the "Zodiacal Man," a medieval concept where each sign of the zodiac governs a specific part of the human body, starting with Aries at the head and ending with Pisces at the feet.</note>, it also operates secondarily through the whole [body] according to the many properties of the person’s age. It operates according to their habit and character, as shown by color; if the sign is hot, it produces in the body those things which are hot, and through that habit, it renders the person sudden <note>Refers to a quick or impulsive temperament</note>—likewise concerning their office and character. Among the signs, some are **Oriental** [Eastern] which are hot; others are **Occidental** [Western] which are hot and moist; others are **Meridional** [Southern] which are cold and dry; and others are **Septentrional** [Northern] which are cold and moist. They are called Eastern or Western and so on because when they are in those [planetary] lordships, they are said to have greater dominion. And among the signs, some are **Commanding** and others are **Obedient**. The Commanding ones are those that ascend directly <note>Also known as signs of "straight ascension," which take longer to rise over the horizon in the northern hemisphere</note>, such as from the beginning of **Aries** to the end of **Sagittarius**. Others are called Obedient, namely those that ascend obliquely <note>Signs of "oblique ascension," which rise more quickly</note>, such as from the beginning of **Capricorn** to the end of **Gemini**.

And not only do the signs have properties of signification, but some are also **masculine** and some **feminine**. They are called masculine because when a planet is in those degrees, it is of greater utility, but also of greater weakness than in other degrees. Some [degrees] are **bright**, others are **dark**; and if the Moon at the birth of a child is in the ascendant at that hour, his affairs will be signaled by whether the sign was dark. Some are **increasing fortune**, others **decreasing** it, because when a planet is in them at the birth of a child, it diminishes or increases his form <note>Referring to physical appearance, stature, or social standing</note>. Others are **certain** [sure], because when a planet is in them, it disposes the matter of any business according to that degree. Others are **azimene** <gloss>that is, degrees of debility</gloss> <note>original: "azimera"; refers to specific degrees of the zodiac believed to cause physical lameness, blindness, or chronic infirmity</note>, and others are of **strength**, because when the Moon is in them at a birth, it gives the child a weak or stable complexion. Others are **wells** <note>original: "putei"; certain degrees that were thought to "swallow" the light of a planet, rendering its influence "void" or "empty"</note> that are void, and when the Moon is in them, it renders the child empty and unstable; for wells render [one] profound in conversation. Others are **pungent**; others are **dusty**, and when the Moon is in them, it signifies a turning to dust in a short time.

The **secondary significance** of the signs happens through their operation, for hatred or love, compatibility or incompatibility, arises from the properties of the signs. For some signs agree in two qualities, some in only one, and some in none. For **Aries**, since it is like **Taurus** in a shared passive quality, there is a pure regard <note>original: "diligencia"; in this context, it refers to the affinity or "friendship" between signs</note>. On the other hand, **Pisces** and **Aquarius** have no regard, for they are incompatible in two qualities. Since Aries [shares] love and agrees in an active quality—namely heat—there is a greater regard [with signs] that behold it in a **sextile aspect** <note>An astrological aspect where signs are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious</note>. On another side is **Aquarius**, which agrees in heat. On another side is **Cancer**, which is cold and moist—that is, it does not match Aries in any quality. On another side is **Capricorn**, which does not seek visibility. On this side is **Leo**, seeking itself in all qualities; from this comes good regard, for they look upon each other with their [trine] aspect, and this aspect is better because it seeks [agreement] in two qualities; and so it is for other aspects and the qualities of the signs.

<margin>
The following concerns figurative power, but some is principal and universal, and other is secondary
</margin>
<insert>and special</insert> namely as that which is principal, by which the signs are assigned to the [charts] of their birth. They begin [to act] as if in the founding of some city; if **Aries** is in the ascendant—that is, in some of its degrees—and it is good, and if Aries is free from conjunction with evil planets and from bad aspects, it disposes the matter toward nobility and utility, and these aspects [increase] it further; and so it is with the others.

The second and specific classification is that which occurs through the signs daily, based on the diversity of the houses <note>In astrology, "houses" are twelve divisions of the sky representing different areas of life, such as wealth, health, or career.</note> in which they are located. Just as the higher things have a natural and accidental [quality] of the signs, so too do the functions and accidents have a natural figurative power. From this, each has a natural quality proper to itself, assigned through the aspects of the <term>planets</term> <note>original: "planethorum"</note> which they act upon. For **Saturn** is cold and dry in excess <note>original: "in excessu"; in medieval medicine and astrology, this means the planet's elemental qualities are extreme rather than balanced</note>. **Jupiter** is hot and humid in excess. **Mars** is hot and dry in excess. The **Sun** is temperately hot and dry. **Venus** is temperately cold and humid, although she herself is said to be hot and humid. **Mercury** is dry on his own, but is adapted to all qualities; for instance, if he is joined to any of the <term>planets</term> <note>original: "planetarum"</note>, he shares their complexion <note>A "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) or qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry)</note>, being bad with the bad and good with the good. The **Moon** is cold and humid. Disproportion proceeds from this natural complexion.

And regarding the accidental [qualities], let us begin from the higher planets. First, with **Saturn**: **Saturn** is unfortunate, masculine, nocturnal, and heavy <note>original: "ponderosus"; referring to Saturn's slow movement across the sky, having the longest orbit of the visible planets</note>. **Jupiter** is fortunate, masculine, and diurnal <note>Diurnal planets are those traditionally considered more effective or "at home" in a birth chart for someone born during the day</note>, and thus truthful. **Mars** is unfortunate, masculine, and nocturnal, and a speaker of falsehoods. The **Sun**, by its aspect, is fortunate, masculine, diurnal, and truthful. **Venus** is fortunate and nocturnal. **Mercury** is mediocre toward all; he always takes on the quality of the <term>planet</term> <note>original: "planeta"</note> to which he is joined. The **Moon** is fortunate, feminine, and participatory <note>original: "parthicha"; likely a variation of "participans," meaning she shares in the nature of others</note>. <insert>Thus we ought to know</insert> that certain <term>planets</term> <note>original: "planete"</note> are friends to others, and others are mediocre. A second significance of the <term>planets</term> <note>original: "planetarum"</note> is of their order, such as the agreement or discord of the <term>planets</term> <note>original: "planete"</note> among themselves or with the signs. In another way, some [friendship] is great, some is small, and some is middling or mediocre. **Great friendship** is that which proceeds from affinity in this manner: **Saturn** loves **Jupiter**, the **Sun**, and the **Moon**, but they themselves hate him. **Mars** and **Venus** also [hate] him. **Jupiter** loves all, and all love him except **Mars**. **Mars** indeed loves **Venus**, because she renders him [acceptable] to all others, except for **Jupiter**, <insert>as</insert> he loves and water loves <note>This likely refers to elemental affinities between the planets and the signs</note>. <meta>This page transitions from the general qualities of the planets and zodiac signs to the specific astronomical arrangement of the 48 constellations. All forty-eight constellations <note>original: "ymagines"; in medieval astronomy, this refers to the 48 classical Ptolemaic constellations or "images" in the sky</note> arrange the entire heavens, and the stars themselves adorn them, yet they do not all appear above the earth at the same time. Instead, some rise and some set, such as those on the opposite side of the world from the rising point. Various stars are visible to many people on any given day because of the sweetness of their brightness, while some are seen only faintly, either due to their great distance from the earth—such as the head of Ophiuchus <note>original: "ofiuntake"; a corruption of Ophiuchus, the Serpent-Bearer</note>—or because many are cloudy, which in some parts of the sky are said to be more so because of the intensity of their fineness. Still others are less visible due to their smallness, like the body of Cancer. There are also many that are seen more rarely and are obscure, either because of the Sun or because of other things passing before them. 

This is granted so that the truth concerning the rising and setting of the signs and constellations might be better known through the Sun, because we are moved by this purpose to make clear the errors of many regarding the twelve signs. Therefore, when the Sun rises, all the stars rise with it, and so forth, so that they remain unknown during its course. This lasts through one month of thirty days, ten hours, and two points <note>original: "punctorum"; a "point" was a medieval unit of time, often a quarter of an hour</note> or more. First, the sign is placed by the Sun, specifically by the most pure rising of the rest, and the other signs follow it equally in their own order. That part of the sky where they are remains present whether they are missing <note>below the horizon</note> or present, and both in the night and the day. It must be known that stars within the sign of the Sun cannot be seen because of its rays. 

Indeed, these things are not only regulated by the stars of the heaven, but also by the daily course of the Sun; not that it is so forward, but from that point into the night, the size of one sign is calculated and then another according to the order of the firmament. It varies as it rises through **Aries**, while **Libra** falls through the same number of points. Here **Cancer** is in the middle of the sky, from whatever part we look toward the south, and here by a similar duration **Capricorn** is underneath, and so it is understood for the others. This is to be understood through the whole sphere <note>original: "phaleri"; likely a corruption of "sphaera"</note> by the astrolabe, which correctly investigates the degrees of any given day. Here the degree of the ascending sign <gloss>that is, the first</gloss> is known at the rising, which is on the opposite side. 

Regarding the arrangement of the twelve constellations of the signs, let us suppose for a moment that the first degree of **Aries** is rising; therefore, the ascending constellation is the head of the Dragon <note>original: "draconis"</note> and the... <unclear>die auday</unclear>... and those figured within the circle of the outer heaven. It is clear, therefore, that there are diverse aspects and influences for both the constellations and the signs, and they are joined together in one to investigate the truth of future things. They also wander, for some signs and constellations appear in the first part of the night in the east, some in the west, some at the height of the heaven, and some in their own [places] on the earth and in other regions. Through the six signs, all constellations are sometimes above the earth and others below the earth, and when one rises, another sets. 

Regarding the rising and setting of the constellations according to the signs, because it is not at one and the same hour for all lands due to the diversity of the climates of the world, we wish to speak more clearly so the present discourse may be better understood. Their influence is governed by the determination of the figures of this member [the zodiac], balanced according to the sign in which the mixture is proven; however, according to the authors, there are a specific number of stars. Yet, some are awaited by the wise, by which the two signs are recognized on a clear night according to their rising, setting, and residence, from the <unclear>setting</unclear> until the white light of the day. There are 12 alphabets and 25 lunar stars [mansions] whose power and beacons we shall note in a single treatise of their houses. So that anyone may sufficiently know and discern the 12 signs and 30 images for themselves by sight alone, we place the planets and the sign in which they move, and one of their stars, for all things in their integrity.

### Aries
**Aries** has many stars. Among these, **20** are more perceptible, arranged as skillfully as can be shown: 3 in the eyes, 4 in the back, 3 in the belly, 2 at the tips of the horns, and 1 in the tail. It has the form shown above in its movement in the heavens.

### Taurus
**Taurus** has many stars, among which **18** are visible in its body. The **Hyades** rise—so called by the Greeks—and the **"Little Pigs"** <note>original: "surrule"; likely a corruption of "suculae"</note> by the Latins. At their rising, vapors are raised in the air and moist showers are turned into heavy rain, of which **Virgil** says: *"Arcturus and the rainy Hyades."* <note>original: "Arcturuz pluuias ꝑ rades"; quoting Virgil's Aeneid</note> They are arranged like a **'Y'** in the forehead of the Bull. In the rear part of the Bull, at the haunch and tail, are what the Greeks call the **Pleiades** and the Latins call the <term>Vergiliae</term> <note>original: "dogmle"; likely a scribe's error for "Vergiliae"</note>. They rise in the springtime, and when they set, the winter season begins to yield. When they appear, navigation across the sea begins in early spring. One can know the coming weather by whether they appear bright or obscure; if they are clear, they predict good weather. The disposition of their stars is confirmed as follows: 2 in the forehead, 1 in the snout (which star represents the <unclear>nostril</unclear>), 1 in each knee, 2 in the hoof of the right foot, 1 in each shoulder, 1 in the neck, 3 in the back (the last of which is very large and splendid), 5 in the breast, 1 in the belly, 1 in the tail, and 2 in the horns.

The Lyre is a stringed instrument <note>original: "instrumentum pulsatile," literally a "struck instrument"</note> made of strings from the nerve of a single sea-turtle's shell and the horns of an ox, just as a hollow bit... it is attributed to the god Mercury, because it is said to have sounded so human that because of its sweetness it moved trees, herbs, and stones. The **Flying Vulture**, which is called the **Eagle** by the poets, is said to be the wonder of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> because it served Jove. It is said to have goodness and a willing grace.

The Flying Vulture is called the Eagle, which, as the poets relate, was the servant of Jove named Ganymede, who by art transformed himself into an eagle <note>In standard mythology, Jupiter transforms into an eagle to abduct the youth Ganymede; here the author suggests Ganymede himself took the form</note>; with his wings extended, he flew outward. In another way, the poet says that Jupiter once transformed himself into a lover... for the sake of overcoming the "stator" <note>A title for Jupiter, "Jupiter Stator," the stayer or stabilizer</note> of bodies, the desertor <note>The sense here is unclear, possibly referring to a specific myth of Jupiter's travels</note> who is everywhere on earth; so that when he held that form, he is said to have gone to places where he found most beautiful ladies. In truth, its appearance in the sky has 4 visible stars. The arrangement of these is confirmed thus: in the head it has 1, very clear and thick; in the part of the beak under the stretch: 2; in the breast 1, small and obscure; in the right part 1.

The natures of those born in this sign are wanderers, more often leaders than poor, yet they will not be well-contented with the goods they obtain. Therefore, such a person will still be a traveler <note>original: "viator"</note> and they will come together for many grand and praiseworthy courses of fortune; and this is its first appearance.

The **Falling Vulture** <note>The constellation Lyra was frequently depicted in medieval maps as a "falling vulture" (Vultur Cadens) carrying a lyre</note> is called the Eagle. The poet Aglosthenes says that when he once transformed himself into an eagle, he extended his wings toward the region of Asia and flew toward the East. In the region of women, his nourishment was transformed into a most beautiful youth. When he was seen standing before a choir of women in that region, an eagle appeared from above and arriving suddenly, took him back to heaven and placed him among the stars. In truth, it has 4 visible stars. The arrangement of these is confirmed thus: in the head it has 1, quite clear; in a certain shoulder another 1; in the breast 1, small and obscure. In the part which it holds in its feet on the left, opposite the right, in which it killed Architoptus <note>This name and the following—Amantros, Rotoman, Gomora—appear to be corrupted names from a lost or obscure mythological source, possibly referring to the giants or specific heroes</note>... and Rotoman and Gomora. Whose stars have 3 points in the middle of the constellation, placed equally: 1. The nature of one born in this sign will be much of a wanderer; they do not hold to... but could stand in a good state through the presence of good turns of fortune, which will prepare for him good entries into many regions. He is pleased with his life, and he will never hoard gold for himself or for another; and this is the form of its appearance in the heavens.

<margin>
...at the end of the region... in the highest region of lovers, they have more... to the highest region of others... he suffers... and fortune... it is similar in... and the hands... wonderful... from the forehead...
</margin>

**Etus** <note>A medieval spelling of "Cetus," the Whale or Sea Monster</note> or the **Whale** is placed between the Bear and Pisces, looking toward the southern part.
