### Sirius (The Dog)
Sirius is in the sky, on the earth, in the water, and in the heights, just like the celestial <term>draconis</term> <note>meaning "serpent" or "dragon-like constellation"</note>. It is both the Greater and Lesser [Dog] by another name: Sirius. The Lesser is called by the other name <term>Anticanis</term> <note>original: "anticanis"; the star Procyon, which rises "before the dog"</note> because it is named for the fact that it rises before [the Greater Dog] in a twofold way and generates agitations in bodies. Many perish at its rising. Two dogs were given [to the stars]. 

**The Dog Days:**
The "Canicular Days" <note>The hot, "dog days" of summer</note> are 40 in number, starting the day before the Kalends of July [June 30] when the heat dominates; where it conquers, it overcomes them with a poisonous plague. It is true that it changes according to the quality of the surrounding [stars]; its rising is harmful when moved by the Lion <note>the constellation Leo</note>. 

**Mythological Origin:**
This dog was not born, but was made into an expectation <note>or a sign</note> that can kill. There is a story that it was previously a fox which was marvelously converted into a dog and given as a guardian to the house of Icarius <note>original: "ycarus"</note>. He was an Athenian and showed the region of the woods to the shepherds. It is said that by the skill of others, at every turn, the dogs of the enemy might easily be guarded against and weakened by those drinking, or those who were made into dogs <note>referring to a myth involving the transformation of the followers of Icarius</note>. And when they recognized themselves, they were lost; and the dog went out to where it sent the dog by rolling through the wounds and revived him by licking. Afterward, out of affection for the fields, Erigone <note>Icarius's daughter</note> was turned into the Virgin <note>the constellation Virgo</note>, and having suffered the underworld, they were made stars in the heavens. From this, the most foul storms are called forth, and it generates and spreads bitter times for youths. This dog girds itself when <term>Anticanis</term> [Procyon] rises.

**The Stars of the Dog:**
It is certified in the heavens having 20 visible stars arranged as follows: in the head, 1. A bright one is called the "tongue," and its name is Sirius, and it is huge. 1. A bright one by whose heat all the air around the earth is inflamed, and therefore the "Canicular" period is then interpolated. From the neck, 2. In the shoulder, 1, which is small and obscure. In the chest, 2. In the left front foot, 3. In the right hind foot, 1. A bright one above the spine of the back, 3. Under the belly, 2. At the joints of the paws, 1. In the left hind foot, 2. At the tip of the tail, 1.

**Astrological Influence:**
One born or conceived under this sign will be a gadfly <note>a pest or provoker</note> to the envious, a flatterer under pleasing words, religious and a faithful friend, a manager of others' affairs, a vagabond, and more likely poor than rich; great things will be given to his soul through much exhaustion.

### The Ship Argo

And it must be noted that these 7 planets are also called "comets," but never the Sun nor the Moon, in which these [planets] show tails—these "tailed ones" are raised up like crowns to be enjoyed, through which they signify signs of future things. For if **Jupiter** and **Venus** are joined as one, it announces the best good things for the world, and Jupiter more so than Venus. But if the **Sun** is crowned with a great [halo], or is obscured, or its color is changed, we can take it as a sign of future events. But it is better if the crown is similar to gold, for then it is a good sign. But if the **Moon** is ever crowned or obscured or changes color, it is a greater sign for the future. A similar thing happens with the air: if it is pure and mild, it is a good sign. And if a rainbow is generated from the clouds, and more than one, if they are straight, they are strong and of much efficacy. When [a planet is] retrograde, it has more power in the questions attributed to it.

# The Explanation of the Position of the Planet Saturn

The explanation of the planet's position is as follows: regarding **Saturn**, it signifies vigor and the capacity to escape into good fortune for the person who is born under its influence. By assigning the sign of the **noose** <note>original: *laquei*</note>, it removes discords and bestows peace. Likewise, one [sign] signifies a master of holiness who is above fate <note>The text here is somewhat obscure, possibly suggesting the influence of the planet over earthly destiny</note> so that one born under it may have perennial glory and good fortune. This same venerable aspect of Saturn signifies for everyone a flight from poverty and from all adversity; from one place into distances, it signifies a path of poverty that does not approach oneself. Seek in another way, and thus it shows not that good may happen, but as if a binding wind might come to him; and its sign in the sand and serpents signifies that one born under it will become someone who appears more powerful than he already is, and he will be able to do many things that he currently cannot.

A **smoking beard** <term>barba fumante</term> signifies a world of honesty and a face of goodness; this sign signifies nothing other than the good fortune and hope that the person born under it possesses by right of their nature. Above this, let there be this figure: having good habits and good hope for every man who is born under it. One truth signifies a bridle in fortune, of good fame and good hope concerning holy security. It is a state through which he attains the divine things above. 

The **staff** <term>virga</term> signifies dignity for many lords, such as civil power, the captaincy of a castle, and the management of affairs; and a destroyed [sign] signifies a way of becoming a judge, a lord of a place, wise and good. The **city** which is in the hand signifies consolations in sustenance and that he will make for himself temporal riches; those who are born under it will be wealthy, and wealth shall not fail them; the man shall eat and rejoice, and by his own effort he will be loved by every person. They shall see the gifts of every stage of his life.

Your hand stops; it possesses all the habits of great hope from one place to another for men born under it. To live bitterly signifies that if such a thing seems to happen to him, it is prepared for the joy of one wishing well; and to the good and peaceful person, it promises good from above. It signifies a weapon for himself to be noted by others for his defense; and in the soul, let him have fortune and let it not teach him of evil power and pride, etc. 

Wherefore, one born under it, if he feels "arms" <note>likely referring to a combative nature or actual weapons</note>, he is a friend of little goodness and much malice. 

Regarding the significance, these are the figures according to the form of the text placed next to it.

# The Nature and Motion of the Sun

The **Sun** moves by its own accord beneath the firmament <note>In medieval cosmology, the firmament was the sphere of the fixed stars</note> through a natural motion, so that it might temper the heat of living creatures, remaining within its own spirit. It is not perceived in the same manner as the other planets in our [brightness], but it completes its course along the obliquity of the **Zodiac**, according to the arrangement of the bodies within the celestial sphere. But just as the **Moon** is illuminated by it, so the **Sun** illuminates the other planets, being superior in virtue to all of them, for it alone was chosen for this reception.

The spirit of the Sun is spiritual—therefore a vegetative condition <note>Referring to the "vegetative soul" that governs growth in plants and animals</note> is brought about, so that the logic of the elements might be introduced into any elemental quantity, unless it is spoken of improperly. By the primary motion of its turning, it grows more hot, and the water of the zodiacal signs is changed by natural [processes] through which it appears to us. This motion in the sphere affects everything through its resonance. Because no reason for its whiteness is assigned, suffice it to say that **Zarohonocbe** <note>This likely refers to a corrupted Arabic or hermetic name for a solar intelligence or a specific astrological degree</note> changes it through the firmness of this [light]. We do not know if it is perfect above the earth, but it is observed to possess a depth in its roots when it germinates beneath the earth and **metals** are composed <note>In alchemy, the Sun's rays were believed to "cook" or mature minerals into gold within the earth</note>. Hence, by natural law, its perfection is recognized.

The **Sun** is said to be the "discerner" <note>original: *diagnosentur*</note> because the entire world is illuminated by it; it is like a man, and is abundantly useful to both the good and the wicked. Its intention is not for itself, but for [the world], even when it is not desired—thus it is with **God**. For this reason, the Gentiles wished to call the Sun **Apollo**, desiring to take its spirit for themselves, though they did not return it. For Apollo is called the god of the moon <note>original: *lune dr p deus* - likely a scribal error or a reference to Apollo's role as a god of light generally</note> because by his fervor he [dispels] all shadows; he is given even to the barbarians. They also wished him to be the god of inundation, or because the Sun makes all obscure things manifest, flowing openly. Thus, by its rising and setting, and by its orbit, it produces many kinds of significations and effects.

He is generally depicted **without a beard** because his countenance does not change by waxing or waning like the **Moon**, which grows and then decreases; the Sun is always round and whole. Whence he is always nimble and fresh for his work, just as the eye is for seeing, the ears for hearing, and all the senses for perceiving. He is positioned as a signifier in a certain way, so that the year <note>original: *anus*</note> may be noted; he contains the differences of the **four seasons** through which he runs to complete the year.

Similarly, the poets figure him with **four horses** pulling a four-horse chariot <term>quadriga</term>, and therefore two heads look toward one part of the world and the other two look toward the other, because all time is either like summer or like winter. The names of the four horses [signify] their effects...

The **Sun** is greater [than the Moon]; we represent him holding the orb of the world in his left hand, and an iron rod burning with three flames <note>original: *terbus flāniz*</note>, as a sign of the **Divine Trinity**. He is the one who "illuminates every man coming into this world" <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 1:9, identifying the Sun with the True Light of Christ</note>. At the end, the figure of the **Moon** is depicted, etc.

It concludes by syncretizing the Sun's light with the Divine Trinity and the "True Light" of Christian scripture.</summary>

# The revolution of the years of the world, or of a person’s birth, or indeed of any thing having a beginning: how to find it in hours and the ratios of hours through the table made for this purpose.

It should be known that the revolution of a year is the revolution of the Sun from the same point back to that same point, or the return of the Sun to the same point in which it was at the beginning of that year. And Note that the **revolution of the year of the world** <note>original: "revolutio anni mundi"</note> is the entry of the Sun into the beginning of the first minute of Aries <note>This refers to the Spring Equinox, the start of the astrological year</note>. The **revolution of a birth** is the return of the Sun to the same point of the zodiac in which it was at the hour of birth. The **revolution of years** for any thing whatsoever that has a beginning—for instance, of a certain town or castle—is the return of the Sun to the same place in the zodiac in which it was at the beginning of its foundation, namely, when the first stone was laid. 

When, therefore, you wish to find the revolutions of the years of the world, first have the entry of the Sun into Aries well-verified from another year known to you, recorded under a certain number of days, hours, minutes, and seconds. Put that time as your root <term>Root: a "radix" or base number used as a starting point for astronomical calculations</term> to hold for your whole life.

When you then wish to find the revolutions of a year, see how many years there are from your root until that year for which you wish to have the revolution. With the number of those years, enter the table titled **"Table of the Revolutions of Years in their Fractions"** and find the number of hours, minutes, and seconds. Add what you find to the hours and minutes you have in your root. If the hours resulting from this addition exceed 24, subtract 24 for one unit <note>Representing one full day</note>. That which remains after the addition will show you the time of the Sun's entry into Aries—namely, the days, hours, and so on. Let it also be known in which year it shall be a leap year <note>original: "bisextilis"</note>. And this applies to any hour of the days preceding that day which you found through your work. 

For the revolutions of the years of a birth, or to find an alteration, you should first have the hour of birth (or of any other thing having a beginning) under a certain number of days and equal hours and minutes. Set that time as your root and operate upon it using the same table in the same manner as you did for the entry of the Sun into Aries. One must, however, be careful regarding the leap year; for if it is a leap year, and the place of the leap day has passed, this revolution is not completed until the hour of the day is adjusted.

---

# The revolutions of any years when seeking to find the degrees of the ascendant.

It should be known that the revolution of the ascendant of the year <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the solar return</note> is nothing other than finding the degree of the rising [sign]—specifically, that which is brought into contact with the eastern horizon when the revolution of the year is completed. And I say that this table ought to be understood as being about degrees of the equation and not degrees of the zodiac, according to a certain opinion; otherwise, there would be a flow <note>original: "flumina," perhaps meaning a discrepancy or flux</note> if it were placed otherwise, because the ascensions of the signs are unequal, but the hours placed in the table of the revolution of years in their fractions are equal hours. 

When, therefore, you wish to know this, first know the degree of the equation coming out at the rising in another year known to you—namely, by calculating a certain number from Aries. Have the number of degrees, minutes, and seconds that were from Aries equally up to the equal point which is first in the rising, and hold that number as your root. 

When you then wish to find the ascending degree of the revolution for another year, take the number of years from the time of the root until the first year for which you seek the ascendant. Look in the table titled **"Table of the Revolutions of the Ascendant of Years"** for the number of degrees you find there, along with the minutes and seconds, and add them to your root—that is, degrees to degrees and minutes to minutes. If after the addition the sum exceeds 360, remove [360].

# To find the motion of the sun, moon, and all other planets, and the mean arguments of the moon, Venus, and Mercury, based on the motion of the access and recess of the eighth sphere <term>Access and recess: also called trepidation, a medieval theory that the fixed stars moved back and forth rather than in a continuous precession</term>; also to find their apogees <note>original: "auges," the point where a planet is furthest from Earth</note> and the "heads" of the fixed stars through tables.

Reduce the total given time from the beginning of the Alfonsine era <note>The Alfonsine Tables were prepared in Toledo, Spain, under the patronage of King Alfonso X in the 13th century</note> from the night until the hour of your calculation into 4, 3, 2, 1 <note>This likely refers to the hierarchical grouping of years, months, and days used in table lookups</note>. And reduce the hours and minutes of hours to the fractions of a day, if you have hours and minutes of hours. When this is done, first write down the **root** <term>Root: a "radix," or the known position of a planet at a specific historical starting point</term> of that motion which you wish to know for the time you are working with. For example: if you seek the mean motion of the Sun, write the root of the Sun; and if you are working with the years of Christ <note>A.D.</note>, write the root of the Incarnation. If, however, you wish to work with other years, write the root corresponding to them. When the root is written from the table as it was found, go back into the table for that motion which you seek with that four-fold number; and whatever is found in the line—the line titled "years" will contain the signs, and the following [will contain] the degrees, then minutes—write them in order under the root previously saved, each under its own kind: namely, signs under signs, degrees under degrees, and so on.

Then, go back in the same way into the same table for whatever is found in the line titled "20," putting the signs under the signs, followed by degrees and the rest; write them under the others previously written, each under its own kind. Afterward, repeat in the same way for whatever is found in the line titled "2," under the signs and so on, and write them in order under the others according to the method described. Then repeat in the same way for whatever you find under the first line <note>The single years line</note> under signs and the following degrees and so on; write them in order under the others in the accustomed order. And if you have minutes of days, repeat in the same way in that same table, and whatever you find in the first line under degrees and the following minutes and so on, write them in order under the others, each under its own kind. Then repeat for the [remaining] fraction of the day in the seventh [column] in the same table, and whatever is found in the first line as minutes and so on, write them in order under the other parts. And you shall do this if you have more fractions of time.

Which fraction of degrees corresponds to each fraction of time is clear from the title below in the first [part] of the table. When this is done, add everything together, beginning from the smallest fraction. And whatever total grows from the addition—if 60 is reached—one unit must be placed in the place of the larger part <note>The author is explaining sexagesimal (base-60) arithmetic: 60 minutes = 1 degree</note>. And this method is to be observed in these tables up to the signs, where 30 degrees equal one sign, and six signs make one revolution <note>The text specifies "six signs," though a full circle is usually 12; this may refer to a specific table structured in 180-degree half-circles</note>. But if from the addition of signs to each other a total grows, you may subtract six from the six as many times <margin>root</margin> as you can, and keep the remainder, because that is what you seek. 

It must be understood that the roots placed in these tables are set for the meridian of the city of Toledo, and therefore you cannot find the motions through them except for the meridian of Toledo. If you wish to find the mean motion and the others named above for your own meridian, know whether your city is further east or further west than Toledo. And know by how much time it is further east or west, and for that much time seek the motion you want; then subtract it from the motion found if the city is further east, or add it if the city is further west. That which results after the subtraction or addition is the motion you seek for the meridian of your city. 

Note, however, that you can greatly shorten this work by finding all the roots for your meridian once, and they will serve you as long as you live. It should also be noted that at the beginning of any month you ought to seek all the mean motions and mean arguments and [record them] on a schedule, and keep it with you for that year; it will be a great relief to your spirit, so that it is not necessary in that year to go back [to the tables] for the first, second, or third months, or for the days, if by chance you have the motions for the days already noted.

# Whether it is possible to know if a solar eclipse in any conjunction or a lunar eclipse in any opposition will occur
Seek the argument of latitude <term>Argument of latitude: the distance of the moon from the "nodes," the two points where its tilted orbit crosses the path of the sun</term> of the moon at the time of conjunction (for a solar eclipse) or opposition (for the hour of a lunar eclipse). If the argument of latitude is 0 signs and less than 12 degrees, or 11 signs and more than 48 degrees <note>These two ranges describe the moon being very close to the North Node</note>, or 5 signs and less than 12 degrees, or 6 signs and more than 48 degrees <note>These ranges describe the moon being close to the South Node</note>, an eclipse is possible. If, however, you find it to be outside these limits, an eclipse cannot occur.

# Method for constructing tables of mean motions from these, converting them from hours into days; the motion of one day for each should be subjoined by itself:
If you wish to construct the motion for one day for a subject whose table you want, but its motion is not written in any fixed table, you may doubt whether a certain line of a table is correctly written. Look at the line immediately preceding the one you doubt and write it aside. Having done this, subtract the motion of one day from the first line of the table and add <note>The author is describing a process of verifying the consistency of the additions in the table</note>; then the result will be the number for the line you doubted. If you doubt the truth of even the first line, take any line you wish in the table and write it down; then take the line immediately preceding it and write it underneath. Subtract the lower from the upper, and the remainder will be the motion of one day for that part of the table. If it matches, then it is correct. If it does not match, take two lines from another part of the table and subtract one from the other, looking for consistency until you are certain of the daily rate. When it is likely the table is correct in most places, you can then verify or construct the whole table yourself. Write the motion of one day, then add it to itself to get the double (two days), and proceed in this way, adding the daily motion to the previous total to get three days, and so on, until you complete 60 lines. Thus the table will be finished.

# How to find the position of the apogee of any planet through the tables:
First find the motion of the apogee <term>Aux: also called the apogee, the point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Earth</term>, which is calculated according to the fixed stars and does not change position relative to them, but has its own mean daily motion already recorded. Next, seek the motion of access and recess <term>Access and Recess: a medieval theory called "trepidation" which suggested the stars and equinoxes oscillated back and forth over centuries</term>. Add this to the "root" of the motion of the eighth sphere <note>The eighth sphere was believed to be the realm of the fixed stars</note>. Once this is found, if there are signs, resolve them into degrees and enter the table for the "equation of the motion of access and recess." Look for the number of degrees closest in its line. If they are fewer than 90, they extend toward 90. If, however, they are fewer, take the 90 degrees in retrograde order <note>The author is explaining how to read a table that peaks at 90 degrees and then counts back down</note>—that is, if you find 1, take 89; if you find 13, take 81, and so on, going back toward the start of the table until you reach 180 degrees, where the equation is 10. If it is beyond 180 degrees, take from the beginning of the table so that 180 is the start: 182 counts as 2, 183 as 3, and so on, reaching 90 again at 210 degrees, where the equation will be zero. If it is more than 210, go backward again from the end of the table toward the first line, so that for 211 you take 89, for 212 you take 88, and so on until the beginning of the table at 360 degrees. However, we do not need this retrograde operation in our work because many years will pass before it reaches 90 degrees. Therefore, seek the degrees of the journey in the minutes of the result... and by this you will write from certain places, ensuring that the minutes beyond the degrees are handled correctly.

## To find the true position of the head of the dragon
It must be understood that the motion of the intersections of the moon's eccentric [orbit] and the ecliptic is called the **head and tail of the dragon** <note>The "Head" (*caput*) and "Tail" (*cauda*) of the dragon are the North and South Lunar Nodes—the points where the moon's path crosses the Sun's path (the ecliptic).</note>. According to its plain motion, when the Head is generated in the mean motion, it moves in truth at that moment [backwards]. By subtracting the mean course of the Head from 12 signs, the remainder is its **true corrected position** according to the succession of the signs. Therefore, if you wish to find the true position of the dragon’s head, look up the mean motion in its table and subtract it from 6 signs. What remains after subtraction will be the true position of the dragon’s head, measured from Aries according to the succession of signs. Having learned this through the canons <note>A "canon" is a rule or set of instructions for using astronomical tables.</note> just preceding, and knowing the true position of the dragon’s head, you can find the **argument of latitude** through this canon: subtract the true position of the Head from the true position of the moon. What remains will be the true argument of latitude. Here, take the distance between the body of the moon and the dragon [the node]; this is called the argument of latitude, and by it, one finds how great the moon's latitude is from the ecliptic <note>The latitude is the moon's distance north or south of the Sun's path.</note>.

## To find the true position of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars
First, seek the mean motion of the planet whose true position you seek; save it. Then find its **apogee** <note>original: "augez". From the Arabic *awj*, this is the point in the planet's orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> through the doctrine handed down in the preceding sections. Subtract this apogee from the mean motion; what remains will be the **mean center**. Save this alongside the mean motion.
<margin>it is worth</margin> Next, seek the **mean motion of the sun**. Subtract the previously saved mean motion of the planet from the mean motion of the sun. What remains will be the **mean argument**. Save this alongside the mean motion and the mean center. From this, you have three values: the mean motion, the mean center, and the mean argument. However, whenever the mean motion of any of these three [planets] is sought, it is taken from the mean motion of the sun so that the mean argument can be obtained. This is because for each of these three, their mean motion is related to the sun’s mean motion... in the time it takes for the sun to return to its mean position, it is necessary that it always be distant from the apogee.

The middle of the epicycle <note>In the Ptolemaic system, an epicycle is a small circle on which a planet moves, while the center of that small circle moves along a larger circle called the deferent.</note> is separated from the mean motion of the Sun by its own mean motion. Otherwise, if the mean center was less than three signs, it indicates it should be subtracted; write "subtract" accordingly. Once written and saved, if it should be added, add it to the mean center and subtract it from the mean argument; if it should be subtracted, subtract it from the mean center and add it to the mean argument. Through this, both the center and the argument will remain equated <note>Meaning they have been corrected from 'mean' values to 'equated' or adjusted values.</note>.

When this is done, return to the same tables to find the **proportional minutes** <note>Proportional minutes are used for interpolation, allowing the astronomer to calculate values that fall between the whole degrees listed in the tables.</note>. Save these and look at the heading for the proportional minutes: if it is written "farther" <note>original: "longior"</note> write that title above your saved minutes. Then, repeat the process for the argument in the same tables and take the **equation of the argument**, which is called the first examined equation of the argument. If there are minutes in the argument, proceed as you did in the rule for the Sun.

Take also from that same place the "diversity of the diameter" for the farthest or nearest distance <note>original: "altitudo longitudinis"</note>. You will take it for the "farther distance" if "farther" was written above the proportional minutes, and "nearer" <note>original: "propinquior"</note> if that was written. From this diversity of the diameter, take a proportional part according to the ratio of the proportional minutes you saved. Add this proportional part to the first equation of the argument if the diversity was for the "nearer distance," or subtract it if the diversity was for the "farther distance." After this addition or subtraction, you will have the **final examined equation of the argument**. Write "add" above it if the argument was less than three signs, or "subtract" if it was more than three signs.

Finally, look at the equation of the center you saved and the equation of the argument. If "add" is written above both, add them together and add the total to the mean motion. If "subtract" is written above both, subtract the total from the mean motion. But if "add" is on one and "subtract" on the other, subtract the smaller from the larger. If the larger one was marked "add," add the remainder; if the larger was marked "subtract," subtract the remainder. The result after this addition or subtraction will be the **true place** of that planet, if God breathes life into the work <note>original: "si deo sperit," likely a pious scribal formula for the successful completion of a calculation.</note>.

### Finding the true place of Venus and Mercury

It should be known that the method for calculating these is the same as for the three superior planets <note>The superior planets are Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, except that their mean motion is the same as the mean motion of the Sun, and the apogee of Venus and the apogee of the Sun are in the same place. The difference between these and the superior tables is in seeking the mean arguments, which for these are not found by subtracting their mean motions from the Sun's, but are sought directly in the tables. 

Therefore, when you wish to calculate the true place for any of these, find the mean motion of the Sun (which is the same as the mean motion for each of them, as stated) and its apogee. Then subtract the apogee from the mean motion, and what remains will be the mean center; save this. Afterward, seek the mean argument and save it...

### To find the Sun’s entry into Aries, or into any Sign you wish to find:

Find the true position of the Sun at a time near the completion—namely, at a time using an **ephemeris** <term>Ephemeris: a table providing the predicted positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals.</term>—and when the Sun is only a small distance from **Aries** <note>Aries is the first sign of the zodiac; the Sun's entry into it marks the spring equinox.</note>. Once found, look at its distance from Aries, which you always subtract from the true motion of the Sun toward the sign. Reduce this distance to the same units: for example, if they are in degrees, minutes, seconds, and thirds, reduce everything to **thirds** <note>In ancient and medieval astronomy, units were divided by 60: 1 degree = 60 minutes, 1 minute = 60 seconds, 1 second = 60 thirds. This is called a sexagesimal system.</note>. Keep this distance so that you may determine the motion of the Sun in one minute of a day. You will know this in this way:

Take the Sun's position for one minute of a day afterward, and compare it with the first equal position; subtract the first motion from the second, and what remains shows how much the Sun moves in one minute of a day. Reduce this to the same genus of minutes, seconds, and thirds to which you reduced the distance earlier. To keep everything consistent, also reduce the motion in one minute of a day; having done so, divide the distance by the motion in one minute of a day. What results will be in minutes of a day; save that part. If there is a remainder less than a minute of a day after division, multiply it by 60 and divide by the same divisor as before; the result will be seconds of a day. Save these after the minutes of the day you previously saved. Then, if another remainder exists after division, multiply it again by 60 and divide by the same as before; the result will be thirds of a day. Save them after the minutes and seconds. If anything further remains to be divided, it can be dismissed, as it is a negligible amount.

Having done this, look at the minutes of the day you found. If they are more than 30, count them as one whole day; if not, let them remain in their place. Then, if you have some days of the year, add them to the time at which you first sought the true position of the Sun. At the resulting time, seek the true position of the Sun again. If you find zeros across the board—zero signs, zero degrees, zero minutes, zero seconds, and zero thirds—that specific time will be the moment of the Sun’s entry into Aries.

If, however, you find it is still distant, determine the distance as before by the motion of a minute of a day. Divide that distance by the motion of a minute of a day, and the resulting numbers will be the number of days. If the distance is so small it cannot be divided by the motion of one minute of a day, multiply it by 60 and then divide. The resulting numbers are parts of a day, and any remainders after division should be multiplied by 60 and divided by the same divisor as before to get the next fractional unit. Always follow this procedure: multiply the remainder of the division by 60 and divide by the same divisor until it is sufficient.

Having done this, add the time found here to the first found time if, through your calculation, the Sun has not yet reached Aries; or subtract it from the first time if the Sun has already passed the point of Aries. The resulting time will be the moment of the Sun's entry into Aries... From this time, the positions of the planets should be sought. Next, enter the table of the **equation of days and nights** <term>Equation of days and nights: Also known as the Equation of Time, this accounts for the difference between solar time (sundial time) and mean time (clock time).</term> at the end of the procedure and look for the specific equation for them. Whatever you find in degrees and minutes, convert it to time: for each degree take 4 minutes of time, and for each minute of a degree take 1 minute of an hour <note>This is the standard conversion where 360 degrees equals 24 hours, meaning 1 degree equals 4 minutes of time.</note>. Add this to the time you found for the entry of the Sun into Aries. The result will be the time of the Sun's entry into Aries in **equal days** <term>Equal days: standardized mean solar days used for precise astronomical timing.</term>.

And with this time, the degree of the **ascendant** <term>Ascendant: the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</term> and all the **mansions** <note>In astrology, "mansions" can refer to the 28 lunar mansions or the 12 houses of a horoscope.</note> and everything else usually done should be sought, just as you would do for any other sign. This also works for any other part of the zodiac you wish to work with—namely, by taking the distance from that sign and calculating with the Sun's motion in one minute of a day. Note that if you wish to create a **figure of the heavens** <note>This refers to casting a horoscope or a celestial chart.</note>, you must apply the equation of the day. It should also be taught that in the same way, the entry of the Moon and other planets into any sign or any part of the zodiac can be found...

If not, see the distance by subtracting the smaller motion from the larger, and find the daily motion of that planet in minutes of a day as described before. Calculate the surplus—if both are direct, subtract them; if one is retrograde and the other direct, add their motions together—and divide the longitude you have now found. The result will be minutes of a day, and if anything remains, multiply by 60 and divide again... and so you arrive at the truth. Once done, add the time found by proportional calculation to the time previously found.

<margin>
Year of Christ 1240 until the year [13]24, in the time of Alfonso. So it was that Johannes <note>Likely referring to Johannes de Saxonia or Johannes de Lineriis, famous 14th-century astronomers who adapted the Alphonsine Tables.</note> was missing on the first day of 1320. He wishes to verify the degrees from Alfonso up to this time: 34 minutes for the motion of the 8th sphere. The time of Alfonso from Christ is 1248.
</margin>

### To find the positions of the fixed stars for any time you wish

First, you must know the positions observed at another time known to you, such as the positions of the "Head" <note>Referring to the "Head of Aries," the vernal equinox point.</note> last observed through the true **Alphonsine Tables** <note>The standard astronomical tables used in the late Middle Ages.</note>. Calculate the equation of the **motions of access and recess** <note>original: "motu[um] accessus & recessus"; the medieval theory of "trepidation," which suggested the equinoxes moved back and forth over time rather than in a constant precession.</note> for the time since Alfonso. To do this, take the **root** <note>The "radix" or starting value for a calculation.</note> of the motion of the **8th sphere** <note>The sphere containing the fixed stars.</note> from the table of roots of Alfonso. Keep it and write it down. Then take what follows in the first line after the root, which is the motion and the equation for that time.

Having kept that, seek the motion of access and recess from the time of Alfonso until the desired time. Add that to the Alphonsine root written earlier. Resolve the resulting sum into degrees (if there are signs, include them). Then, using the table of the equation of the motion of access and recess, find the equation mentioned in the **canon** <note>The set of instructions or rules for using astronomical tables.</note> of the motion of the apogee. Having found it, subtract that equation from the one found for the time of Alfonso.

**How to find any planet with any of the fixed stars in every way:**
First, know the position of that star which you wish to know from the chapter immediately preceding this one. Understand from the preceding chapter that in this work, the position of any fixed star is its place in the **zodiac** and its position on the **ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> through which a line passes, such as a circle passing through the poles of the zodiac and through the body of the star. Their **declinations** <note>Distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> from the equinoctial, however, do vary according to how the declinations of the degrees of the ecliptic vary, as is clear from other diagrams. **How to find the magnitude and duration of a solar eclipse through tables:**

Use this to look in the table for the equation of the sun, seeking its like in the lines of numbers for the equation. Subtract the found value from the mean motion of the sun if the argument was less than 3 signs; add it if it was more than 3 signs. Through the argument, as you <unclear>divide</unclear>, the result will be the true position of the sun at the time of the mean conjunction, which you should save. Then, with the mean argument of the moon, enter the table for the equation of the moon, seeking its like in the lines of numbers. Then, look at the true position of the sun and moon: if they agree in signs, degrees, and minutes, it is the same and true. If they do not quite agree, subtract the smaller from the larger and save the longitude. If the longitude is [small] and the latitude is [consistent], add a twelfth part to the longitude by the motion of the signs, divide the whole by the motion... add the half to the mean argument of the moon if the longitude was of the sun, or subtract it from the argument if the longitude was of the moon; after that calculation or division, it will be the most true time.

# Having seen these things, let us proceed to the work of parallax

<margin>The difference between the hour of the day and equal hours</margin>
Consider therefore whether the sign is in the day or in the night. If it is in the night, then do not concern yourself with **parallax** <note>original: *diversitas aspectus*; the difference in the apparent position of the Moon as seen from the Earth's surface versus its center</note>, because it is not visible during the night, unless it happens that it is visible shortly after sunset when some part of the ecliptic is still seen. If it is during the day, I say: for that instant of the conjunction, move by equal hours. Determine those hours according to the tables of the parallax of the moon, which are made for the **climate** <note>original: *clima*; one of the seven latitudinal zones used in ancient and medieval geography</note> under the sign in which the moon is located, and take the minutes of longitude in the direct and inverse [tables]. And if there are any minutes of an hour beyond the whole hours, take the proportional part for one additional hour and add the minutes of longitude to those previously mentioned. And know the difference between the minutes of longitude previously accepted and those now taken; from which difference take a proportional part according to the proportion of the minutes of the hour to 60. Add this proportional part to the minutes of longitude previously accepted if they were fewer, or subtract it if they were more; the result will be the parallax of the moon in longitude, assuming the moon is at the beginning of that sign under which you entered.

<margin>Know what should be done if it is not at the beginning of the sign</margin>
If the moon is not at the beginning of that sign, then perform the calculation for the following sign in the same manner as was done before. Then consider the difference between the minutes of parallax taken under the first sign and those under the second, subtracting the smaller from the larger. Multiply that difference by the minutes that the moon has traversed in the sign in which it is, and divide the product by 30 degrees. The value will not change its denomination by this reduction, and it will be the proportional part which you add to the parallax found under the first sign (if it was smaller than what was found under the following sign) or subtract (if it was larger). The result will be the parallax equated for the hours and minutes for this position in the zodiac.

<margin>Parallax equated for hours and minutes for the position here in the zodiac</margin>
And if it was not in the upper part of the **epicycle** <note>original: *epicyclus*; a small circle on which the Moon moves, while the center of the epicycle moves on a larger circle</note>, so that the equated argument of the moon found at the hour of the truest conjunction is resolved into degrees, enter the table and take the minutes you find in the table over which is written "small circle" <note>original: *circulus brevis*</note>. Multiply these by the total parallax last found, and divide the product by 60; the result will be the proportional part. This parallax is increased because of the distance of the moon in its epicycle; add this to the parallax last found, and you will have the parallax equated for hours and minutes for the position here in the zodiac and in the epicycle.

<margin>Parallax in the zodiac, epicycle, and the eccentric</margin>
Next, find the distance between the mean motion of the sun and the mean motion of the moon, and what remains will be the mean center of the moon. Enter the same table with this value and take what you find under the column titled "circle of egress" <note>original: *circulus egressus*; referring to the eccentric orbit</note>. Multiply this by the total parallax that you have just found, and divide the product by 60. The result will be the proportional part, which you add to the parallax last found. This will give the parallax equated for the hours and minutes of the position of the moon in the zodiac, the epicycle, and the **eccentric** <note>original: *eccentricus*; a circular orbit whose center is not the Earth</note>. Finally, divide the parallax now found by the **hourly excess** <note>original: *superatio*; the difference in speed between the Moon and the Sun in one hour</note> of the moon over the sun in one hour, and the result will be the hours of parallax. If the parallax is so small that it cannot be divided, multiply it by 60 and then divide it as before; the result will be the fractions immediately following the hours and minutes.

# To find the quality and duration of a lunar eclipse through tables.

**F**irst seek the true mean opposition <note>the Full Moon</note> to see if there is a possibility of an eclipse; if so, seek the true opposition. In exactly the same way as was said above regarding the conjunction <note>New Moon</note>, in [finding] the conjunctions find the distances of length between the sun and the moon. Note that if the distance of length is between the *nadir* <note>the point directly opposite</note> of the sun and the body of the moon—and it is said the work varies somewhat here—one must only repeat the points. Then seek the equations of days by iterating the tables; let half the time of the mean motion be taken because it is added so that the opposition of the moon and earth may come most truly, and the argument of latitude and the equation will arrive. Then seek the equations of days by iterating the tables for this purpose, namely with the degree of the sun, which equation you should reduce to fractions of hours; add this to the time of the true opposition, and the time of the said equated true opposition will arrive, and this is the time of the middle of the eclipse. 

Then, by the argument of latitude and the equation, enter the table of lunar eclipses at the "farther distance" <note>original: *longitudine longiore*; when the moon is at apogee, its farthest point from Earth</note> and take the "points of the eclipse" <note>original: *puncta eclypsis*; a measure of the eclipse's magnitude</note> and the half-diameter. Again, if necessary, take it by the same method above the window of the solar eclipse; take the "minutes of incidence" <note>original: *minuta casum*; the time/arc between the first contact and total obscuration</note> and the "minutes of half-delay" <note>original: *minuta dimidie more*; half the duration of totality</note> if there is a delay. If there are 100 of those which are titled "minutes of delay," then there is no delay. And it must be understood that "delay" is the name for the time from the beginning of total obscuration while the moon is within the shadow, and it is said to last until the beginning of the return of light. "Minutes of delay" are the space of the sky which the moon traverses and moves through from the beginning of the delay until the middle of the eclipse; these minutes are also called the space through which it moves from the beginning of the eclipse until the beginning of the delay. Therefore, when the points of the eclipse, the minutes of incidence, and the minutes of delay are situated at the farther distance, save them. 

If, however, the moon was not at the true apogee in the epicycle <note>a small circle moving along a larger one, used to explain planetary orbits</note>, enter by the same argument of latitude into the table of lunar eclipses at the "nearer distance" <note>original: *longitudine propinqua*; perigee, when the moon is closest to Earth</note> and take there the points of the eclipse, minutes of incidence, and minutes of delay by the same method of operating as you did for the farther distance, and save them. [Calculate] the distance made in the opposite... if it is in the epicycle. To put it briefly, if the moon is at the true apogee of the epicycle, the Earth and Sun are at the farther distance. If it is at the opposite of the apogee, enter at both distances as was just said. Then subtract the points of the eclipse found at the farther distance from the points found at the nearer distance, and the minutes of incidence from the minutes of incidence, and the minutes of delay from the minutes of delay, and save the differences each by themselves. 

Then, with the argument of the moon equated for the hour of true opposition, enter the table of proportions and it is increased by 30 degrees; take the "proportional minutes" <note>interpolation factors</note>. Therefore, find the double entry if necessary. Multiply those proportional minutes by each difference saved separately by 60, and a proportional part will arrive for each, which you should add to the points of the eclipse, minutes of incidence, and minutes of delay found at the farther distance, each to its own kind. If you add the proportional part of the difference of the points to the points, and the proportional part of the difference of the minutes of incidence to the minutes of incidence, and the proportional part of the difference of the minutes of delay to the minutes of delay, you will have everything equated according to the distance of the moon from the earth. Then divide the now-equated minutes of incidence by the [motion] of the moon in one hour; the result will be hours. If there is a remainder, multiply it by 60 and divide by the same as before, and they will be minutes of an hour. If there is a remainder again, multiply by 60 and divide by the same as before, and they will be seconds of an hour, and so on.

When this is done, you have the hours, minutes, and seconds which are from the beginning of the eclipse until the beginning of the delay <note>original: "mora"; refers to the period of totality where the moon is fully within the shadow</note>; and if there is a delay, divide the minutes of the hours by those that remain in the same way, then one hour and the hours, minutes, and seconds will result, such as 72 minutes for that delay which is from the beginning of the return until the middle of the eclipse. When this is done, subtract the hours which were from the beginning of the eclipse (whether until the middle or if there was a delay) from the time of the visible equated day of opposition, and the time of the beginning of the eclipse will remain. And if you add those same hours to the time of the visible opposition, the time of the end of the eclipse will result. 

But if the eclipse has a delay, then take the hours, minutes, and seconds which are from the beginning of the eclipse until the beginning of the delay, and add the hours, minutes, and seconds which are from the beginning of the delay until the middle through the eclipse; subtract the whole sum from the time of the visible opposition, and the time of the beginning of the eclipse will remain. If you add the same, the time of the end of the eclipse will result. Therefore, the time from the beginning of the eclipse and the delay until the middle of the eclipse will result; subtract this from the time of the true opposition and the beginning of the delay will remain; if you add it, the end of the delay will result. If you double it, then you will perceive that from the beginning of the eclipse until the middle, the whole duration of the eclipse from start to finish will result. If you double the time which is from the beginning of the delay until the middle of the eclipse, the whole delay <note>the total duration of totality</note> under the shadow will result.

Next, if you wish to know the hours and minutes from the beginning until the middle, multiply by the motion of the moon in one hour, and subtract the result from the true position of the moon at the time of the visible opposition and from the argument of latitude <note>the moon's distance from its orbital node</note>; the true position of the moon at the time of the beginning of the eclipse will result. Also subtract the "heads of the two fish" <note>a reference to the nodes, specifically the Dragon's Head and Tail</note> from the argument of latitude, and you will have the equated argument of latitude for the time of the beginning of the eclipse. If you add those things which you just subtracted, you will have the latitude at the time of the end of the eclipse. At these three times, you will find the latitude of the moon in the depth of the table [marked] $\sigma$ in that whole area of the argument of latitude, namely at the beginning, middle, and end of the eclipse.

-> Here end the canons <note>instructional rules</note> of the tables of the illustrious King Alfonso, formerly King of Castile, and also the canons of eclipses arranged by Master John of Saxony <note>a student of Lignères who helped popularize the Alphonsine Tables</note>; thanks be to God, amen <-

# Whether a planet is ascending or descending.
The equated confluence of the centers of a planet from 1 degree to 6 $\sigma$ signs will be descending in its eccentric <note>an orbital circle whose center is offset from the Earth</note>, and from 6 to 12 signs, it will be ascending. But if the equated argument of the planet is from 1 degree to 6 signs, it will be descending in its epicycle <note>a smaller circle carrying the planet, which itself moves along the larger eccentric circle</note>, and from 6 to 12 signs, it will be ascending. In that planet, because of the lessening of its curves, it is spoken of regarding their removal.

# Whether the latitude will be northern ascending.
If its argument is from 1 to 3 signs up to the 3rd sign, it is [ascending], and from such 10 to 12 it is descending; because from 6 to 9 it is southern descending, and from 9 to 12 it is ascending.

Subtract the mean motion of any of the three superior planets for one day from the motion of the sun on the same day, and you will have the motion of the argument in one day. For all the latitudes of the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> and Venus: enter the designated double-entry tables with their argument; that which is determined there should be written down separately as signs, and this will be the proper latitude. After this, take the <term>geuzahar</term> <note>from the Arabic *al-jawzahar*, meaning the node of a planet's orbit</note> <term>elaz</term> <note>a specific term related to the calculation of planetary nodes</note> of the equated planet; add to it the second argument of latitude which you find in the four-fold tables. Likewise, whatever you find there in the table of the planet, namely $\sigma$, then take the previously mentioned planet's separately saved value and the result will be the diminished latitude of the planet. If the argument is from 1 degree to 6 signs, it will be northern ascending; from 10 [signs] it is descending; from 12 to 9 it is southern descending; and from 9 to 12 it is ascending. We do the same with the equated argument of Venus and Mercury when entering the double-entry tables as mentioned. But we calculate their argument of latitude thus: we add the mean motion of the sun to the argument of the center, and from the sum we subtract the <term>geuzahar</term> <term>elaz</term>; that is, we add the mean motion of the <term>geuzahar</term> to the same so that the truth may be held.

<meta>This page continues the astronomical calculations from the previous page, shifting from the coordinates of the five classical planets to the specific geometric parameters of the Sun and Moon's orbits. Note that the distance of the Sun's <term>eccentric <note>In the Ptolemaic system, an eccentric is a circular path whose center is offset from the center of the Earth. This offset explained why the Sun appears to move at different speeds through the seasons.</note></term> from the center of the Earth is two and a half degrees, based on the degrees of the entire diameter of the eccentric divided into sixty parts.

Note that the distance of the Moon's eccentric from the center of the Earth is twelve degrees and twenty-eight minutes. These degrees and minutes result from the <term>semidiameter <note>The radius of the circle.</note></term> of the Moon's eccentric being divided into sixty parts, which are called degrees; the minutes result from the division of one degree into sixty parts, and so on.

Note that the motion of the Moon in its <term>epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent). This was used to account for the complex observed motions of the Moon.</note></term> is 13 degrees, 3 minutes, 53 seconds, and 56 <term>thirds <note>original: "tertia." In sexagesimal notation, a third is 1/60th of a second, representing an extremely high level of mathematical precision.</note></term> per day.

The diameter of the Moon's epicycle is 12 degrees and 30 minutes, measured in the degrees of the diameter of the Moon's eccentric.

But let it be well-disposed so that, by its <term>aspect <note>In astrology, an "aspect" is the geometric angle between two planets, which determines whether their influence is harmonious or challenging.</note></term>, it may be as it ought to be; on a journey by sea, take care. And let there be no concern that things will not go well, or even better, regarding these matters. Fortune itself is revealed by the aspect, combined with the experience of the stars, as it applies strength to the endeavor. It is as if the effort would lie dormant without it, or conversely, could cause harm or evil. These are certain paths. For crowning a king:

**W**hen choosing the hour for crowning a king, let it be an hour of a firm aspect, and it is better if it is an aspect of Venus; nor should <term>Fortune <note>original: "fortuna plena"; likely referring to the "Part of Fortune" or a benefic planet like Jupiter being in a strong position.</note></term> in its fullness look toward another planet, and let it already be in a superior position. Neither let the Moon be in a "humid place," but let it be rising above the <term>Lord of the Hour <note>The planet that rules the specific hour of the day according to the planetary hour system.</note></term> such as the Sun; if necessary, let it look by aspect toward those things which are to be done by divine aspect. Let the <term>Mansion of the Moon <note>The 28 divisions of the sky that the Moon passes through during its monthly orbit.</note></term> stand in the six signs that truly flourish. Let it not be in the house of Saturn or Mars. A Question:

**S**eek with diligence whether the hour was chosen by the Sun alone; look to the aspect as they are seen, like the Appian Way. But let it be with the given aspect of Venus, for the Moon finds its aspect as if it were being clothed equally, or because it opposes; nor should Fortune look away from us, nor the Lord of the <term>Triplicity <note>original: "d'm ph'i" (dominum triplicitatis); a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note></term> lose its faith. Therefore Alcherit, or the first mansion, Alcerath:

->The Moon’s First Mansion: Alcerath<-

**T**his is the first day of the month in a certain station, which is the "first horns" in Aries. One ought to choose hours that are good rather than merely faithful to their own nature. Regarding travel, one should move to ride at midday. As for sleeping, it brings no special vows to the sleeper; let him not flee the proper things of Venus. Let nothing be done here or there for his own people. But it is good for those buying clothes or helmets to find them, and other things where they may be. One does not graze on good roses from the number of eight for the others of the man. In war, do not accept <term>pledges <note>original: "spondeas"; promises or guarantees.</note></term> for planting trees, so that in weaving new cloths, they would still be there if they had sprouted, as if through growth and fortune. Mansion 1.

**T**he second is called Albothaim. The Indians say that in this mansion, men should dig wells and lead rivers. It is a time for trading and for leading wars through words. Also for buying servants. It is good for sea-life; those who were held captive and punished by the mallet will be liberated slowly. Mansion 2.

**T**he third is Athoraya <note>The Pleiades.</note>. The Indians say it is good for drinking medicine. For travel, it is moderately good. Sleeping is of no value here; in the lowest words, let our people rejoice through a vow; let him burn for his wife, for buying servants, for planting trees and drawing seeds, and for bringing out garments. But all things are for receiving works; he vows that as the mill had come by depriving. Mansion 3.

**T**he fourth is Aldebaran, called the "Great Eye of the Bull." The Indians in this mansion dig and place buildings so that they may be vast. When placed in the earth, you should sleep with no one for the leading of words. Good things can be purchased. He who is born then will be faithful. Good things are to be sought from the earth. A hard temptation must be overcome, and I shall even conquer, but on the contrary, the courses for regenerating children are seen here. Mansion 4.

**T**he fifth is Albeath <note>Al-Haqa, the "Face" or "White Spot."</note>, the "Countenance." The Indians say it is good for teaching children—unknown sons faithful to sons. And there is nothing for a journey of journeys; it is good for buying favors, nor should it be shaped in a human figure according to the stars for one born of evil. Behold, whatever I may take, he is seen in prison. Mansion 5.
